narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical guarantees rely on low-rank structure, incoherence, sufficient signal relative to noise, and randomized sampling; the main analysis focuses on balanced factor dimensions and ranks. The authors note that continuing tensor-based pruning too far may be unsafe if the reduced tensor no longer follows the low-rank model, and that the switch round must therefore be chosen with care. Their empirical evaluation is an offline semi-synthetic study rather than a live randomized field experiment.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence comes from one small three-factor bundle tensor built from popular items in three categories, with added Gaussian noise, so it does not establish performance for larger, sparser, or changing product spaces. The study does not report results from a live platform deployment, and the theoretical sampling guarantees depend on uniform randomization that may be difficult to maintain when traffic, eligibility, or operational constraints differ across combinations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose formally analyzing data-driven switching rules, such as switching when held-out tensor-prediction error stops improving. They also note that the design can use other low-rank tensor structures, including CP and Tensor-Train decompositions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method in a live experiment with nonuniform traffic, user segments, and operational restrictions on which combinations can be fielded. Further work could also test robustness to approximate or changing low-rank structure and develop sequential rules that adapt both the stage budgets and the final deployment decision.

narrate.summary: The paper extends Pyomo.DoE, a Python tool for model-based optimal design of experiments, to make information criteria based on matrix eigenvalues usable in equation-oriented optimization. The objective is to choose experimental conditions that improve parameter estimates and reduce uncertainty for nonlinear, first-principles models. The method constructs a Fisher information matrix from model sensitivities and measurement-error assumptions, then uses callbacks to evaluate design criteria and their derivatives during optimization. A new Experiment class also labels model inputs, outputs, measurement error, and unknown parameters so the same model can be used in estimation and design workflows. Three case studies show that different criteria select different experiments and that designs targeting weakly informed directions can substantially reduce estimated parameter uncertainty.
narrate.key_results: For the batch reaction model, the reported optimal sample times were 1.78 days for D-optimality, 1.33 days for A-optimality, 1.30 days for E-optimality, and 0.94 days for condition-number optimality. In the TCLab case, the E-optimal profile gave the best reported E score, 3.3834, and A score, -3.36, while the D-optimal profile gave the best D score, 20.28, and the condition-number-optimal profile gave the best condition-number score, 2.91; all scores are reported on a log10 scale. Adding the optimized TCLab experiment reduced uncertainty by 2 to 4 orders of magnitude, as reported in the paper. For the simulated membrane cascade, the E-optimal design selected feed flowrate 110, diafiltrate flowrate 27, and feed concentrations 2.0 and 20.0; its estimated uncertainty regions were reported to shrink by 4 to 6 orders of magnitude. The membrane design reduced uncertainty more than the paper’s comparison experiment at the middle of the flow ranges.

key_equations.name: Information matrix
key_equations.explanation: M is the information matrix for the proposed experiment, Q is the sensitivity matrix, Sigma-y is the measurement-error covariance matrix, the superscript T denotes transpose, the exponent minus one denotes matrix inverse, and M-prior is the prior information matrix.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors assume the information matrix is full rank; if it is singular, the listed criteria may be ill-posed. They note that the method depends on numerical eigenvalue and matrix-inverse routines, and that repeated eigenvalues can compromise the robustness of E-optimality. They also state that the criteria presented do not cover all possible design objectives and that the demonstrated optimization problems can have local optima.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The membrane case study uses synthetic experiments and model predictions rather than measurements from an operating membrane system, so the proposed conditions have not been validated against physical process data in this paper. The design calculations also rely on assumed measurement-error distributions and values, prior parameter estimates, and a local information approximation; performance could differ if these inputs or the model are inaccurate.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring a small random diagonal adjustment to address repeated eigenvalues, adding more design criteria through the callback framework, and replacing finite-difference sensitivities with analytical sensitivities obtained by symbolic differentiation. They also identify further opportunities to apply the framework to complex, many-component mixtures and other emerging applications.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the membrane recommendations in physical experiments and compare observed parameter uncertainty with the predicted reduction. Further work could also incorporate practical operating limits, costs, and experiment replication into the design, then assess whether sequential redesign remains effective as new data update the parameter estimates.

narrate.summary: This paper develops two surrogates for the expected information gain (EIG) in experimental design for controlled dynamical systems described by ordinary differential equations (ODEs). The objective is to select observation times, sensors, and system controls to improve parameter estimation while retaining a form that can be optimized using adjoint-based optimal control. Both surrogates begin with an exact decomposition of information gain across observation times; one uses the prior at every stage, while the other tilts the prior using accumulated Fisher information. The authors show that the tilting surrogate is exact for linear systems with Gaussian prior and observation noise, while the prior-based surrogate can count redundant observations more than once. Simulated examples show that both approaches can perform competitively, with clearer advantages over local Fisher-based designs for multimodal prior uncertainty.
narrate.key_results: In the harmonic oscillator with balanced sensors, the estimated full-sequence EIG was 3.5170 for the instantaneous-surrogate design and 3.4473 for the tilting design, compared with 3.0671 for the A-optimal and local linearized designs. With uneven sensor observability, the instantaneous design's estimated EIG was 2.0250, while the tilting design achieved 3.2529 and the A-optimal design achieved 2.8834; the instantaneous design also concentrated measurements on one sensor. For the Lotka–Volterra examples, the best estimated EIG was 2.8432 for the instantaneous design under the log-normal prior and 1.9087 for the instantaneous design under the mixture prior; in both cases these exceeded the reported A-optimal and local linearized values. narrate.summary: The paper develops a distribution-based method for Bayesian optimal experimental design, with the goal of choosing batches that maximize expected information gain. Instead of optimizing one batch directly, it optimizes a probability distribution over batches, regularized by divergence from a reference distribution. The authors also construct mean-field and independent-and-identically-distributed approximations and use Wasserstein gradient flows and particle algorithms to optimize them. The approach is tested on simulated multimodal design problems and pharmaceutical sampling-time benchmarks. The main finding is that the particle methods can be more robust to poor initialization than pointwise optimization, while structured approximations can be more effective than optimizing the full batch distribution in some tested settings.
narrate.key_results: In the torus experiment, batch sizes ranged from 2 to 1,000, and the distribution-based methods outperformed gradient ascent under local initialization; the repulsive independent-and-identically-distributed method performed best overall in that experiment. In the pharmacokinetic benchmark with 15 sampling times, the mean-field and independent-and-identically-distributed particle methods attained the highest or near-highest expected information gain among the methods compared, including coordinate-exchange methods, stochastic gradient ascent, and annealed sequential Monte Carlo. In the FitzHugh–Nagumo benchmark with 21 sampling times, the mean-field methods had the highest median expected information gain and relatively low variability across seeds; the independent-and-identically-distributed methods did not match them. For the pharmaceutical and FitzHugh–Nagumo comparisons, the authors tuned methods to a common wall-clock budget of 7 seconds; their algorithm uses tuple subsampling to avoid enumerating all particle combinations when estimating interaction gradients. The paper reports numerical plots and qualitative comparisons but does not give exact tabulated expected-information-gain values for these comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a factorization that explains how average coefficient variance and determinant-based precision relate for linear experimental designs. It applies the derivation mainly to coded main-effects screening models, with and without two-factor interactions, and also shows how to extend the result to prediction by whitening the information matrix. The construction separates covariance shape into coefficient-variance balance and a determinant-based component for correlations among estimates. The author evaluates the factorization using five published screening comparisons, an exact seven-run family tied on the determinant criterion, and a response-surface example. The findings show that a design can have better average coefficient precision despite a lower determinant-based value when its covariance shape is more spherical.
narrate.key_results: In all five published screening comparisons, the average-variance-optimal design had a larger correlation component and a slightly smaller variance-balance component; its determinant-based value was lower in three comparisons. In the 12-run example, the average-variance design’s determinant-based value was about 2.6% lower, its variance-balance component about 0.8% lower, and its correlation component 18.6% higher, yielding an average-variance value 14.5% higher. In the seven-run family, all designs had the same determinant-based score of 90.71, while the center design’s average-variance score was 85.71, compared with 76.19 at a same-sign corner. In the 26-run full-quadratic prediction example, the I-optimal design had about 35.4% lower average prediction variance than the D-optimal design.

narrate.summary: This paper develops adaptive experimental designs for combinatorial multi-armed bandit (CMAB) problems, where each decision selects a group of basic actions. Its objective is to balance low cumulative regret against accurate estimation of differences in reward between groups or between basic actions. The authors propose MixCombKL for settings that reveal only a group's total reward, and MixCombUCB for settings that reveal each selected action's reward. Both methods mix reward-seeking decisions with exploration, with the exploration rate controlling the trade-off. The paper proves that both methods are Pareto optimal under stated conditions and finds that richer, action-level feedback improves estimation accuracy while preserving regret of the same order.
narrate.key_results: The theory establishes Pareto optimality for MixCombKL and MixCombUCB when the exploration parameter alpha is between 0 and one-half; MixCombUCB also has this guarantee up to alpha equal to 1 when the authors' large-gap condition holds. For the reported problem classes, both feedback settings have regret bounds of order m times the time horizon to the power one minus alpha, up to logarithmic factors; the paper's table reports lower estimation-error rates with semi-bandit than full-bandit feedback for both group rewards and basic actions. The simulations used 20 independent trials: the full-bandit case had 8 basic actions, groups of size 3, 56 groups, and 5,000 rounds, while the semi-bandit case had 9 basic actions, maximum group size 4, 126 groups, and 2,000 rounds. Across the plotted exploration settings, more exploration generally reduced regret and increased estimation error, illustrating the trade-off rather than establishing superiority over other algorithms in simulation.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how competing sellers’ repeated price experiments and demand learning affect the prices they reach over time. It analyzes linear demand learning, in which sellers perturb a current price, fit a local linear demand model to their own demand and the rival prices they observe, and partially update their price toward the fitted revenue-maximizing target. When a seller cannot observe some rivals, correlated experiments can bias the fitted demand model because omitted rival price changes are associated with observed price changes. Under stated demand and stability conditions, this bias makes prices converge to a conjectural variations equilibrium, with conjectures determined by the feedback and experimentation structures. When the bias is absent, including under full price feedback or suitable independent experimentation, the limiting equilibrium is the standard Nash equilibrium.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove convergence in expectation to the equilibrium selected by the induced conjectures under their stated assumptions; with an interior limit, this is a conjectural variations equilibrium. Their finite-sample result gives mean squared price error of order O(T^-1/2) up to logarithmic factors for a fixed market, the same order as the cited result for related Nash-convergence games with bandit feedback. The theory covers linear demand and multinomial logit demand; for the Nash case with equal price sensitivities in the latter model, a sufficient stability condition is that every seller’s market share remains below 3/5. Full price feedback or zero limiting covariance between omitted and observed experimental variation yields zero conjectures and the Nash benchmark, while partial feedback and correlated experiments can produce positive or negative conjectures. The paper is theoretical and does not report empirical comparisons or rank alternative experimental designs by an optimality criterion.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) for choosing multiple sensor locations over a continuous domain in linear inverse problems. It focuses on A-optimality, which reduces uncertainty by minimizing the posterior covariance trace. The authors relax the batch search over locations to an optimization over positive measures of fixed mass and show that this corresponds to a Gaussian-process observation model indexed by a function space. They derive the expected utility and its gradients, then optimize it using a particle-based Wasserstein gradient flow. Numerical examples show convergence toward useful sensor configurations, while added variance and repulsion penalties help produce concentrated and separated sensor ensembles.
narrate.key_results: The expected utility is proved concave in the design measure, and the paper derives its posterior covariance and first variation. In the one-dimensional Poisson example, a batch of 2 sensors was optimized using 120 particles over 500 steps; the found configuration was approximately (0.1614, 0.8386), close to the reported true optimum (0.1616, 0.8384). In the two-dimensional time-harmonic Schrödinger example, the method used 100 particles for a batch of 4 over 120 steps and found four sensor locations; the paper does not report a numerical comparison against other design methods. In a regularization example with batch size 8, the authors report that a repulsion weight chosen too small allowed the particle ensembles to collapse to only six locations rather than eight.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that stationary points of the Wasserstein flow need not be maximizers and that the maximizing measure is not necessarily unique. They also state that effective regularization weights depend on the model, discretization, number of design variables, time step, and repulsion-kernel settings.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method relies on a linear observation model, a Gaussian prior, and Gaussian noise, so the reported conclusions may not carry over directly to nonlinear or non-Gaussian experiments. Evaluation is limited to two simulated inverse-problem examples, without comparisons against alternative optimization methods or validation in physical experiments; regularization weights and numerical settings also require problem-specific tuning.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying convergence properties in greater generality, extending the method to other optimality criteria, and applying it to high-dimensional inverse problems in large-scale scientific and engineering systems.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the approach with non-Gaussian priors, nonlinear observation models, and practical constraints such as forbidden regions or specified minimum sensor spacing. Comparisons with established design algorithms, sequential design extensions, and validation using real experimental data would clarify its practical value.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a faster way to generate treatment assignments for rerandomized experiments, where an assignment is retained only if measured covariates meet a prespecified balance threshold. It targets fixed-size treatment and control groups and uses the Mahalanobis distance to assess balance, with treatment effects estimated from the resulting randomized experiment. The method proposes pair-swaps through a Metropolis-Hastings chain, whose stationary distribution favors balanced assignments, and corrects that sampling bias through a second acceptance step. Its practical version, Pair-Switching Rejection Sampling Rerandomization (PSRSRR), checks candidates during the chain and stops when one passes both checks. The authors report much faster assignment generation than classical rerandomization, with estimation and inference results broadly comparable to or better than the tested alternatives.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with a covariate-outcome relationship setting of 0.5, the proposed method's relative mean squared error was 33%–61% of that under complete randomization, and its relative interval length was 58%–74%. For generating 100 assignments, it was a median of 4 times faster than the Gram-Schmidt walk method and more than 1,800 times faster than classical rerandomization. In the Student Achievement and Retention Project data, generating 10,000 assignments took 2.95 seconds or 3.63 seconds under the two proposed threshold-selection strategies, compared with 193.65 seconds for classical rerandomization. The authors report that coverage and Type I error were generally satisfactory in simulations, and the proposed method produced balance and variance reduction in applications to the Student Achievement and Retention Project and the reserpine data.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal non-asymptotic guarantee that the practical algorithm, which checks every step with no explicit burn-in, produces a uniform assignment. They hypothesize that its waiting time before acceptance acts as an implicit burn-in, and leave a rigorous characterization of that behavior for future work. They also note that the theoretically justified procedure that runs a full chain for each candidate can be computationally slow.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The practical algorithm's near-uniformity depends on the chain mixing sufficiently before its early stopping event, but the paper does not provide a general diagnostic or finite-run bound for deciding that this has occurred. Its main comparisons focus on fixed treatment-control allocation and selected covariate-balance criteria, so performance under operational constraints such as blocked allocation, limited treatment capacity, or nonstandard assignment rules is not established. The real-data applications evaluate generated assignment balance rather than validate treatment-effect performance against outcomes from new experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring more advanced Markov chain Monte Carlo kernels, including adaptive tempering and hybrid proposals, to improve mixing and exploration. They also propose extending the framework to factorial, clustered, stratified, and sequential experiments, and combining it with hardware-accelerated rerandomization tools.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could develop practical mixing diagnostics and run-length guidance that quantify the error of the early-stopping sampler for the thresholds and assignment sizes used by practitioners. It could also test the method in prospective experiments with real allocation constraints and provide an independently reproducible implementation and validation workflow.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a sequential data-collection method for predict-then-optimize problems in which predictions become cost coefficients in a downstream linear optimization problem. Its objective is to reduce decision loss, rather than merely improve prediction accuracy. The proposed method measures disagreement between predictions after normalizing them, then samples designs in proportion to this directional uncertainty and removes models with poor observed decision loss. The authors prove risk and stopping-time guarantees under stated geometric and optimality-gap conditions. Their theoretical and experimental results indicate that the method can identify decision-effective models earlier than prediction-focused alternatives.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that, under a directional-margin condition, excess decision risk decreases at a rate proportional to the inverse square root of the number of runs, up to logarithmic factors; the corresponding sample complexity is of order the inverse square of the target tolerance, up to logarithmic factors. Under an additional positive optimality-gap assumption, the proposed method eliminates suboptimal models after a finite number of runs with high probability, whereas a decision-blind benchmark can retain a suboptimal model with probability bounded away from zero. In the cardiovascular classification study, which used 100 trials and tested cost ratios from 1 to 15, the reported percentage increase in decision risk at cost ratio 3 was 0.29% for directional uncertainty with decision-loss training, compared with 10.45% for Euclidean uncertainty with squared-error training. In the language-model allocation study, also run for 100 trials, the proposed method had lower test decision loss than the benchmarks; the study used 50 texts and a test set comprising 20% of the data.

narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical risk guarantee depends on a directional-margin condition, and the stronger result on earlier elimination of suboptimal models also requires a positive optimality gap. The paper focuses on linear downstream optimization and primarily analyzes finite candidate model classes, while noting that the analysis can be extended using a complexity measure for infinite classes.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The design is presented for a finite pool of candidate inputs and a maintained set of candidate models, so the paper does not establish how the method scales when either set is very large. The empirical evidence is limited to one public cardiovascular dataset and one small language-model allocation study using 50 texts; it does not validate performance in prospective clinical experiments or across a broad range of engineering applications. The experiments also do not report computational-time comparisons, despite the method's stated computational advantage.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors say that directional uncertainty offers insights for future studies of uncertainty in predict-then-optimize problems. They do not identify a specific follow-on method or application.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method with larger candidate pools and model classes, and measure computation as well as the number and cost of experiments. It could also study constraints on which experiments may be run, sequential updating when labels arrive with delay, and prospective validation in real clinical or industrial settings.

narrate.summary: The paper designs sequential A/B tests in which treatment and control policies are assigned over time and outcomes may carry over to later periods. Its objective is to minimize the mean squared error of the estimated average treatment effect. The proposed method uses a transformer to represent the full observed history and reinforcement learning to learn treatment assignments in a simulation environment, rewarding allocations that bring the estimate closer to a Monte Carlo reference. The authors also prove that, for a class of doubly robust estimators, an optimal allocation can require the full history. In synthetic, ridesharing-data-based, and dispatch-simulator evaluations, the proposed method generally achieved lower estimation error than the tested alternative designs.
narrate.key_results: The paper reports results from 400 simulation replications in its main comparisons. In the synthetic setting with 30 days, the reported mean squared error was 27 × 10⁻⁴ for the proposed method, compared with 36 × 10⁻⁴ for the daily treatment design and 37 × 10⁻⁴ for its related design. In the real-data-based simulator with 35 days, 12 intervals per day, and a 5% policy improvement, the 7-day warm-up version had a mean squared error of 37.9 × 10⁻⁴, compared with 46.5 × 10⁻⁴ for the best listed alternative. In the public dispatch simulator with 35 days, the plotted mean squared error was 49 × 10⁻² for the proposed design versus 53 × 10⁻² for each of the two closest alternatives; training took a little over 3 hours in the reported smallest synthetic configuration, while generating a design after training typically took less than one minute.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method uses a simulation environment that approximates the data-generating process; when no simulator is available, the authors propose building and updating one from sequentially collected experimental data. They report that training can be time-consuming, taking more than 45 hours for the longest tested synthetic horizon, and state that data-use agreements prevent public release of some real-world data.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence is based primarily on simulators, including one fitted to a ridesharing dataset, rather than a prospective randomized field experiment using the learned allocation. The method’s performance therefore depends on whether a simulator and its Monte Carlo reference capture the actual policy effects and temporal dependencies; the robustness experiments examine only selected, moderate forms of misspecification.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework beyond time-series experiments to settings with multiple experimental units, where spillover effects between units may occur.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the learned allocation prospectively in operational A/B tests and compare estimated effects with the simulator-based predictions. Further work could also develop explicit safeguards for operational constraints and uncertainty about the simulator, and report statistical inference guarantees for estimates produced under the adaptive design.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an adaptive experimental design approach to find process settings that produce successful prints of the GRCop-42 copper alloy. The authors apply it to directed energy deposition, a metal additive manufacturing process, and focus on finding feasible settings at lower laser powers. The approach learns from prior success or failure results using a probabilistic classifier, then selects experiments by combining estimated feasibility with the value of further exploration. Domain knowledge is used to constrain parameter ranges and remove physically infeasible candidates. In laboratory deployment, the approach found successful configurations at four laser power settings, including 500 watts.
narrate.key_results: The authors report testing laser powers of 950, 700, 600, and 500 watts, with an experimental budget of 10 at each setting. The number of feasible configurations discovered was 1, 1, 3, and 1, respectively, and each setting yielded at least one feasible configuration within the reported budget. The parameter space at each setting contained over 100 million configurations; the table reports an explored fraction of 10 × 10⁻⁸. By comparison, collaborators tried 37 configurations over several months without finding a feasible one. The paper reports completing the adaptive-design deployment within three months.

narrate.summary: The paper designs randomized treatment assignments for estimating the global average treatment effect (GATE) when outcomes may be affected by network interference, homophily, and heterogeneous variation. It studies the Horvitz–Thompson estimator and seeks designs with low worst-case mean squared error (MSE) over a specified class of potential outcomes. The design criterion combines graph-based penalties for interference and homophily with a matrix-norm penalty for robustness. The authors construct assignments in two ways: by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying Gaussian rounding, or by adapting the Gram-Schmidt Walk (GSW). They give theoretical guarantees and report simulations on synthetic networks and a real village network, with the designs performing better in worst-case comparisons over a range of conditions.
narrate.key_results: For symmetric assignment, the paper derives a worst-case MSE upper bound with a factor of 28 divided by the square of the number of units; its terms penalize assignment covariance associated with the all-ones vector, the Laplacian pseudoinverse, heterogeneous variation, and the graph Laplacian. The SDP followed by Gaussian rounding has a theoretical approximation guarantee relative to the best achievable design covariance, subject to a non-degeneracy condition on the SDP solution. The adapted GSW method has a direct worst-case error bound, but the authors note that its bounds can grow with the number of units and may be loose for larger problems. In simulations and the village-network analysis, the authors report that their designs can outperform unit-level and cluster-level randomization in worst-case MSE across broad ranges of interference and heterogeneous variation; the paper does not give a single numerical improvement or run-size figure for these comparisons.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method requires bounds on homophily, interference, and heterogeneous variation, which the authors say may need to be informed by domain expertise or historical data. The SDP can become computationally burdensome on large graphs, and the authors identify faster, structure-exploiting algorithms as outside the paper’s scope. Their main treatment focuses on the vanilla Horvitz–Thompson estimator for GATE estimation, while broader estimators and estimands are left for future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The design’s worst-case guarantees depend on the chosen outcome-model class and trade-off bounds, so inaccurate assumptions or parameter estimates may produce a design that is poorly matched to the experiment. The empirical comparisons described in the paper do not establish performance across a wide range of operational constraints or real-world experiments, and the paper reports no single numerical gain or run-size summary for the comparisons.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to online experiments in which treatments are assigned sequentially and the trade-off parameters are learned adaptively. They also suggest developing algorithms that exploit graph structure to accelerate the SDP for large networks, and extending the framework to more general estimators and estimands.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess how the designs perform when treatment capacity, implementation groups, or other practical assignment restrictions must be met. Validation on additional operational datasets, including sensitivity analyses for misspecified network structure and trade-off parameters, would help establish how reliably the theoretical worst-case advantages transfer to practice.

narrate.summary: This paper compares Kullback–Leibler divergence and Wasserstein distances as criteria for Bayesian experimental design. The goal is to select measurement locations that improve estimates of an unknown contaminant-source location, both when the forward model is accurate and when it has model discrepancy. The authors construct a sequential design procedure that alternates physical-parameter inference with model-error correction, using automatic differentiable ensemble Kalman inversion for high-dimensional error parameters. They also calculate Wasserstein utility using an entropically regularized discrete optimal-transport method and demonstrate a location-related false reward that can occur with a uniform prior. In the simulated examples, Kullback–Leibler divergence generally updates beliefs faster when the model is accurate, while Wasserstein-based designs are more robust when model discrepancy is present.
narrate.key_results: In the source-inversion comparisons without model discrepancy, the actual-utility and expected-utility studies used six sequential stages; Kullback–Leibler-based designs generally reduced uncertainty faster, and in the main expected-utility case the Wasserstein-based designs needed one additional measurement to reach the same uncertainty level. This was not universal: an appendix case with the source near the Wasserstein-selected design found lower uncertainty from Wasserstein in the first stage and across later updates. With model discrepancy, the expected Wasserstein design covered the true source by stage 3, while the expected Kullback–Leibler design did so by stage 4, and the Wasserstein approach corrected the source-strength error faster in the reported case. In the additional acoustic example with model discrepancy, Wasserstein-based criteria located the true source in two stages, one stage earlier than the Kullback–Leibler criterion; the paper reports no general runtime comparison or single numerical efficiency measure.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The main numerical comparisons use simulated source-inversion problems, a small set of parameter settings, and six-stage sequences, so they do not establish how the criteria perform across real environmental monitoring systems or larger experiments. The main discrepancy example is parametric, and the comparisons do not benchmark total computation time or experimental cost against alternative robust-design methods.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing formal convergence criteria and denoising or regularization strategies for the alternating model-correction procedure. They also identify comparison of long-term or accumulated reward under the greedy sequential strategy as future work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the competing criteria in real monitoring campaigns, including practical limits on sensor locations, measurement budgets, and model calibration. Further comparisons could test alternative design objectives and discrepancy models, and examine whether the methods can be used sequentially with stopping rules and reported computational costs.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Implicit Bayesian Markov Decision Process (IBMDP), a method for planning which drug-discovery assays to run when there is no simulator or record of past sequential decisions. It is designed to reduce assay resource use while reducing uncertainty about a target property and keeping the candidate’s estimated likelihood of success above a chosen threshold. The method compares the candidate’s known predictions and assay results with historical compound profiles, samples likely outcomes from similar cases, and updates those weights as new results are considered. It uses an ensemble of Monte Carlo tree search planners and combines their recommendations by majority vote. In a central nervous system drug-discovery case study it found lower-cost plans than a rule-based approach, and in synthetic tests its recommendations matched a known optimal policy more often than a deterministic planner using the same similarity model.
narrate.key_results: For four representative brain-penetration cases, the rule-based approach was described as costing USD 5,200 for a full assay panel, while IBMDP plans cost USD 400 to USD 800 and achieved the same or higher decision confidence, with up to 92 percent lower resource consumption. In the opportunity-discovery case, IBMDP recommended a USD 800 plan for a compound the heuristic would have discarded; the other cases had plans costing USD 400 or USD 400 to USD 800. Across 100 synthetic trials, IBMDP’s most frequent first action matched the theoretical optimum in 47 percent of trials, compared with 36 percent for deterministic value iteration using the similarity-based estimates; the optimum appeared in IBMDP’s top two recommendations in 66 percent. A single-compound policy took approximately one hour to generate in the reported setup, which used 50 ensemble runs and 20,000 search iterations per run.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that results depend on the coverage and representativeness of historical data, and that similarity-based sampling cannot discover strategies absent from that data. They note that the normalized Euclidean-distance kernel may not capture nonlinear or threshold biology, that computation can become burdensome as the data or feature set grows, and that performance is sensitive to hyperparameter choices.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-world case study reports plans for four representative compounds, rather than prospective execution and evaluation of the recommended assay sequences on new candidates. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify empirical validation of alternative similarity kernels, including kernels that can better handle heavy-tailed outcomes or outliers, as an important future direction. They also note that domain-tailored similarity metrics may be needed to represent structure–activity relationships more appropriately.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective validation across a larger set of compounds and assay programs, tracking actual spend, turnaround time, and decision outcomes against existing practice. Further work could also test how the method handles missing or censored assay results and practical constraints such as assay availability, scheduling, and fixed budgets.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces a method for selecting informative preference queries to personalize generative models. It models prompt construction and other generation processes as a Markov decision process, with a user's reward represented by a linear function of known features. The method chooses several exploration policies by optimizing an approximation to the information in preference feedback over state visitation measures, using a convex optimization procedure for the fixed-vocabulary case. The authors also present a vocabulary-free extension that optimizes language-model prompt generators with REINFORCE. In the reported studies, the method generally improves preference learning over random query selection, although results vary by style and the main preference evaluation uses a simulated user.
narrate.key_results: In the language-model-simulated study, using 50 training episodes, the method achieved 60.4% average held-out preference accuracy across 10 styles, compared with 51.1% for random exploration; the paper reports a 9.4 percentage-point difference, while random guessing was 25%. The advantage was not universal: at the same setting, the method did worse than random exploration for the forest and landscape styles, and was slightly lower for noir. In the vocabulary-free experiment, optimized policies had between-policy embedding similarity of 0.140 ± 0.006, compared with 0.185 ± 0.012 for the unoptimized baseline, which the paper describes as 24% lower similarity. For a vocabulary of approximately 5,000 tokens, the one-time design optimization took around 10 minutes on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors describe the study as a proof of concept and say that the effect of bias in the queries and collected data requires further investigation before deployment. Their primary preference evaluation uses language-model-simulated feedback rather than human participants. They also note that the static version does not update policies using feedback from earlier queries, and that the vocabulary-free REINFORCE extension has a non-convex optimization landscape.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The information design relies on a linear preference model and, for its tractable fixed-vocabulary objective, approximates choice probabilities as uniform; performance may be weaker when real users have sharply unequal choice probabilities or preferences that are not well represented by the chosen features. The main quantitative preference study uses one simulated feedback model and a limited set of styles, while the preliminary human evidence is qualitative, so the reported gains do not establish effectiveness across real users or applications. The fixed-vocabulary design also depends on the selected token categories and embedding representation, which may restrict the kinds of prompts it can discover.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose an adaptive version that uses earlier preference feedback to update the estimated choice probabilities and re-optimize policies. They also say that bias should be investigated before deployment and describe the evaluation protocol as transferable to future studies with human participants.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be a larger, controlled study with real users across varied tasks, measuring both preference-model accuracy and the number and burden of queries required. narrate.summary: The paper presents hdrm, an R package for testing hypotheses about mean vectors in high-dimensional repeated-measures and split-plot designs. It covers one-group and multiple-group settings, including settings with either equal or unequal covariance matrices across groups. The tests assume multivariate normal observations and use quadratic-form statistics, with critical values based on a Pearson approximation. The package estimates required quantities from the data and uses subsampling and smaller equivalent hypothesis matrices to reduce computation. The authors illustrate the software with a real medical dataset and report tests for measurement-location and diagnostic-group effects.
narrate.key_results: The real dataset included 160 patients, measurements in 40 dimensions, and group sizes that were smaller than the dimension. In the one-group example, 30 women with mild cognitive impairment were tested for a measurement-location effect; the reported test statistic was 18.4195, the estimated degrees of freedom were 1, and the p-value was below 0.0001. In the four-group comparison of 101 women, the unequal-covariance analysis reported a test statistic of 0.5851 and a p-value of 0.2199; assuming equal covariances gave 0.4095 and 0.2451, respectively. The paper gives theoretical asymptotic validity results and describes subsampling and reduced hypothesis matrices as ways to limit computation, but it does not report a numerical runtime or a comparative benchmark.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that estimating higher-order trace quantities can require many summations and substantial computation, particularly for large dimensions and group sizes, although subsampling and alternative hypothesis matrices can reduce this burden. narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess test calibration and power under departures from multivariate normality and across a wider range of covariance structures. A systematic runtime and accuracy study of subsampling choices and reduced hypothesis matrices, followed by validation in additional real experiments, would help guide practical use.

narrate.summary: The paper designs an adaptive experiment for choosing the better of two treatments, with the objective of minimizing expected regret. Its proposed two-stage Neyman allocation (TSNA) first assigns treatments uniformly so their outcome variability can be estimated, then allocates the remaining rounds in proportion to the estimated standard deviations. At the end, it recommends the treatment with the higher observed sample mean. The analysis covers worst-case and prior-averaged performance for specified exponential-family outcome models. The paper shows that this design asymptotically attains both minimax and Bayes lower bounds.
narrate.key_results: For worst-case performance, the paper gives a bound on regret multiplied by the square root of the sample budget: the bound is the sum of the two maximum standard deviations multiplied by the standard normal cumulative probability at negative one. The authors show that this upper bound matches their minimax lower bound. For Bayes performance, the corresponding bound is one quarter of the prior-weighted sum of the squared sums of the treatment standard deviations, weighted by conditional prior densities; it matches the derived Bayes lower bound as the first-stage fraction tends to zero. These are asymptotic theoretical results, not empirical comparisons.

key_equations.name: Expected regret

The design and results concern two treatments and do not report validation using simulated or real experimental data.
narrate.future_work_stated: The paper identifies applying sequential estimation of the ideal allocation ratio to treatment choice as an important direction for future work, noting that such methods have improved finite-sample performance in average treatment effect estimation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Finite-sample comparisons of the proposed fixed two-stage design with sequential allocation rules would help establish its practical performance across run sizes. narrate.summary: This review surveys design-based causal inference for randomized experiments, primarily using a finite-population perspective. Its objective is to estimate and test causal effects using the known randomization mechanism while relying less on outcome-model assumptions. It describes designs that balance covariates, including stratification and rerandomization, along with randomization tests, large-sample inference, and regression adjustment. It also reviews extensions for high-dimensional covariates, noncompliance, network interference, and effects that persist over time. The review finds that the field has developed a broad set of theoretically grounded methods, while practical challenges remain for complex experiments and interference.
narrate.key_results: The review covers design and analysis methods rather than presenting a new experiment or a single comparative evaluation. It reports that nearly 70 percent of 224 randomized trials published in major medical journals in 2014 used stratified randomization. For pair-switching rerandomization, the cited theory establishes unbiasedness when treatment and control groups are equal in size and describes a variance-reduction guarantee that depends on covariate predictive strength and the acceptance threshold. The review also reports that one network partitioning approach covered about 35.59 percent of network edges, illustrating that grouping alone may leave substantial interference unresolved.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that Fisher randomization tests rely on a sharp null hypothesis and that enumerating all treatment assignments becomes computationally impractical for large experiments. They also describe limitations of network methods: some depend on correctly specified exposure mappings or sparse networks, while conditional randomization tests can lose power by excluding individuals or assignments.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper does not report a systematic search or selection protocol for the research it reviews, so readers cannot assess how comprehensively the literature was identified. It also provides no common empirical benchmark across the many methods, and the practical computational demands and implementation details are not compared consistently.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose research on more complex experiments, design-based conformal inference, and stronger integration of causal machine learning with design-based methods. They also call for methods addressing missingness, noncompliance, censoring, ethical constraints, disruptions, and spatiotemporal interference, as well as approaches for combining evidence across trials and data sources and improving extrapolation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be reproducible software and a shared simulation benchmark comparing the reviewed methods under realistic sample sizes, covariate structures, and assignment constraints. Researchers could also validate these methods in real experiments and report how design choices affect implementation burden, computation time, and the resulting uncertainty.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for choosing sensor locations to improve parameter estimation in distributed systems described by partial differential equations. It is designed for physics-informed neural networks, which estimate unknown parameters while representing the governing equations. A sensitivity network takes both the system coordinates and parameter values as inputs, calculates sensitivities using automatic differentiation, and uses them to select locations with a D-optimality criterion. A separate network then estimates parameters from simulated measurements at the selected locations. In two reaction, diffusion, and advection examples, the selected locations generally produced more accurate estimates than intuitive sensor placements.
narrate.key_results: For the one-dimensional steady-state example, a sensor at the selected location produced a Péclet number estimate with 0.20% relative error, compared with 84.7% for a sensor at the outlet. For the two-dimensional transient example with noiseless data and three sensors, the selected locations gave relative errors of 1.67% for the Péclet number and 2.32% for the Damköhler number; intuitive locations gave errors of 7.58% and 8.05%. With five sensors, selected-location errors were 0.17% and 1.00%, compared with 5.50% and 5.82% for intuitive locations. In noisy-data tests repeated five times, the three-sensor selected design estimated the Péclet number as 12.01 ± 0.26 and the Damköhler number as 21.97 ± 0.75, against true values of 12.0 and 22.0; the intuitive design estimates were 11.18 ± 0.60 and 19.59 ± 1.94.

key_equations.name: Parameter sensitivity
key_equations.explanation: The sensitivity s is the derivative of the system state u at spatial coordinate x and time t with respect to parameter lambda indexed by j.

key_equations.name: Information matrix
key_equations.explanation: The information matrix F for sensor locations x one through x N is the time integral from zero to observation horizon T of the sensitivity vector M multiplied by its transpose; M collects sensitivities at the sensor locations.

key_equations.name: D-optimal sensor selection
key_equations.explanation: The selected sensor locations x one star through x N star maximize the determinant of information matrix F over candidate locations, where N is the number of sensors.

key_equations.name: Steady-state sensor selection
key_equations.explanation: For the steady-state case, the selected locations maximize the trace of information matrix F over candidate locations, where N is the number of sensors.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that sensitivity-network training is computationally intensive, taking approximately 270 minutes in the two-dimensional example. The method uses prior parameter estimates and assumes that sensitivity-maximizing locations remain qualitatively similar at the prior and true parameter values; they propose an iterative procedure when those locations differ substantially.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses two illustrative simulation cases and virtual measurements rather than measurements from physical experiments, so the reported advantages are not validated under real sensor behavior or process variation. The placement comparisons also do not appear to impose practical constraints such as sensor accessibility, installation cost, or restricted locations, and the reported alternatives are limited to the intuitive arrangements used in the examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the framework to more complex systems with multiple unknown parameters or partially defined models, including unknown reaction kinetics. They also describe transfer learning as a way to adapt the models to changes in boundary or initial conditions, geometry, or physics without restarting training.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on physical experiments and assess whether the selected locations remain effective under realistic sensor errors, process variation, and model mismatch. It could also incorporate installation and access constraints into placement optimization and compare alternative design criteria or sequential sensor placement strategies.

narrate.summary: This paper develops concatenated orthogonal minimally aliased response surface (cOMARS) designs for screening quantitative factors at three levels while also allowing estimation of second-order effects. Each design is built by stacking two definitive screening designs (DSDs), with optional center runs, and the authors adapt a column-change and variable neighborhood search (CC/VNS) algorithm to reduce aliasing among second-order effects. The method is intended for cases where existing enumeration methods cannot practically produce designs for many factors. The authors provide designs for seven to 20 factors and compare them with existing designs and with non-orthogonal designs in simulations. They find that the new designs are competitive in the comparisons, with advantages that depend on the number of factors and the effects of interest.
narrate.key_results: The authors construct cOMARS designs for seven to 20 factors, with run sizes from 33 to 81 in the catalog. For nine- to 12-factor designs, the reported D-efficiency for estimating the intercept, all linear effects, and all quadratic effects is higher than 171% relative to the compared DSDs; correlations between quadratic-effect columns are also lower for the cOMARS designs. In the seven-factor, 34-run comparison, the cOMARS design has a maximum absolute correlation of 0.367 between second-order effect columns, matching the lowest maximum among the compared designs, and its median correlation is zero. In 1,000 simulation repetitions, the seven-factor cOMARS analysis had higher average power for linear effects than the 36-run D-optimal design and the 34-run Bayesian D-optimal design; its interaction power exceeded 91% when there were one or two active quadratic effects, but with three such effects its interaction type-I error was 0.073 and its interaction FDR was 0.236.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that cOMARS designs may have limited efficiency for estimating quadratic effects as run size increases, because the proportion of zero entries in quadratic-effect columns becomes low. They also show that detecting quadratic effects can be difficult in the simulations, especially when their signal-to-noise ratios are small, and recommend considering axial runs to improve quadratic-effect estimation in some response-surface applications.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence is centered on a seven-factor setting with particular patterns of active effects, weak heredity for interactions, normally distributed errors, and effect sizes generated by the stated protocol; the results may not transfer to other practical conditions. The CC/VNS search is repeated a finite number of times and returns the best design it finds, but does not establish that the globally best concatenation has been found.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose constructing larger cOMARS designs by using DSDs derived from conference designs with larger run sizes. They also suggest augmenting designs with axial runs when feasible, particularly to improve quadratic-effect estimation and response prediction in experiments with three or four factors.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the designs under model misspecification, non-normal errors, practical restrictions on factor combinations, and additional patterns of active effects. Sequential augmentation strategies and validation in real experiments would also help establish how the designs perform beyond the paper's comparisons and simulations.

narrate.summary: This paper develops sequential sampling methods for best-arm identification: choosing the arm with the highest mean reward from several alternatives under a sample budget. The methods target minimax error-rate performance, with a closed-form allocation specifically established for the paper’s standard H1 complexity measure. The allocation assigns sampling proportions using the current empirical means, and the proposed Almost Tracking method distributes each batch among arms that have received fewer samples than their target proportions. This batch-based approach is designed to work without knowing the final budget in advance and without discarding observations. The authors prove rate-optimality under stated conditions and report that their tracking methods outperform many comparison methods in synthetic and real-dataset evaluations.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 40 Gaussian arms across 10 instances, the estimated worst-case rate for H1 was 0.537 for Simple Tracking and 0.509 for Almost Tracking, compared with 0.456 for Successive Rejects, 0.435 for Continuous Rejection A, and 0.114 for Double Sequential Halving. For the H2 measure, the reported rates were 0.260 for Simple Tracking, 0.255 for Almost Tracking, and 0.256 for Successive Rejects, so these methods were closely matched. In evaluations based on the Open Bandit Dataset with 80 arms and MovieLens 1M with 31 arms, the tracking methods generally had lower error probability than the anytime and fixed-budget elimination methods; Continuous Rejection was comparable on MovieLens. The paper proves that its allocation for H1 is a constant-factor approximation and that Almost Tracking is rate-optimal under its theoretical conditions; experiments used 10,000 simulation runs per setting and set the batch size to twice the number of arms.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their technical results do not cover rewards that are not sub-Gaussian. Their explicit closed-form allocation and constant-factor guarantee focus on H1; finding efficient optimization methods for a broader class of complexity measures is left open.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical comparison is limited to ten synthetic instances with 40 arms and two real datasets converted into Gaussian-arm instances, so it does not establish performance on live experiments or on a broad range of reward distributions. The theoretical guarantees require growing batch and horizon conditions, while the experiments use batches of twice the number of arms; the paper does not show how the guarantees translate into practical finite-budget performance under those experimental settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing an efficient optimization algorithm that achieves rate-optimality for a larger class of complexity measures.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the allocation on live experiments and on data with non-Gaussian or nonstationary rewards, while checking whether its sampling proportions remain effective under practical constraints such as arm-specific costs or limited availability. Further work could also quantify finite-budget performance for the tested batch settings and evaluate sequential stopping or budget-adaptation procedures.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for estimating treatment effects when experimental treatments include many semantically related variants, such as content generated by large language models (LLMs). It models the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) as an inner product of a low-dimensional treatment representation and a user-covariate representation, with each representation learned using a separate kernel. The authors estimate the representations by alternating between penalized regression updates. For online experiments, they use an explore-then-commit strategy: first randomize assignments to gather data, then assign each user the treatment predicted to work best for that user. In semi-synthetic evaluations, their method generally achieves lower prediction error than the compared methods that model treatment and user interactions, and the paper proves estimation and regret guarantees under stated assumptions.
narrate.key_results: In the Upworthy semi-synthetic experiment, at rank 2, double-kernel representation learning (DKRL) had training error 0.0019 and test error 0.0036, compared with 0.0105 and 0.0104 for the neural-network-based structured intervention method, and 0.0043 and 0.0080 for product-kernel regression. Its runtime was 0.1907 seconds, compared with 8.4686 seconds for the neural-network method and 0.0014 seconds for product-kernel regression, so it was faster than the neural network but slower than product-kernel regression. In the MIND semi-synthetic results, at decay level q=4, DKRL had test mean squared error 0.003, compared with 0.004 for the best listed baseline with combined treatment and user features. The authors prove a sublinear regret bound proportional to the time horizon to the two-thirds power, with additional factors determined by the number of treatment and user bases and the representation rank; they also report that adaptive assignment without user covariates has linear regret in their Upworthy simulation. The Upworthy setup used 50 candidate treatments, 500 simulated users, and treatment and user feature dimensions of 384 and 200, respectively.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify the need to address delayed responses and interference between participants, and note that their theoretical guarantees are for fixed bases rather than infinite-dimensional bases. They also identify privacy and fairness as important concerns for experimentation involving generative artificial intelligence.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence is largely semi-synthetic: the Upworthy user covariates and outcomes are simulated, and the MIND evaluation uses a synthetic outcome model rather than observed outcomes from a deployed adaptive experiment. The adaptive procedure also relies on randomized exploration over the candidate bases and on the low-rank interaction structure, so its reported performance may not transfer directly to experiments with restricted assignment, substantially misspecified embeddings, or strong departures from low rank.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the theory to infinite-dimensional bases and studying settings with delayed outcomes or participant interference. They also suggest improving the embeddings through language-model fine-tuning or contrastive learning, and identify privacy and fairness as issues requiring attention.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method in prospective experiments with real user outcomes and compare it with adaptive designs that account for assignment costs, safety limits, or unequal treatment availability. Further work could test robustness to poor semantic embeddings and model misspecification, and investigate sequential updates that adapt throughout the experiment rather than using a single explore-then-commit split.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for Bayesian experimental design that estimates expected information gain by estimating the differential entropy of the evidence distribution. It targets problems with additive Gaussian noise, where the noise entropy is known, and where expensive forward-model evaluations dominate computation. The method approximates the evidence with a Gaussian mixture built from prior samples mapped through a surrogate forward model, then estimates the mixture’s entropy. The authors analyze both Monte Carlo and randomized quasi-Monte Carlo ways of selecting the points used to build that mixture. Theory and two numerical examples show that quasi-Monte Carlo can reduce the number of expensive forward evaluations needed for a given accuracy.
narrate.key_results: For independent random training points, the authors prove that the entropy estimator’s RMSE is bounded in order by the forward-model approximation error plus M to the power of minus one-half and N to the power of minus one-half. For randomized quasi-Monte Carlo training points with a uniform prior, their theorem gives a squared-error contribution that decreases at least as M to the power of minus two plus a small rate adjustment; the authors describe this as approximately first-order convergence in M for RMSE. In a linear deconvolution example with dimension 20, 30 realizations supported the predicted Monte Carlo and quasi-Monte Carlo trends, with the latter converging faster. In a nonlinear diffusion PDE example with 100 prior dimensions, 30 realizations showed approximately first-order convergence for shifted-lattice training points and approximately second-order convergence for tent-transformed lattice points; the study used 8,192 finite elements and 4,225 mesh nodes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not prove the proposed convergence rate for the Gaussian-prior quasi-Monte Carlo case; they validate its hypothesized dependence on M numerically. narrate.summary: The paper proposes the Backfill time-to-Event Bayesian Optimal INterval design (BE-BOIN), a clinical dose-finding design for trials in which toxicities may occur late. It combines sequential dose escalation with backfilling patients into doses that meet safety, preliminary efficacy, and sample-size requirements. The method estimates toxicity using observed outcomes and partial follow-up from patients whose toxicity assessments are still pending, and it includes rules for handling conflicting toxicity evidence across doses. After escalation, the design supports selecting the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and, following a randomized dose-optimization stage, the optimal biological dose (OBD). Simulations found that it selected doses comparably to established designs while shortening trial duration relative to the backfill design that does not make real-time decisions.
narrate.key_results: Across eight simulated scenarios, each repeated 10,000 times, BE-BOIN correctly selected the MTD in an average of 55.4% of trials, compared with 52.6% for the time-to-event Bayesian Optimal Interval design (TITE-BOIN) and 56.1% for the Backfill Bayesian Optimal Interval design (BF-BOIN). Across scenarios 1–6, correct OBD selection averaged 63.9% for BE-BOIN, compared with 61.8% for TITE-BOIN and 64.6% for BF-BOIN; all designs had correct OBD selection below 22% in scenarios where the OBD was two dose levels below the MTD. BE-BOIN treated an average of 9.7 more patients than TITE-BOIN, and its average trial duration was 15.0 months shorter than BF-BOIN’s 64.5 months. Compared with the model-based backfill design, BE-BOIN had better average MTD selection and fewer overdosed patients by an average of 3.9, although that comparator had higher MTD selection in the scenario where the MTD was the highest dose.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an offline experimental-design method to reduce the time needed to identify nuclear spins coupled to a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond. The authors validate the approach experimentally in a high-field regime and evaluate it with simulated data in a low-field regime. They report substantial reductions in measurement time, with some loss of performance at the shortest high-field measurement time and low-field validation limited to simulations.

For low-field simulated data at 40.4 gauss, the SIG-selected 8-hour model outperformed the 8-hour reference model, and the 3.2-hour case was reported as comparable to the reference while reducing time by 60%. Models were trained on 5 million simulated samples; selection used 50,000 simulated samples, with 4,000 points selected per signal at high field and 8,000 at low field.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a simple posterior approximation for Bayesian testing of control and experimental groups, intended for treatment-effect analysis in online experiments. It bins each group’s observed metric values and treats the bin counts as categorical data with a Dirichlet prior, producing a Dirichlet posterior for each group. Posterior draws are mapped from bin proportions to metric values and used to estimate the chance that one group has a higher average, expected loss, and quantile differences. They report that the method performs well with sufficient bins and is practical enough to use as their standard internal analysis method.
narrate.key_results: The authors ran 10,000 simulations, with the number of visitors in each simulated group ranging from 8,000 to 25,000. For average differences, chance to beat, and expected loss, roughly 32 bins were enough for offsets from the ground truth to be near zero and have variance similar to the comparison methods. Quantile estimates required more resolution: the Dirichlet-Categorical approximation was similar to bootstrapping at roughly 256 bins. With a few dozen bins or more, the reported 99% credibility intervals contained the ground-truth mean difference in about 99% of simulations; the normal-based intervals for the mean were narrower than the bootstrap or Dirichlet-Categorical intervals.

narrate.summary: This paper develops foldover screening designs for experiments that need to identify important main effects while accounting for second-order effects and estimating error variance before model selection. A search algorithm uses the expected confidence interval criterion to choose designs, and an augmentation method adds runs when the run budget or model-estimation needs make a complete foldover unsuitable. The simulations show that these designs can perform similarly to traditional designs under sparse, hierarchical effects and can perform better when those principles do not hold; a 20-run chemical-process experiment illustrates their use.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with five two-level factors and 16 total runs, the traditional half-fraction design had true-positive rates below 0.10 when ten effects were active, while the three augmented foldover designs had main-effect true-positive rates from 0.710 to 1.000 across the reported scenarios. Each simulation setting used 500 generated responses. For variance effects, it replaces an approximate variance with the exact variance of the log sample variance to calibrate tests. narrate.summary: The paper develops online experiment-design methods that choose system inputs to identify linear and nonlinear dynamic models efficiently. It adapts active learning for regression to nonlinear autoregressive models with exogenous inputs and recurrent neural network state-space models, updating model parameters recursively with a Kalman filter. At each step, the method chooses an admissible input using a criterion that balances predicted uncertainty and exploration, with optional penalties for predicted output-constraint violations. The authors test the approach on simulated two-tank, ethylene oxidation, and industrial robot arm systems, comparing it with random excitation and other active-learning strategies. Their inverse-distance-based approach generally improves prediction as samples are collected, although its computation can be slower than the comparison methods.
narrate.key_results: In the two-tank benchmark, the nonlinear autoregressive model was run for 1,000 samples after 80 initial samples, over 30 runs; without output constraints, the mean test coefficient of determination was 98.17% for the proposed method and 97.92% for passive sampling, while the greedy input-space method also reached 98.17%. In the ethylene oxidation benchmark, the proposed method reached 92.96% for the nonlinear autoregressive model without constraints, compared with 92.57% for passive sampling. For the robot arm recurrent neural network, the proposed method reached 95.79% without constraints, compared with 92.04% for passive sampling; the experiments used 500 samples after 40 initial samples and 10 runs. Computation was a trade-off: in the two-tank nonlinear autoregressive experiment, the proposed method averaged 90.8 milliseconds per sample, compared with 22.8 milliseconds for the input-space greedy method and 25.2 milliseconds for the incremental greedy method; the authors also report that penalties reduced output-constraint violations.

narrate.summary: This paper designs a fast-and-slow experimentation framework for optimizing long-term outcomes in online systems with Bayesian optimization. It is intended for tuning parameterized systems such as recommendation and ranking policies, where treatment effects can change over time and reliable measurement may take weeks. The design runs a long experiment to measure long-term outcomes while running shorter experiments in parallel to test candidate settings. Gaussian process models link short-term measurements and other proxy data to the long-term objective, with a target-aware model that can downweight unhelpful proxies. The authors report that this approach improves optimization in their benchmark studies and can reduce experimentation wall time by over 60 percent compared with sequential experimentation.
narrate.key_results: Across four real-world-based simulation benchmarks, the parallel design significantly outperformed sequential optimization, and including additional proxies with the target-aware model further improved results in some tasks. In a video playback and a retrieval benchmark, reported out-of-sample prediction log-likelihoods were -298275 versus -831 and -952 for sequential, intrinsic-coregionalization, and target-aware models in video playback; for retrieval, the corresponding values were -22799742, -461, and -456. In a real deployment example, retrieval-system tuning saved over 2 megawatts of capacity while improving ranking performance; the authors also report more than 30 major launches per year from the framework’s broader deployment. The authors report over 60 percent lower experimentation wall time than a traditional sequential design, and accounting for time-of-day effects improved log-likelihood on 12 of 14 engagement metrics and mean squared error on 6 metrics.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the framework prospectively across more live systems and report uncertainty for the optimization gains, not only model-prediction measures and simulated results. narrate.summary: The paper designs an adaptive acquisition procedure for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), using sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) to choose which k-space measurements to acquire. Its objective is to select measurements with high expected information gain (EIG) about the image being reconstructed and, where relevant, a downstream analysis such as segmentation. The method represents feasible sampling patterns with a design parameter and optimizes that parameter using diffusion-based posterior sampling and stochastic optimization. In tests on MRI datasets, the method attained a mean structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 91.34 on the fastMRI knee test set when sampling 25% of k-space. The paper also presents segmentation examples and reports that this task can be inferred from less sampling than is needed for high-fidelity image reconstruction.
narrate.key_results: At 25% k-space sampling, corresponding to four times acceleration, the method achieved a mean SSIM of 91.34 on the fastMRI knee test set. The reported comparison scores were 91.26 for active diffusion subsampling, 91.08 for sequential MRI sampling, 90.2 for random sampling, 90.13 for fixed-mask diffusion posterior sampling, 89.52 for LOUPE, and 87.97 for PG-MRI. On brain fastMRI data, at iteration 9 the paper reports 15.6789% k-space sampling, a PSNR of 20.6784, and an SSIM of 0.9104. For white matter hyperintensity segmentation, the paper provides visual examples but no numerical segmentation score; it reports that segmentation can be inferred from less data than detailed image reconstruction requires.
