narrate.summary: This paper develops lattice-based designs for large computer experiments, with the objectives of improving space coverage, numerical integration, and prediction. It constructs optimized lattice-based Latin hypercube designs by searching over lattice generators and using faster formulas to evaluate design quality. It also introduces regularly repeated lattice-based Latin hypercube designs, whose translated local designs can be used to fit Gaussian process models around prediction locations. The authors evaluate the methods through mathematical results and numerical comparisons, including integration, physics-informed neural network training, and computer-model emulation. They report better space-filling and prediction performance in their tests, together with substantial savings in design-search and model-fitting computation.
narrate.key_results: For lattice-based designs, the new evaluation formulas reduce the cost of assessing design criteria from quadratic in run size to linear, or to logarithmic in run size for the bivariate projection criteria. In tests with 100 runs and 4 factors and with 1,000 runs and 10 factors, the lattice-based search typically reached its reported optimum in about 500 and 5,000 iterations, respectively, while the unrestricted Latin hypercube search had not converged within 100,000 iterations. The optimized lattice-based designs generally had better space-filling criteria than the optimized unrestricted and power-generator designs, and the lattice-based designs optimized for wrap-around discrepancy performed best for mean integration error across the four test functions; they also gave the lowest reported physics-informed neural network errors when run size was at least 1,000. In emulation tests using 500-point local models and 1,000 prediction locations, the regularly repeated designs had the lowest reported root mean squared prediction errors: 9.54e-6 for Ackley, 0.017 for Shekel, and 0.478 for Emichalewicz, compared with partitioned designs, nearest-neighbor designs, local approximate Gaussian process models, and sparse grids.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes a way to estimate variance components for response surface analyses of multi-stratum experiments, including split-plot and split-split-plot designs. The method, called pure error residual maximum likelihood (PE-REML), fits the full treatment model when estimating variance components, rather than relying on the assumed polynomial response surface model. Those estimates are then used with generalized least squares (GLS) to estimate response surface effects, with a Kenward-Roger adjustment available for their standard errors. The authors compare the method with standard response surface residual maximum likelihood (RS-REML) using three examples and simulations. They find that both methods perform similarly when the response surface model is correct, while PE-REML is more robust when it is misspecified.
narrate.key_results: In simulations of 10,000 data sets where the assumed model was correct, fixed-effect estimates were similar between methods, and empirical standard errors for the quadratic effects differed by less than 0.001 in the reported table. With a large omitted third-order effect in the whole-plot stratum, PE-REML standard-error biases were no greater than about 10%, while RS-REML biases exceeded 40% for several whole-plot effects; the mean whole-plot variance estimate was 4.0358 with PE-REML and 9.6323 with RS-REML. When the omitted effect was in the subplot stratum, PE-REML variance estimates were close to the true values, while RS-REML standard-error biases for several subplot effects were about 76% to 89%. In the ceramic-pipe experiment, which had 12 whole plots with four runs each, PE-REML gave smaller standard errors for some effects and larger ones for others than RS-REML.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify the search for better corrections to standard errors, p-values, and confidence intervals as a useful direction for further research, since the Kenward-Roger correction helps only a little.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could quantify when a design has enough replicated-treatment information for stable pure-error variance estimates, and compare design choices that increase this information against their run cost. narrate.summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design procedure for identifying the anode rate constant in a lithium-ion cell electrochemical model. A reinforcement learning policy adjusts the applied current during the experiment to increase the voltage sensitivity to that parameter, using a hardware-in-the-loop setup for testing. The procedure uses a reduced-order electrochemical cell model and a data-driven estimator of cathode surface concentration as an input to the controller. The authors compare the resulting experiment with constant-current discharge tests and a relaxation current interrupt discharge test. The adaptive design identifies the parameter with low drive-cycle voltage prediction error in a much shorter experiment than the relaxation current interrupt discharge test.
narrate.key_results: The reinforcement-learning hardware-in-the-loop design had Fisher information of 0.08 volts squared, a median drive-cycle verification error of 12.32 millivolts, and an experiment length of 1800 seconds. The relaxation current interrupt discharge test had higher Fisher information, 0.42 volts squared, and a 13.33-millivolt error, but required 103333 seconds, or about 28 hours. The 1C and 5C discharge tests had errors of 47.98 and 47.31 millivolts, Fisher information of 0.01 and 0.05 volts squared, and durations of 3781 and 701 seconds, respectively. The data-driven state estimator achieved an R-squared value of 0.9987 and mean squared error of 1.16 × 10^-4 on training data, and 0.9951 and 4.28 × 10^-4 on validation data.

narrate.summary: This paper presents an input-design method for nonlinear dynamic system identification that aims to improve model prediction by filling the relevant regions of the model-input space with data. It uses a surrogate model and a receding horizon control (RHC) procedure to choose inputs, repeatedly selecting the next input from an optimized future sequence. Its objective is to make supporting points spread through the region of interest while respecting input and model-space constraints. The procedure can run offline with a fixed surrogate model or online with a model updated from process observations. In a simulated nonlinear example, the authors report better space-filling performance than the comparison methods they tested.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used a simulated Hammerstein process and compared the proposed method in adaptive and fixed-surrogate modes with incremental dynamic space-filling design (IDS-FID) and amplitude-modulated pseudo random binary signals (APRBS). For each method, the study generated 50 signals, each with a dataset size of 300. The paper reports that the proposed method outperformed the comparison methods on both the largest-empty-ball radius and distribution uniformity measures, but does not give numerical summary values for those metrics in the text. The adaptive version increasingly improved on the fixed-surrogate version as data accumulated, while the IDS-FID comparison used the same fixed linear time-invariant surrogate as the proposed offline method.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential design of experiments (DoE) method to estimate seismic fragility curves when only a binary indicator of state (BIS) is observed for each intensity measure (IM). It uses a Bayesian probit-lognormal model and a constrained reference prior to estimate failure probability while addressing degenerate likelihoods that can arise with small samples. At each step, the method selects an intensity measure value expected to have a large effect on the posterior estimate, then tests or simulates the structure and records its outcome. The authors evaluate the strategy using simulated responses for a nuclear-industry piping system, with peak ground acceleration and pseudo-spectral acceleration as the intensity measures. They report that the sequential method usually estimates the curve more efficiently than standard sampling, particularly with fewer than 100 observations, while reducing likelihood degeneracy.
narrate.key_results: In 100 replications, the authors compared standard sampling with sequential selections for sample sizes up to 250; the sequential approach reduced estimation error more quickly, with its clearest advantage below about 50 observations. With pseudo-spectral acceleration, estimation bias approached the probit-lognormal model-bias level by about 50 observations, and decreased little beyond about 100; the paper reports that around 80 observations gave a reasonable estimate. With peak ground acceleration, the method outperformed standard sampling up to about 100 observations, but its performance degraded beyond that point because of model bias and the limited range of that measure. The proposed stopping indicators suggested about 60 observations for pseudo-spectral acceleration and about 40 for peak ground acceleration at the stated information-index threshold; the authors caution that such thresholds depend on the case study.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the influence of the seismic signal generator is outside the scope of the study. They also note that the probit-lognormal model can be biased, that peak ground acceleration does not fully describe the fragility curve in their case, and that their proposed stopping thresholds are case-specific rather than established guidance. The constrained prior does not guarantee against estimates whose spread parameter tends toward zero in very small samples.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation centers on one piping-system model and synthetic seismic signals calibrated to a limited collection of real accelerograms, so it does not establish performance across other equipment or seismic settings. narrate.summary: The paper introduces BLADE, a Bayesian method for discovering sparse governing equations of dynamical systems from measurements. It assumes the system can be represented as a linear combination of candidate functions and estimates coefficient uncertainty using replica-exchange stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics. For limited-data settings, it chooses additional observations by combining predictive uncertainty with a space-filling criterion, then refits the model as data are added. The authors test the method on simulated Lotka–Volterra, Lorenz, Burgers, and convection–diffusion systems, comparing it with sparse regression, a Bayesian sparse-regression method, and alternative samplers. In the active-learning tests, the combined selection strategy reaches the reported error target with substantially fewer measurements than random sampling.
narrate.key_results: For the Lotka–Volterra system, the hybrid uncertainty and space-filling strategy reduced the number of measurements needed to bring the total error bar below 10 to the power of minus 2 from 70 with random sampling to 30, a reduction of about 60%. For Burgers’ equation, the same target required 50 measurements with the hybrid strategy versus 90 with random sampling, a reduction of 44%; at 50 points, the hybrid strategy identified the correct candidate functions while the other strategies retained extra terms or an incomplete model. In the convection–diffusion test, the hybrid strategy recovered the correct equation structure with 50 points and reported coefficient estimates of 1.002 and minus 0.996, while random sampling missed the diffusion term. In a matched-throughput test on the Lorenz system, replica-exchange sampling achieved 25.29 steps per second compared with 1.14 for the No-U-Turn Sampler.

key_equations.explanation: The coefficient vector at iteration k plus one is updated from its value at iteration k using step size eta, the gradient of the approximate negative log-posterior L, temperature tau, and Gaussian random noise zeta.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that replica-exchange sampling costs more computation than deterministic optimization and may be prohibitive for very large systems or real-time applications. The candidate-function library is specified in advance, and finite-difference derivative estimates can be fragile for noisy partial differential equation data. They note that the partial differential equation tests used lower noise levels than the ordinary differential equation tests, so those results do not comprehensively test robustness to high noise.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The active-learning evaluations use simulated data pools, and the authors calculate response derivatives from the original regular data even in scenarios framed as having difficult or costly derivative acquisition. Thus, these tests do not establish the full real-world cost or feasibility of acquiring each selected measurement. The evaluation also covers a small set of known benchmark systems and does not show how performance changes when the candidate library or the assumed sparse model is wrong.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose improving sampling through adaptive temperature scheduling and parallel chains, and exploring neural operators or manifold-learned features to discover candidate bases automatically. For noisy partial differential equation problems, they suggest weak-form or integral methods, transformed-domain methods, filtering, and neural-network-based denoising with automatic differentiation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test BLADE on physical experiments where each selected measurement has a recorded acquisition cost and derivatives are not available from a full underlying trajectory. It would also be useful to test alternative design constraints and acquisition criteria, and to evaluate sequential use when observations arrive over time and the system may change.

narrate.summary: This paper studies Bayesian optimization (BO) for finding the minimum of intrinsically noisy response surfaces, such as those encountered in physical experiments. It models the response with a Gaussian process (GP) and compares choices of initial sample size, replication, acquisition function, and covariance function. The study varies the problem, noise magnitude, and noise form using simulated functions, and evaluates performance by the gap between the selected and true optimum. Across the tested settings, the Matérn covariance function performs best, while the available experimental budget strongly affects other design choices. The authors provide recommendations for selecting initial samples, replicates, and acquisition functions according to that budget.
narrate.key_results: The study reports 18,225 experiments, using five repetitions of each unique experimental setting, and evaluates results after 25, 37.5, and 50 times the problem dimension in samples. The Matérn covariance function performs better on all test problems than the Gaussian and power exponential alternatives. A larger initial sample size generally improves the optimum gap, while replication has a minor overall effect but becomes more useful as the experimental budget grows. The preferred acquisition function also depends on budget: probability of improvement is favored for smaller budgets, while the upper confidence approach is more suitable for larger budgets. The authors report that objective-function type and the studied noise properties do not interact with the controllable choices in the way that total budget does.

They also call for new statistical methods for optimizing noisy response surfaces when data are sparse.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate the recommendations in physical experiments and test them on a wider range of response surfaces and noise distributions. It could also assess whether the design guidance remains effective under practical constraints such as restricted or costly input settings.

narrate.summary: The paper extends a result about mixtures of noncentral chi-square distributions to mixtures of noncentral Wishart distributions. It applies that result to testing random effects in balanced, two-factor factorial designs with multivariate normal observations. The design separates the response variation into sums-of-outer-products for each factor, their interaction, and error, then uses the derived finite-sample distributions to test whether factor covariance components are zero. The method applies when the degrees of freedom in the mixed and mixing Wishart distributions are the same. The authors show that the resulting factor test statistics have exact matrix-variate Beta Type II null distributions and illustrate the tests with two real datasets.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical result establishes that a noncentral Wishart mixture of noncentral Wishart distributions with equal degrees of freedom is itself noncentral Wishart; the paper uses this to obtain exact finite-sample tests for random effects in multivariate factorial models. In the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey example, there were 150 observations, 2 response variables, and 5 observations per cell; the multivariate p-values for the two main effects and interaction were 0.4993, 0.9556, and 0.0704. In the diamonds example, there were 105 observations, 2 response variables, and 3 observations per cell; the corresponding multivariate p-values were 0.0000, 0.0000, and 0.0153. Both examples used 10,000 Monte Carlo draws to estimate p-values, and comparisons with separate univariate variance-component tests showed that multivariate and univariate analyses can yield different conclusions.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a more efficient sampling step for Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), which approximates a complex model locally with a linear explanation. It focuses on regression with tabular inputs and uses a D-optimal design to place sample points near the instance being explained. The construction fixes a small design weight at the reference point, places the other design points symmetrically around it in one dimension, and adds small random perturbations around those points when more samples are needed. In an illustrative one-feature example, the optimal-design approach generally matched or improved explanation quality and reduced run-to-run variability relative to standard random LIME sampling. The authors present it as a way to obtain useful explanations with fewer costly model evaluations, while noting that the evidence is limited to the illustrative example.
narrate.key_results: The numerical comparison used 11 sample points per explanation and 100 runs at each of 11 reference points. Across those reference points, the optimal-design approach had lower average NWISE at 8 points and higher weighted correlation at 6 points; at the other points, the reported results were equal or worse on at least one measure. For unit 9, average NWISE was 34,245 for the optimal-design approach and 48,558 for LIME, while weighted correlation was 0.9502 and 0.9312, respectively. Unit 10 showed a boundary-related exception: NWISE was 316,728 for the optimal-design approach versus 174,770 for LIME, with weighted correlation equal at 0.9722. The paper also shows that the optimal-design approach has less variability as sample size increases, but does not report a direct measurement of runtime, energy use, or model evaluations saved.

They also suggest studying feature selection, including penalized models, distribution-aware sampling, and designs that are jointly optimal for multiple reference points.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on real engineering and other tabular datasets, comparing it with LIME across multiple primary models and dimensions. Future evaluations could measure model calls, runtime, and energy directly, and investigate constrained or sequential designs that respect feature dependence and practical input limits.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a two-stage robust optimal design framework for toxicology experiments, using sea urchin embryo dose-response studies as its main application. It models ordinal embryo outcomes with a proportional odds model and uses particle swarm optimization to select dose levels and allocation weights. After an initial experiment, the method uses several fitted parameter sets to construct a robust second-stage design, with options to prioritize parameter estimation or precision for a target dose. The authors also include practical dose levels such as a zero-dose control and an extremely high dose, and derive conditions for checking design optimality. Their real-data results show that the designs can provide useful precision, but do not consistently outperform conventional or locally optimal designs when biological variation may shift between experiments.
narrate.key_results: The initial sea urchin dataset contained 8,163 observations, the locally dual-optimal December dataset contained 2,070, and the two robust-design datasets contained 889 and 927 observations. In the robust-design datasets, the estimated RD50 was 2.650 with a standard error of 0.154 for the robust D-optimal design, compared with 2.955 with a standard error of 0.123 for the robust dual-optimal design. Across four parameter estimates in the relative-efficiency comparison, the robust D-optimal design's D-efficiencies ranged from 0.902 to 0.986, but it was never the best D-efficient design; the locally dual-optimal design had the highest c-efficiency in some comparisons. In the bivariate probit simulations, the authors report that particle swarm optimization often improved on the published benchmark designs; for example, the one-stage D-optimal criterion without penalty was 8.332 for their design and 8.654 for the reported design.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data evaluation is confined to sea urchin embryo experiments, and comparisons across dates may confound design effects with changes in organisms or experimental conditions. The paper does not provide a controlled comparison of time or cost savings, and the additional experiments still require substantial sample sizes; the method's performance under plausible alternatives to the proportional odds model is not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors call for better control of genetic shifts in experimental organisms, accessible tools for practitioners, and designs that incorporate practical requirements such as control groups and endpoint doses. They also advocate continued collaboration between statisticians and toxicologists to adapt design methods to real experimental settings.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Prospective studies could compare the designs using standardized organism cohorts and controlled conditions, while tracking total cost, labor, and estimation quality against conventional designs. Further work could test sensitivity to model misspecification and operational constraints, and provide reproducible code and tools for applying the robust procedure in sequential experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops active hypothesis-testing methods for situations where a valid test statistic is costly to obtain but an inexpensive, possibly invalid proxy is available. It considers multiple hypothesis testing and aims to reduce the number of costly tests while retaining valid inference and false discovery rate control. The methods randomly decide whether to query the valid test based on the proxy, then combine the queried result or proxy into a valid active statistic. The authors also develop procedures that use these statistics with multiple-testing methods and apply them to causal-effect tests in single-cell CRISPR screening. Their theory establishes validity under stated conditions, and their simulations and data analysis show that the methods can reduce computation while retaining useful power.
narrate.key_results: For e-values, the active construction remains valid under arbitrary dependence between the proxy and true statistic, and applying e-BH controls the false discovery rate at the target level under arbitrary dependence. For p-values, the active construction is valid under arbitrary dependence between each proxy and its true p-value; the paper's active BH false discovery rate bounds depend on the dependence across hypotheses and can exceed the target level. In the scCRISPR analysis, the expensive proximal 2SLS test took about 34 seconds per test, compared with about 0.0046 seconds for the proxy OLS test; the active density-based method queried the expensive test for 34% of null tests and 72% of alternative tests. In simulations, the density-based method had a false positive rate of 0.072 at a 0.05 cutoff when proxy and true p-values had rank correlation 0.95, illustrating that its independence assumption matters; the arbitrary-dependence active p-value avoids that particular assumption.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify choosing proxy statistics to maximize power as an open theoretical problem. The density-based p-value method requires independence between proxy and true p-values and a known or estimated proxy density; the joint-distribution extension requires enough true tests to estimate the conditional distribution. They also note that it remains open whether the active BH false discovery rate bound under independence or positive dependence can be improved to the target level.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data evidence comes from one scCRISPR dataset, and the reported savings depend on the particular proxy accuracy, query rates, and computation-time benchmarks, so they may not transfer directly to other applications. The paper does not evaluate a planned experimental run allocation or show how operational constraints, such as limited batches or test-specific costs, would affect the randomized querying strategy.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further theoretical work on choosing proxies to maximize power. They also identify improving the active BH false discovery rate guarantee under independence or positive dependence as an open question.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the methods in additional laboratory applications and compare observed savings and discovery performance against practical cost-aware allocation plans. It would also be useful to evaluate query policies that account for unequal test costs, batching constraints, or an evolving budget, while checking error control under those operational conditions.

narrate.summary: This paper presents a diagnostic for deciding when standard uncertainty estimates are trustworthy in online randomized A/B tests. It focuses on the average treatment effect and on the assumption that the Central Limit Theorem makes its sampling distribution approximately normal. The method repeatedly resamples synthetic A/A tests from observed user data and checks whether their p-values follow a uniform distribution using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The authors demonstrate the approach with operational data from a consumer application. They find that most measured outcomes pass the diagnostic, while some show evidence that standard confidence intervals and tests may be unreliable.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used data from approximately 2 million users, about 17 million logged event instances, and 50 event types; each event was assessed with 5,000 synthetic A/A comparisons, using roughly 1 million users per group. The uniformity null hypothesis was not rejected for most outcomes, but several outcomes showed substantial departures, including after a crude Bonferroni correction. Event frequency had a Spearman rank correlation of approximately 0.45 with the D statistic, while sample skewness had a correlation of approximately 0.43; neither was a monotonic or fully reliable substitute for the resampling diagnostic. The authors conclude that the D statistic provides additional diagnostic information beyond event frequency and that frequency and skewness are useful but imperfect indicators.

key_equations.explanation: ATE is the average treatment effect, which is zero by design when the two groups receive the same condition.

key_equations.name: Expected p-value distribution
key_equations.explanation: The p-values are those from repeated resampled A/A tests, and the uniform distribution on the interval from zero to one is expected when the test is calibrated under the null.

key_equations.name: Kolmogorov-Smirnov diagnostic
key_equations.explanation: D is the largest difference between the empirical p-value cumulative distribution function F_emp and the uniform cumulative distribution, p is a value from zero to one, and sup denotes the supremum over that interval.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that interpreting the Kolmogorov-Smirnov p-values across outcomes requires a multiple-testing correction. They also state that alternative methods such as permutation sampling or bootstrapping can be computationally demanding, and that exploring their applicability is outside this paper's scope.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation comes from one proprietary consumer application, with 50 event types, so it does not establish how the diagnostic performs across other industries, outcome structures, or experiment platforms. The analysis also relies on resampling the available user data; it does not validate the diagnostic against a broad set of independently run experiments with known treatment effects.

narrate.summary: This paper describes how to analyze randomized A/B tests with ordinary least squares (OLS) regression using aggregated, k-anonymous equivalence-class data instead of individual records. Its objective is to support treatment-effect and regression-parameter estimation while minimizing the amount of individual-level data stored or shared. The construction aggregates observations by treatment and selected covariates, then uses class counts and outcome sums to build the regression matrices; for numeric covariates, the class counts also weight the covariate calculations. The paper demonstrates partial F-tests for interactions and heterogeneous treatment effects, as well as covariate-based regression adjustment. In the worked examples, the aggregate approach reproduces the individual-data coefficient estimates, while also offering lower computational and data-storage requirements when the number of classes is much smaller than the sample size.
narrate.key_results: For the dummy-variable example, 18 observations were represented in 6 equivalence classes, and the paper reports that the aggregate-data regression results match those from Excel on individual-level data. The worked interaction example gives a partial F statistic of 41.705. The authors state that construction of the regression matrices can reduce computational complexity from O(n squared times k) to O(m squared times k), when the number of equivalence classes m is much smaller than the number of subjects n. In the numeric-covariate example, the estimated sample average treatment effect is -0.1871; its reported t statistic using the authors’ variance approach is -0.6568, while the individual-level pooled OLS output gives a t statistic of -0.6551, with the difference attributed to the variance estimators rather than aggregation.

narrate.summary: The paper develops three weighted informativity conditions for using multiple signal segments to identify and control linear time-invariant systems when one long, persistently exciting input is impractical. The authors construct inputs by selecting signal values to build rank-sufficient Hankel matrices, while allowing each individual segment to remain insufficiently exciting. In the model predictive control comparison, reported optimization times were 3.1657 seconds for mosaic, 0.1919 seconds for cumulative, and 1.8771 seconds for hybrid; the authors report nearly consistent closed-loop tracking across the three. narrate.summary: The paper presents an R package for constructing and analyzing covariate-balanced assignments in randomized treatment-control experiments. Its objective is to improve treatment-effect precision while preserving design-based inference conditional on assignment acceptance. The package batches assignment generation and balance checks, can use graphics processing units (GPUs) or tensor processing units (TPUs), and stores compact random-number keys rather than all accepted assignment vectors. It supports exact enumeration when feasible and Monte Carlo generation for larger problems, with randomization tests and optional fiducial intervals. The paper reports faster pool generation in its benchmarks and derives how stricter acceptance can reduce the imbalance contribution to estimation error under its stated model assumptions.
narrate.key_results: For 100 units, 100 covariates, and an acceptance probability of 0.005, the authors report that pool generation takes about 5 seconds on the GPU backend, compared with 112 seconds for a baseline R workflow, a speedup of about 24 times. For 1,000 units and 1,000 covariates at the same acceptance probability, generation takes 7 seconds on the GPU and 91 seconds on the package's CPU backend; GPU runtime reductions reach 96% at 1,000 covariates. The authors report speedups over baseline implementations exceeding 42 times in some high-dimensional, high-unit-count, stringent-acceptance settings, while noting that baseline results are shown only where those implementations finish in a reasonable time. Under the paper's theoretical example with an outcome variance share of 0.5, acceptance probability 0.01 yields an estimated root mean squared error reduction of about 15% at 30 covariates and about 3% at 1,000 covariates.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an optimal experimental design for learning how to rank a large set of items from a limited number of human comparisons. It assumes that feedback ranking groups of items follows the Plackett-Luce model and that item rewards are linear in their features. The design chooses a probability distribution over groups of items to maximize a determinant-based information criterion. The authors introduce DopeWolfe, a randomized Frank-Wolfe algorithm that searches a sampled set of candidate groups and uses efficient matrix updates. In synthetic tests and public ranking datasets, the chosen comparisons generally produce better learned rankings than the tested sampling and clustering baselines.
narrate.key_results: In synthetic experiments on three datasets, the paper reports lower ranking loss for DopeWolfe than for uniform sampling and, generally, the clustering baselines; it evaluated each setting over 100 random runs. With real feedback from two public datasets, DopeWolfe also had lower ranking loss than uniform sampling, with results averaged over 10 trials. For one runtime comparison, DopeWolfe took 1,646.70 seconds for 1,000 iterations, compared with a reported total of 4,927.38 seconds for the DBSCAN baseline; the authors note these runtimes are not directly comparable because their tuning parameters differ. They report that DopeWolfe typically reached similar performance in about 100 iterations, taking 164.67 seconds in that comparison. For 100 items and comparisons of 10 at a time, the paper estimates about 17 trillion possible subsets, illustrating why enumerating all candidate groups is impractical.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an approach to optimize thermoelectric performance by adjusting antimony and tellurium contents in silver antimony telluride. The approach combines design of experiments (DoE) with machine learning (ML) to guide composition choices. A Latin square design and a Monte Carlo search spread experiments across the selected composition space, while support vector models use measurement results to narrow the search in later cycles. The authors synthesized and measured eight compositions over three optimization cycles. Their best composition had a peak thermoelectric figure of merit more than 30% higher than earlier reported values for this material system.
narrate.key_results: The optimization used eight samples over three cycles and found a best composition with a peak thermoelectric figure of merit of 1.61 ± 0.24 at about 600 K and an average value of 1.18 ± 0.18 from 300 to 623 K. The authors report that these values are more than 30% above the previous best values for this material system, which were a peak of 1.22 and an average of 0.9. The best sample had thermal conductivity of about 0.4 W per meter per kelvin and showed no evidence of secondary phases, although it contained two phases with similar lattice constants. The authors also released their optimization software as an open-source graphical interface and made the code available in a public repository.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a determinant-based D-optimal design method for discretizing norms and recovering functions from samples. For a finite-dimensional space of continuous complex-valued functions, it constructs points and nonnegative weights that exactly reproduce the L2 norm using a Marcinkiewicz–Zygmund identity. The construction maximizes a Gram-matrix determinant and uses a convex-geometric reduction to bound the number of points. The method also constructs tight frames and provides a deterministic sampling recovery procedure for functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space when leading eigenfunctions are available. The authors establish general bounds and test the construction numerically for trigonometric polynomials, while also showing that lattice designs cannot have a point-count bound based only on the number of frequencies in complete generality.
narrate.key_results: For a space of dimension n, the paper proves an exact weighted L2 discretization with at most n squared plus 1 points; for trigonometric frequencies in a finite index set, the bound is the size of the difference set, at most the frequency count squared minus the frequency count plus 1. In the recovery setting, the method uses at most n squared plus 1 samples and gives worst-case squared L2 error at most 3 times the tail sum of squared singular values. The paper reports recovery computation requiring order n cubed arithmetic operations for its direct implementation, and notes that prior sharp probabilistic approaches can have a large sampling constant and do not construct verifiable point sets. In numerical tests, the authors obtained a discretization with 41 points for a 41-frequency set and 45 points for a 33-frequency set; for a challenging 10-frequency example, they found a 91-point design and did not find one with fewer points, which they present as numerical evidence for sharpness rather than a proof.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that equal-weight exact discretization for every trigonometric frequency set with a number of points depending only on the set’s cardinality remains an open question. They also show that lattice rules cannot, in general, have a point-count bound depending only on that cardinality without additional structure on the frequency set. For function recovery, their deterministic construction uses a quadratic-in-dimension sample bound, while some earlier probabilistic methods have better sample scaling but nonconstructive or unverifiable point sets.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical construction relies on iterative optimization and repeated initializations, so the theoretical existence result does not ensure that a practical search will find a design efficiently or reliably for large problems. The method assumes a specified function space and target measure and permits unequal weights; the paper does not establish performance when experiments impose run costs, restricted feasible settings, measurement noise, or other operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors leave open whether equal-weight exact discretizations can be obtained for arbitrary trigonometric frequency sets using a number of points depending only on the frequency count. They also note that constructive subsampling could reduce the recovery design to a number of samples proportional to the dimension, while retaining the error bound up to constants.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to adapt the construction to practical design constraints such as forbidden settings, unequal run costs, replication limits, and noisy responses, then validate it in real experiments. Further work could also compare the optimization’s runtime and reliability with alternative design algorithms across larger spaces and test whether sequentially adding runs preserves the exactness or recovery guarantees.

narrate.summary: The paper develops alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithms to compute convex relaxation bounds for the 0/1 D-optimality problem (D-Opt) and maximum-entropy sampling (MESP). D-Opt selects a fixed number of design points to maximize information for parameter estimation, while MESP selects variables to maximize the information in a covariance submatrix. The algorithms split the relaxations into simpler updates, including bounded least-squares steps and closed-form matrix updates based on eigenvalues; the factorization-bound update is supported by new theoretical results. Numerical tests show strong performance for the natural D-Opt bound, the MESP factorization bound, and the MESP Boolean quadratic programming bound, with the linear-algebraic MESP bound less competitive. The authors position these methods as tools for faster upper-bound calculations within branch-and-bound optimization.
narrate.key_results: For the natural D-Opt bound, the algorithm solved random instances with 15,000 candidates in 1.0 second, compared with 35.5 seconds for KNITRO and 27.3 seconds for MOSEK; on the quadratic-response instances with 50,000 candidates, it took 219.1 seconds, compared with 430.0 and 1,226.7 seconds, respectively. For the factorization bound on MESP instances with 2,000 variables and covariance rank from 150 to 300, the algorithm was faster than KNITRO on most tested ranks; when varying the selection size from 50 to 150 at rank 150, it took about 0.6 to 2.5 seconds and was faster than KNITRO throughout. For the Boolean quadratic programming bound, it solved tested instances up to 400 variables in 3,279.3 seconds, while SDPT3 ran out of memory above 300 variables and MOSEK ran out of memory at 250 variables. In a 100-step D-Opt diving test, warm-starting reduced cumulative time from about 600 seconds to about 100 seconds, a reported speedup of about six times; the computed relaxations used a target duality gap of 0.05.

narrate.summary: The paper extends mixture and component-amount experimental designs to include order-of-addition effects while accounting for process differences through orthogonal blocks. The proposed models combine mixture proportions or component amounts with pairwise-ordering factors and their interactions. The authors construct designs by adding order-of-addition settings to existing two-block designs based on Latin squares. They assess the designs using parameter-estimation criteria and prediction measures, including G-efficiency and fraction-of-design-space plots. Their three worked examples show moderate prediction efficiency and indicate that order effects may be important for the responses considered.

The reported G-efficiencies are 58.8% for the yarn example, 58.8% for the vinyl example, and 53.5% for the tablet example; the conclusion reports 59% for vinyl. The paper does not report a numerical comparison against alternative designs; its examples evaluate the constructed designs, and the authors report high power for several order factors in their power analyses.

narrate.summary: This paper develops multiple-comparison tests for right-censored time-to-event outcomes across treatment groups. The objective is to identify which groups differ in their cumulative hazard functions while controlling the familywise error rate (FWER), including when proportional hazards (PH) do not hold. One method takes a maximum across weighted log-rank statistics, while the other extends Cumulative Aalen Survival Analysis-of-Variance (CASANOVA) to user-selected contrasts and uses a wild bootstrap. The authors compare both methods with adjusted log-rank and multidirectional log-rank procedures in simulations and a multiple-myeloma data example. The new methods generally control the FWER and show good power in non-proportional-hazards settings, though the maximum weighted-log-rank method can be liberal at smaller sample sizes.
narrate.key_results: The main simulations used four groups with 100 subjects per group, considered four hazard scenarios and Dunnett- and Tukey-type contrasts, and ran 10,000 simulation replicates with 1,000 resampling iterations. At this sample size, nearly all methods controlled the FWER; the adjusted multidirectional test was slightly liberal for Dunnett-type contrasts, and the new methods were more conservative, especially for Tukey-type contrasts. In crossing-hazard scenarios, the adjusted log-rank test lost power substantially, while the methods intended for non-proportional hazards retained high power; the adjusted log-rank test performed best under proportional hazards, and the adjusted multidirectional test performed best in the mixed scenario. In the smaller-sample analysis with 50 subjects per group, the maximum weighted-log-rank approach showed inflated FWER, whereas both bootstrap CASANOVA variants maintained strong control. In the seven-group multiple-myeloma example with 21 pairwise comparisons, all methods rejected the global hypothesis; the adjusted log-rank and multidirectional tests each rejected six local hypotheses, the maximum weighted-log-rank method rejected six, and the two bootstrap CASANOVA variants each rejected five.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that the maximum weighted-log-rank method can have inflated FWER at 50 subjects per group, likely because of its normal approximation. They also note that the new methods can be conservative, particularly for Tukey-type contrasts, and that the adjusted multidirectional test showed slightly liberal behavior for Dunnett-type contrasts.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulation evidence covers four groups, equal group sizes in the main study, specified censoring conditions, and a limited set of hazard patterns and contrasts, so performance in other trial structures is not established. The real-data illustration is one retrospective multiple-myeloma dataset; it does not validate the methods across prospective clinical trials or other application settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose evaluating the methods in unbalanced designs and exploring more efficient use of the FWER, for example through closed testing. They also suggest that alternatives such as the Holm procedure could improve the balance between error control and power for adjusted tests.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess the methods with more groups, unequal censoring patterns, and practical allocation or recruitment constraints. Evaluation in prospectively planned clinical experiments, including whether the local contrast findings are useful for treatment decisions, would test their practical value beyond the single illustrative dataset.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Incremental Dynamic Space-Filling Design (IDS-FID), a method for choosing input excitation signals for nonlinear dynamic system identification. It aims to spread training data across the approximator’s input space while also controlling the signal’s frequency content. The method builds a signal by repeatedly selecting a piecewise-constant input sequence, scoring it with a space-filling measure and a penalty that favors dynamic sequences, and appending the selected sequence. The authors evaluate the approach using a simulated nonlinear Hammerstein process and trained data-driven models. They find that matching excitation dynamics to the anticipated operating frequencies can improve model accuracy, with a trade-off between dynamic and steady-state accuracy.
narrate.key_results: The authors trained 100 models for each excitation using training sets of 300 samples, and evaluated them on test sets of 500 samples. Increasing lambda shifted the excitation toward higher frequencies and improved results on the higher-frequency multisine test, whose band was 0.25 to 0.3 hertz, but generally worsened steady-state accuracy and results on lower-frequency tests. IDS-FID was competitive with the comparison methods, including the existing OMNIPUS method, pseudorandom binary signals, and multisine signals; even its highly dynamic settings performed better than the multisine on the higher-frequency test. The paper reports that settings with lambda values of 0.5 and 2 had notably worse steady-state approximation than OMNIPUS and pseudorandom binary signals, illustrating the trade-off rather than a universal best setting.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the approach on real processes and multivariable systems, including practical input limits and actuator constraints. narrate.summary: The paper develops experimental designs for estimating coefficients in complex-valued linear regression when predictors lie on a compact, connected Lie group. The regression functions are eigenfunctions of the negative Laplace-Beltrami operator, and the authors show that normalized Haar measure is approximately optimal for Kiefer's Phi-p criteria and related eigenvalue-sum criteria. For fixed run sizes, they use equal-weight lambda-designs, which integrate appropriate functions exactly and yield optimal information matrices. They give constructions and examples for the circle, tori, the special unitary group of two by two matrices, the special orthogonal group of three by three matrices, and a product involving the sphere and rotation group. Their examples show that these designs can achieve comparable estimation accuracy with substantially fewer runs than equally spaced angle sampling or rounded approximate designs.
narrate.key_results: For the 55-parameter model on the three-dimensional sphere, a 97-point lambda-design has an information matrix numerically close to the identity, whereas rounding a competing approximate design with 225 support points produces a nearly singular information matrix; the rounded design's reported A-optimal and D-optimal efficiencies are about 2.59 percent and 33.93 percent. For a model on the special orthogonal group of three by three matrices with the first ten coefficients, a 12-point design is optimal, while equally spaced Euler-angle designs at the same run size do not permit estimation of all parameters. Compared with an equally spaced design of 144 runs, the paper reports that 96 runs at the 12 selected points match its minimum-eigenvalue criterion performance, and 132 runs give approximately the same A-optimal performance. In the 90-parameter example on the product of the sphere and rotation group, the optimal design has 168 points; compared with a 3,456-run equally spaced design, 2,016 runs match its A-optimal accuracy and about 1,008 runs suffice for similar minimum-eigenvalue performance.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a global optimum-informed greedy algorithm for choosing sensor locations in a Bayesian inverse problem. Its objective is to minimize average posterior uncertainty, using the criterion known as A-optimality. The method first uses a relaxed global design to identify sensor locations that appear redundant, removes those locations from a greedy design, and then fills the available sensor slots greedily. The authors test the method in a simulated acoustic inverse-source problem with sensors measuring wave fields at multiple frequencies. In that example, the modified method improves the objective and reconstruction accuracy over the standard greedy method, but takes substantially longer to run.
narrate.key_results: The test used 334 candidate sensor locations, and compared designs with up to 36 sensors. The standard greedy sequence took 100.0 seconds, while the global optimum-informed sequence, evaluated for sensor budgets from 6 through 36, took 701.4 seconds; 629.1 seconds of that time was spent computing relaxed global optima. The modified sequence had a 4.2 percent average and 22.3 percent best-case improvement in the objective over the standard greedy sequence, and the authors report a better design at every compared sensor budget. For the 12-sensor reconstruction, the reported error decreased from approximately 4.69 × 10^-2 with the standard greedy design to approximately 4.57 × 10^-2 with the modified design, an improvement of about 2.7 percent.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest using locations assigned weight one by the relaxed optimum, preventing the greedy update from reintroducing locations assigned weight zero, and performing the global-informed update less often to improve efficiency.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method across other inverse problems and compare it with additional design algorithms and criteria. It could also evaluate practical placement constraints and validate the gains using measurements from real experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper presents a method for sequential Bayesian experimental design (BED) that learns a policy to choose experiments over time, aiming to maximize expected information gain (EIG) about unknown model parameters. It focuses on non-exchangeable experiments, where outcomes follow Markovian dynamics and each design can depend on the experiment history. The proposed Inside–Out Nested Particle Filter (IO-NPF) uses a recursive nested particle-filter procedure, with particle jittering, and adds backward sampling to reduce trajectory degeneracy. The authors prove consistency under stated technical conditions and report a simulation study using a stochastic pendulum. In that study, IO-NPF with backward sampling achieves higher information gain than the earlier particle-filter method while reducing its amortization-iteration runtime.
narrate.key_results: The authors report computational complexity of O(NMT) for IO-NPF, compared with O(NMT²) for IO-SMC2. In the 50-experiment pendulum simulation, IO-NPF with backward sampling achieved an EIG estimate of 3.47 ± 0.18, compared with 3.35 ± 0.20 for IO-SMC2 and 3.54 ± 0.20 for the exact IO-SMC2 baseline; the random policy achieved 1.37 ± 0.08. The reported runtime per amortization iteration was 2.73 ± 0.07 seconds for IO-NPF with backward sampling, 5.71 ± 0.08 seconds for IO-SMC2, and 1.36 ± 0.04 seconds for exact IO-SMC2. Without backward sampling, IO-NPF had an EIG estimate of 2.98 ± 0.19 and runtime of 0.34 ± 0.01 seconds; results were reported as means and standard deviations over 25 seeds.

key_equations.name: Computational complexity

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their approach, like IO-SMC2, requires the Markovian outcome likelihood to be known, which may not be available in some applications. They also say they aim to derive stronger non-asymptotic error bounds for IO-NPF, including results that use recent work on backward-sampling stability.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison is limited to a simulated, conditionally linear-Gaussian pendulum setting with a Gaussian parameter prior, so it does not establish performance in other application domains or under nonconjugate models. Runtime is reported for a single amortization iteration, and the paper does not provide a broader study of total training cost or of how the method performs under practical design constraints beyond the pendulum setup.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose addressing settings where the Markovian outcome likelihood is unavailable. They also propose deriving stronger non-asymptotic error bounds for IO-NPF, particularly by incorporating results on backward-sampling stability.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the method with additional design objectives and outcome models, and evaluate it in real experiments rather than only the simulated pendulum. It would also be useful to assess the method under operational constraints on allowable designs and to report the total computational cost of training and sequential deployment.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a variant of approximate D-optimal design for polynomial regression and parameter estimation. Instead of using only the usual information matrix, its criterion combines information matrices that incorporate polynomials describing the design space and its boundary. For the unit ball, unit box, and canonical simplex, the authors show that the equilibrium measure is optimal at every degree and dimension. A finite design can therefore be constructed as a positive-weight cubature that matches the equilibrium measure's moments through degree 2n. The resulting sequence of atomic designs converges to that measure, while for other compact basic semi-algebraic design spaces the paper gives an optimization relaxation and an asymptotic connection to the equilibrium measure.
narrate.key_results: For the unit ball, unit box, and canonical simplex, the equilibrium measure is optimal for the proposed criterion at every degree and dimension; any positive-weight cubature exact through degree 2n gives an optimal finite design. In the disk example at degree 4, the proposed design has 9 support points, 5 of them interior, whereas the standard D-optimal design shown has 9 points with only 1 interior point. In the two-dimensional simplex example at degree 4, the standard design has 6 points, while the proposed design has 9, including 8 boundary points and 1 interior point. For the unit interval at degree 16, the proposed design uses the 9 roots of a degree-9 Chebyshev polynomial; the paper reports no efficiency percentages or real-experiment prediction results.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say that the statistical comparison between their criterion and the classical D-optimal criterion remains to be investigated. narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper provides theoretical results and a small number of illustrative numerical comparisons, but does not evaluate estimator variance, prediction performance, or implementation in a real experiment. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify comparison with the classical D-optimal criterion from a statistical perspective as future work. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare estimator and prediction performance under the proposed and classical criteria across realistic noise models and constrained design spaces. Further work could also test the method in physical experiments and develop software that automates cubature construction while reporting numerical stability and run requirements.

narrate.summary: The paper develops an adaptive method for allocating a campaign’s daily advertising budget across its ad lines to maximize expected returns. It treats each campaign as a combinatorial bandit task and shares information across campaigns through a Bayesian hierarchical model. A shared feature-based reward function is combined with an ad-line-specific random effect to represent differences not explained by available features. The method discretizes budget shares and uses Thompson sampling to balance trying uncertain allocations with using promising ones. In offline simulations and an online advertising experiment, the authors report higher click performance or lower cost per click than the existing system.
narrate.key_results: In simulations averaged over 100 random seeds, the proposed method achieved approximately 18% more clicks than the existing Hibou system in the concurrent-campaign setting and 16% more in the sequential setting. The concurrent simulation used 50 campaigns with five ad lines each; the sequential simulation used campaigns with five ad lines lasting 50 days each. In the online randomized comparison, 3% of an active campaign’s budget was used across 30 constructed campaigns containing 300 ad lines in total. After three weeks, the proposed method had reduced cost per click by 12.7% compared with standard practice.

They also assume independence between campaigns, although internal competition for limited ad resources can make separate campaign optimization fall short of a global optimum.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The offline comparisons use simulated rewards generated from a fitted model based on campaign data, so the reported advantages may depend on how well that model represents actual rewards. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to contextual bandits that incorporate temporal factors such as week of the month, day of the week, and holidays. They also identify modeling internal competition across campaigns as worthwhile for pursuing a global optimum.

The method could also be assessed under practical allocation constraints beyond its discretized budget shares, including whether coordinated decisions across campaigns improve outcomes when campaigns compete for resources.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential experiment-design method to characterize soft material properties from cavitation bubble dynamics. It uses inertial microcavitation rheometry (IMR) simulations and chooses experimental settings by maximizing expected information gain (EIG), with Bayesian optimization (BO) searching for informative settings. Material properties and constitutive models are inferred from bubble-radius measurements using an ensemble-based four-dimensional variational method (En4D-Var) and Bayesian model probabilities. In synthetic polyacrylamide (PA) hydrogel examples, the approach identifies material properties and distinguishes between competing models in a small number of sequential designs.
narrate.key_results: For the synthetic stiff-gel case, material-property relative error reaches about 1% within 10 sequential designs, and the paper reports model correctness above 99% within the same number of experiments. At one reported design, the generalized quadratic Kelvin–Voigt model has probability 0.999 while the Neo-Hookean Kelvin–Voigt model has probability 0.001; at another design, their probabilities are 0.587 and 0.413. For the synthetic soft-gel case, 12 designs characterize the underlying model and properties; compared with random designs, the information-based designs improve viscosity estimation and give comparable shear-modulus results. A design with 15 optimization trials and 1,000 EIG samples, followed by data assimilation, requires approximately 200 CPU hours for the quadratic model and an additional 200 CPU hours for the Neo-Hookean model.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their data-assimilation method is most effective when material properties follow a multivariate normal distribution, and that performance deteriorates when this assumption does not hold. The numerical examples restrict the candidate model library and experimental settings, which may limit how well the reported efficiency transfers to other materials, model sets, or practical design constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest assessing test samples in advance to help balance the constraints of the material-property distributions against the measurements needed for posterior estimation. narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the sequential designs in real cavitation experiments and compare predicted information gains with observed parameter and model improvements. Further work could also test other constitutive-model libraries and experimental constraints, and assess whether designs can be updated during an experiment as measurements arrive.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a sequential design method for maximum a posteriori (MAP) parameter estimation in linear structural dynamics, using frequency response data. To reduce costly evaluations of the structural model, it represents each response with a rational polynomial chaos expansion (RPCE), constructed as a ratio of polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs). Sparse Bayesian learning estimates the surrogate coefficients and their uncertainty, while Bayesian optimization adds new model evaluations at points selected using expected improvement (EI). The method is demonstrated on a two-degree-of-freedom system with simulated measurements and on a cross-laminated timber plate using measured data. In both examples, adaptive sampling produces more accurate MAP estimates than a fixed experimental design at comparable run sizes.
narrate.key_results: For the three-parameter two-degree-of-freedom example, with 15 initial evaluations and a budget of 50, the active method's global reward estimate had a median relative MAP error of 2.8 × 10^-5, compared with 2.2 × 10^-2 for the fixed-design RPCE estimate. The global reward estimate reached an error on the order of 10^-4 from about 35 training samples, while the simple reward estimate converged less accurately. In the four-parameter timber-plate example, with a budget of 35 evaluations, the global reward estimate had a median error on the order of 10^-4, compared with about 10^-2 for fixed design. The authors report that including surrogate-model error in expected-improvement sampling slightly improves accuracy, with little added cost.

narrate.summary: The paper develops bounds on causal treatment effects in randomized factorial experiments when some participants do not take up their assigned treatments. It focuses on the average main effect of one focal factor among participants who would comply with that factor under every assignment of the other factors. The authors derive the bounds, study them in simulations, and illustrate them using an experiment of cognitive behavioral therapy and cash transfers in Liberia. Under the stronger assumptions used in prior work, the point estimates were -0.096 for therapy and -0.015 for cash, both inside the corresponding bounds. In simulations with 2 and 5 factors, average bound widths fell as the proportion of perfect compliers increased: for proportions of 0.2 and 0.9, widths were 0.351 and 0.084 with 2 factors, and 0.696 and 0.154 with 5 factors. narrate.summary: The paper develops a method to reduce the input and output dimensions of a nonlinear model together, with particular attention to Bayesian optimal experimental design (BOED). An alternating eigendecomposition updates the input and output subspaces, while goal-oriented sensitivity analysis is another application of the framework. For the Burgers’ equation sensor study, they used 1,000 prior samples, selected 10 sensors, and evaluated EIG using 30 inner samples and 1,000 outer samples; the proposed sensor sets almost always had higher EIG than 250 random placements. The proposed selections generally performed similarly to sensors from the Fedorov–Wynn method, and outperformed that comparison for two of the reported goals where model linearization could be inaccurate. narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for causal inference and experimental design when people’s outcomes can be affected by other people’s treatments through a network, but the network is only partly observed. The approach uses a structural causal model for outcomes and estimates the missing network structure with a generative graph model. It averages estimating equations over possible networks to estimate outcome-model parameters and supports inference for effects such as the global average treatment effect. For experimental design, it uses Bayesian optimization to select cluster treatment saturation levels that reduce estimator variance, and it also constructs model-based seeding strategies. Semi-synthetic studies based on village networks in India and Malawi show that partial-network methods can estimate effects and improve treatment allocation, although results depend on the assumed outcome and network models.
narrate.key_results: In semi-synthetic studies of the global average treatment effect, the aggregated relational data approach reduced estimation bias and error compared with difference-in-means and Horvitz–Thompson estimators, although regression using the full network performed best. For estimating the diffusion parameter alpha one, optimized designs using partial network data reduced root mean squared error by 38% (plus or minus 12%), compared with an 11% (plus or minus 2%) reduction for optimized designs with complete network data, both relative to uniform random designs. Across all model parameters, the corresponding reductions were 45% (plus or minus 10%) and 18% (plus or minus 2%). In the complex-contagion seeding study, the reported optimal strategy increased adoption by 1.50 times (plus or minus 0.16) relative to degree-based seeding; optimal blocks alone achieved 1.13 times (plus or minus 0.12), and selecting high-degree nodes within blocks achieved 1.28 times (plus or minus 0.13).

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that valid inference and causal identification require correctly specified exposure maps, confounders, outcome models, and graph models; misspecification can introduce bias. They also note that their analysis focuses on outcomes at a single time point, and that their graph-misspecification bound depends on good alignment between observed traits and latent clusters.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluations are semi-synthetic: they use observed village networks but simulate outcomes, so they do not establish performance in a prospective field experiment with real outcomes. The design search is also restricted to cluster saturation levels and depends on estimated models and repeated network simulations, so its practical value may differ when treatment constraints or network-estimation uncertainty are more complicated.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose semiparametric estimation with partial network data and further structured assumptions on potential outcomes. They also suggest extending the work to panel data and staggered rollouts, and developing outcome models that represent temporal dynamics more explicitly.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective validation of the design and seeding procedures in field experiments, comparing planned effects with observed outcomes. Further work could also test designs under operational constraints such as unequal treatment costs, limited cluster capacity, and changing saturation decisions as outcome data arrive.

narrate.summary: This paper develops fixed-budget experimental designs for multi-fidelity computer experiments that use an autoregressive Gaussian process model. It extends the model to infinitely many fidelity levels by representing each level as the previous level plus an independent response increment whose variance decreases geometrically. The proposed multi-level Gaussian process (MLGP) design allocates runs across nested fidelity levels to reduce integrated prediction error under a cost budget. Its run allocations are derived from an error bound and use a simple construction rather than a numerical search over designs. The authors’ theoretical analysis and simulation studies support lower cost or improved prediction accuracy compared with the single-fidelity and other multi-fidelity designs they examine.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that, asymptotically, the proposed design reaches a given prediction accuracy with lower cost order than any single-fidelity design under their assumptions. In the one-dimensional misspecification studies, mean root mean squared error (RMSE) was 0.2831 for MLGP versus 0.3441 for the classical multi-fidelity method and 0.3789 for the single-level method with a misspecified variance-decay parameter; with a misspecified smoothness parameter, the respective errors were 0.1652, 0.2127, and 0.2064. In the two-dimensional study, average RMSE was 0.1510 for MLGP, 0.1735 for the multi-fidelity comparison, and 0.1658 for the single-level design. In higher-dimensional studies, MLGP had average RMSEs of 0.3702 versus 0.4621 in dimension 4, and 1.074 versus 1.181 in dimension 8, compared with the single-level design.

key_equations.explanation: Here y_i is the response at level i, x is an input location, y_-1 is the zero starting response, δ_i is the level increment, GP denotes a Gaussian process, λ controls the decay in increment variance, σ is a scale parameter, and Φ is the shared correlation function; the increments are mutually independent.

key_equations.explanation: Here n_i is the run count at level i, C_i is the cost per run at that level, K is the highest included level, and ε is the required prediction-error tolerance; the objective minimizes total simulation cost.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical comparisons are based on simulated Gaussian-process response functions, with a limited set of dimensions, parameter settings, and competing designs; the paper does not validate the method on real computer-code experiments. narrate.summary: This paper develops design-based causal inference methods for experiments with multiple treatments when it is not practical to assign every treatment within every block. It studies incomplete block designs and the balanced incomplete block design, assuming fixed potential outcomes and the stable unit treatment value assumption. The design assigns treatment subsets to blocks in one randomization stage, then assigns units within each block to the treatments in that subset. The authors derive Horvitz–Thompson and Hájek estimators, a finite-population central limit theorem, and conservative variance estimators, and compare them with an additive linear-model estimator. Their main conclusion is that incomplete block designs are practical options, while the design-based estimator is less dependent on assumptions about treatment effects across blocks than the adjusted alternative.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, the authors used 10,000 random assignments per setting and varied the number of blocks across 10, 20, 50, and 100; for a nominal 95% confidence level, coverage tended to be low with 10 blocks and approached or exceeded 95% as the number of blocks increased. Under an additive outcome model, the adjusted estimator could be more precise than the design-based estimator when between-block variability was sufficiently large, but that advantage diminished or reversed as treatment-by-block interaction increased. In the Tennessee STAR data illustration, averaged over 500 reconstructed assignments using all blocks, the balanced design gave a block-level effect estimate of 11.290 with estimated standard error 4.030 for the design-based estimator, compared with 11.097 and 3.422 for the adjusted estimator. For the unbalanced incomplete design using all blocks, the design-based block-level estimate was 12.369 with estimated standard error 3.607; these are illustrative reconstructions from an existing experiment, not results from a newly randomized incomplete-block trial.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their asymptotic results require the number of blocks to increase while the number of treatments and the set of treatment subsets stay fixed; they do not cover settings with a fixed number of blocks and increasing block sizes. Their variance estimators also require sufficient replication: treatments must appear in at least two blocks, and some variance estimators additionally require treatment pairs to co-occur in at least two blocks and at least two units per assigned treatment within each block.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulation comparisons use a particular balanced design and a limited family of generated potential-outcome patterns, so they do not establish performance across the range of block structures and outcome behavior encountered in practice. The data illustration reconstructs incomplete designs by reallocating treatment subsets and dropping classrooms from an existing study, rather than evaluating an experiment originally randomized under those designs.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the framework to generalize beyond the experimental units, including studying random sampling of blocks or units within blocks and using weighting methods. They also propose incorporating covariate adjustment to improve efficiency and generalizability.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could develop design-selection procedures that account for operational constraints such as unequal treatment costs, limited capacity, and required treatment comparisons, while ensuring the variance estimators remain usable. Software and validation in prospective experiments would help assess whether the reconstructed-data findings and theoretical coverage behavior carry over to routine practice.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes an adaptive design of experiments (DoE) method for selecting runs to build accurate metamodels of unknown functions, including when experimental results contain noise. The method uses a Higher-Order Local Maximum Entropy Scheme (HOLMES) metamodel and selects new points by combining measures of curvature, distance from existing points, and estimated metamodel error. It can recommend a batch of distinct runs by updating the spacing measure after each proposed point. The authors also introduce an estimate of local node spacing that accounts for uneven point distributions and domain boundaries. In numerical tests, the method reduced prediction error faster than full factorial and latin hypercube designs in selected examples, and showed greater noise resistance than a comparable adaptive method.
narrate.key_results: For the two-dimensional Gaussian hill example, the design started with a 5 by 5 full factorial grid; adding 8 adaptive points reduced the reported error by a factor of 5. In comparisons on that example, the adaptive design reduced error more quickly than full factorial design and latin hypercube sampling; the latin hypercube results were averaged over 100 tests. In a noise comparison using 36 initial points and 40 batches of 4 points, the proposed method had lower error than the Mackman adaptive method as noise increased, with the difference becoming notable at moderate noise levels. For the time-varying wave example, adaptive designs improved accuracy by around 10–15% over the full factorial design when point placement was updated frequently; the advantage diminished with longer update intervals.
