narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that HOLMES derivative estimates are distorted near domain boundaries, so they exclude a region close to the boundary from point selection; this can be problematic when the region of interest is itself near a boundary. HOLMES may also become difficult to solve for highly clumped data, and the authors note practical convergence problems as dimension or polynomial order increases. For time-dependent use, future projection is only suitable over short intervals and depends on the accuracy of the projection; physical experiments may not allow enough time to run the algorithm and reposition measurement equipment.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Most evaluation is on two-dimensional analytical functions and simulated noise, so the results do not establish performance on real industrial experiments or high-dimensional problems. Performance depends on the initial design and on choosing the spacing parameter, while the boundary exclusion can leave important regions under-sampled; the paper does not evaluate these effects under practical factor constraints or varied experimental budgets.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose adapting the method to solve partial differential equations, especially in particle-based continuum mechanics simulations such as smoothed particle hydrodynamics, where it could dynamically increase resolution during a simulation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further research could test the method in real physical experiments, higher dimensions, and designs with operational restrictions such as cost, safety, or discrete factor settings. It would also be useful to compare alternative selection criteria and initial designs, and to assess reliable automated choices for tuning parameters and updating runs sequentially.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a sequential method for choosing monitoring-well locations for carbon dioxide (CO2) sequestration. Its objective is to select locations that maximize expected information gain (EIG) about the uncertain CO2 plume, while also learning a conditional normalizing flow to infer the plume from observations. The BEACON method jointly trains the inference model and a probability density for well locations, using fluid-flow simulations to generate training examples. The authors test it in a synthetic digital-twin case study with realistic permeability models and compare it with randomly selected well locations. They report reduced plume uncertainty and consistently lower inference errors for optimized placement in that study.
narrate.key_results: The synthetic case study used four sequential iterations, with one optimized well drilled at each iteration. The authors compared the resulting placements with randomly selected well locations and evaluated inference using the RMSE between the posterior mean and the known synthetic ground truth. They report that optimized placement consistently produced lower errors than the random-placement baseline and reduced uncertainty in the plume inferences. The paper does not report exact numerical error values in the text.

narrate.summary: This paper develops locally determinant-optimal subsampling designs for estimating the parameters of a Poisson regression model with a log link and one covariate. The design is built using the assumed covariate distribution and a specified value of the regression slope, and selects a fixed proportion of the covariate distribution to maximize information. For a negative slope, the optimal support is either one interval or a left-tail interval together with a second finite interval; units in the support can be selected deterministically when their covariate values are known. The authors derive how the design changes under location and scale transformations and give numerical examples for exponential and uniform covariates. Their comparisons show that the optimal design can substantially outperform uniform or heuristic subsampling at small subsampling proportions, although performance can decline when the slope used to construct the design is misspecified.
narrate.key_results: For exponentially distributed covariates, the paper reports that uniform random subsampling and the one-sided and two-sided heuristic designs have low efficiency at subsampling proportions of 0.1 or less in relevant settings; the one-sided and two-sided heuristics can be less efficient than uniform sampling at very small proportions. For a two-sided heuristic under the exponential model, reported efficiency is 0.07974506 near a slope-to-rate ratio of negative 3.64 and 0.9988009 near negative 0.40. With the exponential model and a nominal slope-to-rate ratio of negative 1, the locally optimal design retains efficiency above 0.98 at a subsampling proportion of 0.01 when the true ratio is negative 0.8 or negative 1.2. For larger parameter deviations, particularly when the true ratio is closer to zero, the reported efficiency can fall substantially; the numerical illustrations cover exponential and uniform covariate distributions rather than real experimental data.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a Bayesian design method for nonlinear models when the experiment is intended to improve predictions rather than estimate model parameters for their own sake. Its objective is to choose the design with the greatest expected information gain about predictive quantities of interest. The method uses nested sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo to draw parameter samples after simulated observations, kernel density estimation to approximate predictive densities, and Bayesian optimization to search the design space. Tests include nonlinear examples and a simulated sensor-placement problem for a convection-diffusion field. The results show that designs selected for predictions can differ substantially from designs selected to learn parameters.
narrate.key_results: The standard nested-sampling settings were 1,000 outer and 1,000 inner samples; in one-dimensional tests, increasing both counts to 2,000 and 3,000 reduced variation while preserving the general utility trends and optimal design locations. In a non-bijective prediction example, the parameter-information optimum was at design value 1.0, while the prediction-information optimum was around 0.2, demonstrating that the two objectives can select different designs. For the convection-diffusion example, the neural-network surrogates had reported testing mean-squared errors around 10^-6 and 10^-7 for the two modeled times and accelerated each forward-model evaluation by about 10^5 times compared with the finite-volume solver. In the computational cost tests, at 1,000 outer and inner samples, the sampling share of per-iteration cost exceeded 65% and increased toward 100% as dimension increased; in the one-dimensional sample-size test, that share fell from about 80% at 1,000 inner samples to about 40% at 4,000.

key_equations.explanation: Expected utility U at design d is the average, over observations y at that design, of the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the predictive density p of z after observing y and its prior predictive density.

key_equations.name: Nested sampling estimate
key_equations.explanation: The estimated utility is an average over nout simulated observations and nin posterior predictive samples per observation, using estimated posterior and prior predictive densities for z.

key_equations.name: Optimal design
key_equations.explanation: The optimal design d star is the design in the design space D that maximizes expected utility U.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method depends on Markov chain Monte Carlo and kernel density estimation. Sampling can be slow for complex posterior distributions and high-dimensional parameter spaces, leading to high estimator variance; finite density-estimation error and imperfect bandwidth tuning can bias utility estimates and shift the selected design, while frequent bandwidth retuning is expensive.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The sensor-placement examples use simulated model outputs and a trained surrogate, so they do not establish performance with field measurements or model error in an operating environmental system. The design examples also do not evaluate practical placement constraints such as sensor access, cost, minimum spacing, or restrictions on allowable locations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose more efficient information-gain estimation using methods such as Gaussian mixture models, transport maps, and normalizing flows. They also propose deriving and optimizing bounds on information gain and developing density-ratio estimators that can handle implicit likelihoods.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could incorporate installation costs, inaccessible regions, and minimum distances between sensors directly into the design search, then test the resulting designs in real monitoring systems. It would also be useful to evaluate sequential redesign after observations arrive and to assess how errors in the convection-diffusion model or its surrogate affect the selected sensor locations.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a cost-efficient batch-sequential design for estimating two parameters in a binary response model with a complementary log-log link. It is motivated by switching measurements on Josephson junctions, where changing the current-pulse setting takes substantial time compared with a measurement. The authors use the dynamic programming principle (DPP) to choose when to update covariates, using a two-point D-optimal design and an approximate model for information growth. narrate.summary: This paper designs sequential experiments to improve Gaussian process (GP) surrogates used in Bayesian inverse problems, where costly computer models link unknown inputs to observed outputs. Its objective is to reduce prediction uncertainty in regions that matter to the posterior distribution of the inputs. It proposes Inverse Problem Stepwise Uncertainty Reduction (IP-SUR), which minimizes the expected future value of a posterior-weighted uncertainty measure, and Constraint Set Query (CSQ), which maximizes predictive uncertainty within a region near the posterior maximum. The methods are intended to refine an existing surrogate rather than build its initial training set. Across three simulated test cases, both methods generally outperform standard D-optimal and I-optimal designs; IP-SUR also has a theoretical guarantee of almost sure convergence for its uncertainty measure.
narrate.key_results: The methods were tested for 20 added points per design strategy, with 100 repetitions and an initial training set of 10 input-output pairs. Average runtime per test case was 16, 14, and 18 seconds for CSQ, versus 235, 265, and 1,676 seconds for IP-SUR; the corresponding D-optimal runtimes were 3, 2, and 16 seconds, and the I-optimal runtimes were 136, 92, and 440 seconds. Both proposed methods generally improved the reported uncertainty and posterior-comparison measures more than D-optimal and I-optimal designs, particularly for the bimodal and four-dimensional neutron-noise cases. Against the Bayes-risk design of Sinsbeck and colleagues, the authors report broadly similar performance for the banana-shaped and neutron-noise cases, and more reliable results for their methods in the bimodal case; IP-SUR alone has the stated convergence guarantee among these compared methods.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say the proposed methods are for fine-tuning a surrogate and should not be used to construct its initial training set. IP-SUR is computationally more intensive than CSQ, while CSQ has no convergence guarantee and its performance can depend substantially on the chosen region-width parameter. The methods are developed for GP surrogates; the authors note that approximating the criterion for other surrogate types could jeopardize the convergence guarantee.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evaluation uses simulated examples, including an analytical approximation for the neutron-noise application, rather than a real experiment or a full transport-model run. The comparisons cover three cases, only 20 added points per strategy, and a limited set of competing designs, so the results may not establish performance across other model structures, input dimensions, or operational constraints. IP-SUR also depends on posterior sampling and costly optimization, which may limit its practicality when those computations are themselves difficult.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring the method with surrogate models other than Gaussian processes, including approximate evaluation of the criterion, and investigating the robustness of such approximations and their effect on convergence guarantees. They also present a tempered version connecting the inverse-problem criterion to integrated mean squared prediction error as a possible extension.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate both designs on real engineering experiments and on cases where observations, priors, or the surrogate model are misspecified. It would also be useful to study practical constraints such as restricted or batch runs, sequential updating with changing observations, and ways to reduce the posterior-sampling and optimization burden.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) method for selecting a fixed number of observations from a larger candidate set. Its objective is to maximize mutual information (MI) between the selected observations and unknown model parameters, which is also an expected measure of information gained about the parameters. The proposed logarithmic Sobolev inequality greedy (LSIG) method uses an inequality to bound information gain and then selects observations greedily using score and covariance matrices. This avoids repeatedly estimating MI during selection, a costly step for nonlinear, non-Gaussian models. Simulations show that LSIG is competitive with greedy selection based on nested Monte Carlo (NMC) MI estimates, and can outperform a Gaussian approximation in the nonlinear examples.
narrate.key_results: For the linear Gaussian example with 50 parameters and 50 candidate observations, LSIG produced MI values nearly indistinguishable from standard greedy selection, while random selection performed worse. In the epidemic example, the goal was to select 10 of 50 time points; LSIG and NMC-greedy had similar MI, and both outperformed the Gaussian approximation, which was only comparable to or slightly better than random selection. In the spatial Poisson example, which had 25 candidate cells and selected up to 10, LSIG’s MI exceeded the Gaussian approximation for every tested design size and exceeded NMC-greedy except at sizes 1 and 2. The reported leading costs are O(Mm) sample draws and model evaluations and O(nk³) linear algebra for LSIG, compared with O(nkMinMout) sample draws and model evaluations for NMC-greedy and O(nk⁴) linear algebra for the Gaussian approximation; for the nonlinear experiments, LSIG used 1,000 joint samples and 1,000 prior samples, whereas NMC used 10,000 inner and 1,000 outer samples.

narrate.limitations_stated: The bound relies on reference distributions satisfying the assumptions of the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, and the paper notes that determining the relevant reference measure and constants can be difficult in general. The method also requires gradients of the likelihood and estimates the observation-density score using Monte Carlo; the authors report that neural-network score estimates can make the score-matrix rankings sensitive. The authors state that they do not focus on theoretical optimization guarantees for the greedy procedure.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparisons cover three simulated models, with candidate pools of 50 observations or 25 spatial cells, so performance in larger or real industrial experiments is not established. The method’s rankings depend on estimated score and covariance matrices, but the paper does not provide a systematic study of how sampling error in those matrices changes the selected design or its achieved information.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the approach to implicit models, where only samples are available and the likelihood and its gradient are intractable. They plan to use score-estimation tools that are more consistent and stable.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on real experiments and candidate sets with practical constraints, such as costs, forbidden combinations, or limited measurement capacity. Further work could also evaluate sequential updating and compare alternative design objectives, while quantifying how score-estimation error affects design quality.

narrate.summary: The paper develops rerandomization methods for randomized experiments designed to improve covariate balance while preserving randomization-based inference. It focuses on experiments with covariates grouped by importance, stratified assignments, and multiple treatment arms, with treatment-effect estimation as the objective. The proposed method orthogonalizes contrast groups, calculates a squared Mahalanobis distance for each group, and accepts assignments using a weighted sum of those distances. Under stated asymptotic symmetry conditions, conditionally affinely invariant balance rules have equal percent variance reduction within each group. The authors show that their weighted-distance method is admissible, while common intersection rules can be inadmissible, and illustrate the method using a stratified factorial experiment dataset.
narrate.key_results: The theory shows that conditionally affinely invariant balance rules reduce variance equally across linear combinations within each relevant contrast group, under the paper’s asymptotic assumptions. The authors establish that weighted sums of the group-specific squared Mahalanobis distances form an admissible complete class for minimizing their conditional means, and show that intersection rules using separate thresholds are inadmissible when there is more than one group. In the dataset example, after 1,000,000 rerandomizations with an asymptotic acceptance probability of 0.001, the proposed weighted rule had lower mean distances than the intersection rule in all six groups: 2.16 versus 2.65, 85.34 versus 88.60, 18.86 versus 23.25, 0.99 versus 1.04, 38.13 versus 45.57, and 7.78 versus 12.46. The corresponding means under complete randomization were 8.41, 110.51, 33.89, 4.34, 55.90, and 15.36, respectively.

key_equations.name: Weighted-distance acceptance rule
key_equations.explanation: The acceptance rule phi equals the indicator 1 when the sum over tiers m from 1 to M of each tier’s weight pi_m times its squared Mahalanobis distance D_m is no greater than threshold a.

key_equations.name: Squared distance for a canonical contrast

key_equations.name: Asymptotic distance distribution
key_equations.explanation: As the sample size grows, the distances D_m converge jointly in distribution to independent chi-square variables, with k_m degrees of freedom for tier m.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors evaluate balance criteria at a fixed asymptotic acceptance probability and note that finite-sample imbalance can remain when perfect balance is not achieved. They also note that collecting more covariates adds to experiment costs and identify the trade-off between covariate-collection cost and efficiency gain as future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantees depend on asymptotic central limit and conditional ellipsoidal-symmetry assumptions, so their performance under substantial departures from those assumptions is not established here. The numerical illustration uses one dataset and focuses on the first blocking variable; it does not provide broad comparisons across varied sample sizes, covariate structures, or practical assignment constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing a framework for studying the trade-off between the efficiency gain from covariates and the cost of collecting them.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method under departures from the assumed limiting distributions and under uncertainty in the weights used to prioritize balance groups. It could also assess performance under a wider range of allocation constraints and validate the procedure in additional operational experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for estimating low-rank matrices and for using those estimates in low-rank bandit problems. Its main estimator, LowPopArt, assumes the measurement distribution is known and uses its population covariance to form robust estimates, followed by hard thresholding of small singular values. The authors also choose a sampling distribution by minimizing a covariance-based measure of estimation difficulty, rather than relying only on E-optimality. They use the estimator and design to construct two bandit algorithms for general operator-norm-bounded arm sets. The theoretical results give recovery and regret guarantees that adapt to the geometry of the available arms, and the reported experiments generally favor the proposed estimator and designs over the tested alternatives.
narrate.key_results: For matrix recovery, the paper bounds the operator-norm estimation error by a quantity proportional, up to logarithmic factors, to the noise scale times the square root of design difficulty divided by sample count; the warm-started version achieves this without retaining a large reward-bound term in the final rate. The optimized design has difficulty of order d squared for the unit operator-norm ball and d cubed for the unit Frobenius-norm ball, where d is the larger matrix dimension; its criterion is no worse than the classical covariance-based comparison in the paper and can be much better for a constructed arm set. LPA-ETC has a regret upper bound proportional, up to logarithmic factors, to the cube root of noise variance times the reward bound times rank squared, design difficulty, and horizon squared. Under an additional lower bound on the smallest nonzero singular value, LPA-ESTR has a square-root-in-horizon regret bound; simulations report lower matrix recovery error and cumulative regret than the compared methods, using 60 random instances in the main experiments and also testing a MovieLens-derived setup with 30 repetitions.

key_equations.name: LowPopArt one-sample estimate and recovery guarantee
key_equations.explanation: The one-sample estimate uses the inverse population covariance, response Yi, pilot estimate Theta-zero, and measurement Xi; the final estimate Theta-hat has operator-norm error bounded in terms of noise scale sigma, design difficulty B of Q, and sample count n-zero, up to logarithmic factors.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their general-purpose algorithms can have weaker guarantees than methods tailored to special arm sets, such as the unit Frobenius-norm ball. They identify matching specialized guarantees while retaining generality, and establishing regret lower bounds that depend on arm-set geometry, as open directions; they also leave precise guarantees for estimating the covariance from observed samples as future work.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method’s direct use requires access to the measurement distribution and its covariance, and the design optimization assumes the available arm set is known; the paper does not establish how estimation and design behave when these inputs are inaccurate. The matrix inversion in the estimator scales steeply with both matrix dimensions, while the experiments cover small dimensions and a limited set of simulated or transformed-data settings, so practical performance at larger scales and in real response-generating processes remains uncertain.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose designing algorithms that retain generality while matching the stronger guarantees available for specialized arm sets. They also propose deriving low-rank bandit regret lower bounds that reflect arm-set geometry and analyzing the case where the covariance matrix must be estimated from observations.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test robust or approximate versions of the design when the arm set or measurement distribution is only partially known, including operational constraints on which measurements can be run. Further work could study sequentially updating the sampling design, benchmark the computational cost at larger matrix dimensions, and validate prediction and decision quality on real experiments with actual observed outcomes.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a Bayesian method for choosing how clusters are allocated to intervention sequences in a stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial with binary outcomes. It targets precise estimation of the intervention effect using a generalized estimating equation analysis and a log-variance design criterion. The method averages that criterion over prior distributions for the period effects and intervention effect, while considering simple exchangeable and exponential-decay working correlation structures. The authors use approximate design theory, Latin hypercube sampling, and interior-point optimization to find sequence proportions. They find that allocations can be asymmetric and depend on time trends and correlation assumptions, although simpler normal-approximation designs are often nearly as efficient.
narrate.key_results: For the Washington State trial example with five periods and four sequences, the Bayesian allocations were 0.3493, 0.1761, 0.1780, and 0.2966 under simple exchangeable correlation, and 0.3401, 0.1882, 0.1817, and 0.2900 under exponential decay. The normal-approximation allocation was less than 1 percent less efficient than these Bayesian designs in that example. In the hypothetical settings, balanced allocations could require substantially more clusters than the Bayesian design, especially with smaller cluster-period sizes and low correlation parameters. With strong decreasing time trends, the Lawrie normal-approximation design could require approximately 15 percent more clusters than the Bayesian design for some settings with cluster-period sizes of 50 or 100.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors did not investigate how misspecification of the correlation parameters affects design performance, or how the choice of priors affects the resulting design. They assumed the same number of patients in every cluster-period and considered only cross-sectional designs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method returns approximate sequence proportions, which may not translate directly into feasible integer cluster allocations, especially when the total number of clusters is small. Its Bayesian averaging covers the mean-model parameters, but the correlation parameters are fixed; therefore the result may be sensitive to correlation values that are uncertain in practice.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the method to other outcome types, such as count outcomes, and applying it to optimal sequence weights for cluster crossover trials.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could assess integer allocation strategies and operational constraints, including unequal cluster sizes and restrictions on which sequences can be used. Sequential adaptation and prospective validation against observed outcomes in real trials could also establish whether the proposed allocations retain their efficiency in practice.

narrate.summary: This paper introduces a method for designing sequences of experiments in dynamical systems when the goal is to learn unknown model parameters. It seeks to maximize expected information gain, or the expected reduction in uncertainty about those parameters. The method learns a stochastic policy that chooses each design using the outcomes and designs observed so far. It constructs an inference problem whose target favors informative trajectories, then uses the Inside-Out SMC2 nested particle-filter algorithm and a particle-based optimization procedure to learn the policy. In simulations of pendulum, cart-pole, and double-link systems, the method generally performed better than the tested alternatives, although it did not lead every comparison.
narrate.key_results: In the conditionally linear pendulum, the method’s expected information gain estimate was 3.53 ± 0.15, compared with 2.58 ± 0.17 for implicit deep adaptive design; its exact variant reached 3.63 ± 0.18. For the nonlinear pendulum, the estimate was 3.72 ± 0.17, compared with 3.01 ± 0.29 for implicit deep adaptive design. For the cart-pole, it reached 21.23 ± 0.62, compared with 18.99 ± 0.68 for implicit deep adaptive design; the paper reports obtaining its estimate with 1,024 parameter particles, whereas estimating an sPCE bound near 21 would require about 1.3 billion regularizing samples. For the double-link system, its estimate was 11.53 ± 0.49, slightly below the 11.73 ± 0.45 reported for implicit deep adaptive design. The evaluations used sequences of 50 experiments and reported means and standard deviations over 25 seeds.

They also note that state-dimension scaling may be problematic with the bootstrap proposal and that the choice of the tempering parameter eta remains an open research question. Their analysis gives time complexity O(NMT²), or O(MT³) when accounting for the particle count needed for stability, with the outer particle loop parallelizable.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from three simulated mechanical systems with specified priors and design bounds, rather than experiments on physical systems or a broader range of industrial processes. The comparison also does not establish how robust the learned policies are to misspecified dynamics, prior distributions, or operating constraints that differ from those used in training.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify the choice of tempering parameter eta and its bias-variance trade-off as an open research question. They also suggest that their approach could be useful for other parameter-marginalized smoothing problems and that it could be combined with related particle-based methods.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method with model-misspecification checks, additional dynamical models, and constraints such as safety limits or discrete operating choices. It would also be useful to validate learned policies in physical experiments and assess whether they can be updated efficiently as new data arrive.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a Bayesian nonparametric method for predicting future user activity in online A/B tests. It models daily re-trigger counts with a negative binomial distribution and places a stable-beta scaled-process prior on users’ activity rates. From pilot-period data, the method predicts both the number of new users expected in a future period and future re-trigger activity for new and previously observed users. Its posterior and predictive distributions have closed-form representations, allowing the authors to avoid Markov chain Monte Carlo for these calculations. The authors report that its predictions of future user counts are competitive with existing methods and that it also predicts re-trigger activity, which competing methods considered do not provide.
narrate.key_results: The method derives closed-form posterior and predictive distributions, and the authors describe fitting as computationally inexpensive; they report avoiding Markov chain Monte Carlo. Evaluation included 1,774 production experiments from a technology company and 76 treatment arms from a public dataset, using 7 days of pilot data and predicting 21 days ahead for the production data. On the production experiments and the public dataset, the proposed method was reported as competitive with the best available alternatives for predicting new users; an additional evaluation on 1,340 production comparisons reported that Bayesian nonparametric methods performed best for a 35-day forecast horizon. narrate.summary: The paper develops designs for crossover trials in which each subject provides several correlated responses over multiple periods. Its fixed-effects model includes response-specific period, subject, direct treatment, and first-order carryover effects, and it studies two error covariance structures: proportional covariance and generalized Markov-type covariance. The authors derive information matrices for direct treatment effects and assess Type I, strength 2 orthogonal arrays, including their performance under several covariance patterns. Under proportional covariance, these arrays are trace-optimal within a specified class of binary designs; under Markov-type covariance, they perform very close to an upper bound in the numerical examples. A gene-expression crossover study illustrates that the design used in that study performs poorly compared with an orthogonal-array design.
narrate.key_results: For proportional covariance and equal numbers of periods and treatments of at least 3, a Type I, strength 2 orthogonal array with n = λt(t − 1) subjects is trace-optimal for direct effects among the stated binary designs. For the generalized Markov-type structure, the authors evaluate seven covariance combinations and find the array’s maximum relative difference from their information-trace upper bound is about 0.39% for 3 periods and 3 treatments with 6 subjects, and at most 2.02% for 4 periods and 4 treatments with 12 subjects. In the 18-subject gene-expression example, the existing design’s maximum relative difference is around 99.70%, compared with around 0.38% for the orthogonal-array design under the reported Markov-type comparisons. For the proportional structure, the authors report that the existing gene-study design’s efficiency relative to the orthogonal-array design is around 2.78%.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a model-aware reinforcement learning method for choosing experimental controls in quantum metrology and estimation. For the Dolinar receiver, the neural-network strategy improved on the earlier reported result for both 4 and 8 reference states, and nearly reached the theoretical bound in the paper's main region of interest, at signal amplitude around or below 1 with 4 reference states. narrate.summary: The paper develops a framework for optimal experimental design that selects sensor locations to estimate uncertain parameters in Bayesian inverse problems governed by partial differential equations. The three-dimensional case used 35,937 discretized parameters and selected 8 sensors from 512 candidates; the two-dimensional case selected 10 from 100. For the two-dimensional example with 1,024 training samples, the expected information gain criterion had a mean relative error of 1.81 percent with derivative training, compared with 48.61 percent for a neural network trained without derivatives. narrate.summary: The paper presents two data-driven ways to recommend the assumed effect size used to plan online experiment durations. The second approach chooses an effect size that maximizes expected utility by balancing experiment costs against customer impacts and the accuracy of launch decisions. In simulations and an analysis of Amazon experiments, the mixture approach estimated the positive effect more accurately, while the utility approach achieved the highest reported reward in the real-data analysis.

The reported two-sample test comparing the three-layer and two-layer estimates had a p-value of 0.036. In the analysis of 3,300 Amazon experiments, the utility method achieved the highest average reward, 2.2, and the shortest average duration, 2.3 weeks; the two-layer model achieved reward 2.01 over 3.63 weeks, the three-layer model 1.91 over 3.83 weeks, and pooled maximum likelihood 1.61 over 3.99 weeks. narrate.summary: This paper develops an online Bayesian experimental design method to characterize a three-level transmon system, or qutrit, described by an open-system quantum model. In the simulated study, pulse extension improves estimation of decoherence times, and the method produces accurate population predictions despite parameter uncertainty and finite shots.

The authors report that iterative extension reduces the mean errors in decoherence-time estimates by about an order of magnitude relative to fixed pulse parameterization when parameter uncertainty is present without shot noise; with shot noise, the estimation accuracy is comparable to the fixed approach. narrate.summary: The paper evaluates whether a surrogate index can support faster product decisions than directly measuring long-term treatment effects. It uses real data from 200 Netflix personalization algorithm tests, covering 1,098 test arms. The index is a linear auto-surrogate model that predicts a user's 63-day average outcome from the user's daily outcomes during the first T days, with models trained either on pre-test data or data from a similar test. The authors compare decisions based on 14 days of data with decisions based on direct measurement at 63 days. They report about 95% agreement in statistical conclusions, while the surrogate-based launch decisions recover some, but not all, of the launches identified using the 63-day results.
narrate.key_results: Statistical conclusions from the surrogate index agreed with the 63-day directly measured results about 95% of the time; about 86.5% of surrogate reads and about 79% of 63-day reads were not statistically significant. For decisions to launch based on a positive, statistically significant result, the surrogate approach had 79% precision and 65% recall relative to the 63-day decision. The authors report no case in which the surrogate indicated launch when the directly measured result was statistically negative. They estimate that changing from a 2-month to a 2-week testing cycle could increase experimentation capacity by up to 300%; under their stated assumptions, about 53% more 2-week tests would be needed to achieve the same gains as the 2-month cycle.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The study evaluates agreement with the 63-day estimate, not whether the surrogate decisions are correct relative to the unknown true treatment effects. narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.

narrate.summary: The paper designs the Mixture Adaptive Design (MAD) for adaptive experiments that use bandit algorithms to assign treatments. Its objective is to estimate the average treatment effect (ATE) while allowing ongoing monitoring and data-dependent stopping. At each assignment, the design mixes the chosen bandit algorithm with randomized assignment, using a deterministic sequence to set the balance between learning and reward. The authors derive an asymptotic confidence sequence and theoretical conditions under which its width shrinks and it eventually excludes zero when the long-run effect is nonzero. Simulations show that the design can support monitoring while retaining rewards closer to a bandit than to a purely randomized design.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 100 replicates and up to 10,000 assignment steps, the authors report empirical anytime coverage near the intended 95% level for the MAD across their main Bernoulli-outcome examples; the standard bandit comparison did not maintain coverage when the effect was nonzero. The MAD’s interval width and stopping behavior were generally similar to the Bernoulli design, while its average reward was closer to the standard bandit. In a stopping-rule comparison, the Bernoulli design stopped at most 88 steps earlier than the MAD in the high-effect setting and at most 3,895 steps earlier in the low-effect setting; the median stopping-time differences were 0 and 275 steps, respectively. The study also reports that intervals based on the compared non-asymptotic method were generally wider and stopped later, while Cauchy-outcome examples could be unstable because the treatment-effect mean is undefined.

narrate.limitations_stated: The theoretical results assume bounded realized potential outcomes and cumulative conditional variances that grow at least linearly. The finite-stopping-time result for excluding zero additionally assumes that the average treatment effect converges to a nonzero value. The authors note that their asymptotic confidence sequence does not itself provide exact finite-sample error control, and that the exact alternative discussed requires assignment probabilities bounded away from zero and one.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evidence comes from simulations with selected outcome models, algorithms, and mixing schedules rather than real online experiments, so it does not establish performance under operational constraints or across the full range of bandit algorithms. The paper gives examples of choosing the mixing sequence but does not optimize it for a specified reward-versus-precision target or report a broad sensitivity analysis of that choice.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the design in real experiments and under operational constraints such as delayed outcomes, clustered assignment, or limited treatment capacity. It would also be useful to develop and validate data-driven ways to tune the mixing sequence to a stated precision and reward target while preserving the inference guarantees.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces ExPT, a method for optimizing an expensive black-box objective when only a few scored designs are available. It is designed for few-shot experimental design in a domain where many candidate designs are available without scores. ExPT is pretrained using unlabeled candidate designs and synthetic functions sampled from Gaussian processes, then conditions on the few labeled examples and a specified target score to generate candidate designs. Its transformer encoder and variational autoencoder decoder learn to generate inputs directly rather than optimize a learned prediction of the objective. On the tested benchmark tasks, ExPT generally outperforms the compared methods, particularly when the few labeled examples are deliberately chosen from low-scoring designs.
narrate.key_results: The benchmark experiments used 1% of each task’s public data for few-shot examples, a budget of 256 proposed designs, and averages over 3 runs. In the poorest-data setting, ExPT achieved an average mean score of 0.639, compared with 0.375 for the next-best baseline, which the authors report as a 70% improvement; it led on 10 of 12 task-and-metric comparisons. In the random-data setting, ExPT’s average mean score was 0.614 and its average best-achieved score was 0.888, compared with 0.587 and 0.847, respectively, for the next-best method on those aggregate measures. Sequential sampling also improved results on D’Kitty and Ant; in the poorest Ant setting, it raised median and mean scores by 20% and 19% relative to simultaneous ExPT sampling.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that ExPT assumes access to a larger unlabeled dataset and knowledge of the optimal objective value. They also note that the model is pretrained separately for each domain.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is limited to four Design-Bench tasks with available exact oracles, plus synthetic tests; the paper does not validate ExPT in real physical experiments. Its synthetic pretraining relies mainly on smooth Gaussian-process functions, so target objectives with substantially different structure may be harder to learn despite the reported tests on several other synthetic kernels. Supplying the target optimum and evaluating 256 candidate designs may also be impractical in settings where the optimum is unknown or evaluations are costly.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose relaxing the requirements for a large unlabeled dataset and a known optimal value, fine-tuning the pretrained model on downstream data, and investigating one model that works across domains. They also suggest validation and early stopping using held-out out-of-distribution synthetic functions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method in real experiments and on domains with practical constraints such as safety, feasibility, or limited candidate availability. It could also assess how to use the method when the target score is uncertain and compare adaptive sampling with simultaneous proposals under realistic evaluation costs.

narrate.summary: The paper develops augmented block designs for experiments with unreplicated test treatments and replicated controls, under a fixed-effects model with uncorrelated errors of common variance. It seeks precise estimates of comparisons among controls, among test treatments, and between controls and test treatments, using average-variance and maximum-variance criteria. The authors derive design-independent lower bounds and use the ratio of a bound to a design’s criterion value to assess its efficiency. They evaluate balanced and partially balanced incomplete block designs and their duals, and propose adding or deleting blocks when the required design parameters do not permit equal control replication. The results show that many readily available block designs have high efficiencies and compare well with algorithmically constructed designs.
narrate.key_results: Among the 781 two-associate-class partially balanced incomplete block designs enumerated from Clatworthy’s tables, 505 (65%) met the authors’ high-efficiency thresholds when used as primals, and another 140 met their less stringent thresholds; the corresponding counts for their duals were 542 (69%) and 123. In the large example with 12 controls, 12 blocks, block size 6, and 228 test treatments, the SR68 design had average-variance efficiencies of 0.998, 0.999, and 0.998 for control-control, test-test, and control-test comparisons, respectively. Its maximum-variance efficiencies for those comparisons were 0.978, 0.996, and 0.979, respectively, and it compared favorably with the two algorithmically constructed designs reported by Haines. For designs obtained by adding or deleting blocks in the example with five controls and block size three, the average-variance efficiencies were generally high, ranging from 0.986 to 0.994 for control-control comparisons, 0.997 to 0.998 for test-test comparisons, and 0.994 to 0.995 for control-test comparisons.

key_equations.name: Design efficiency
key_equations.explanation: Efficiency is the ratio of the design-independent lower bound for a criterion to the criterion value for the design being assessed; the equals sign denotes equality and the fraction bar denotes division.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that their efficiency measures can be conservative, particularly the maximum-variance measures when the total number of control plots divided by the number of controls is not an integer. They also state that sharper maximum-variance bounds and direct constructions for that setting need further study.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The derivations rely on the stated fixed-effects model and uncorrelated, homoscedastic errors, so performance under spatial dependence, unequal error variance, or model misspecification is not established. The numerical comparisons focus on selected examples, a catalogue of two-associate-class designs, and an existing algorithmic comparison; they do not report validation in real field experiments or evaluate operational constraints beyond the stated design setup.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying direct constructions when equal control replication is impossible and deriving sharper maximum-variance bounds for that case. They also suggest extending the approach to augmented row-column designs, including space-filling primals, and to fixed-effects models with intraclass or more complex correlation structures.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test these designs in real agricultural trials and assess whether randomization, spatial layouts, missing plots, and other field constraints preserve the predicted efficiencies. It would also be useful to provide practical software for generating and evaluating the designs and to study sequential or adaptive allocation of test treatments.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Gibbs optimal design, a way to plan experiments when inference uses a loss-based Gibbs posterior rather than requiring a fully specified response model. The framework is presented for estimating target parameters, including when the model used for analysis may be misspecified. The designer specifies a loss, a designer distribution for generating possible responses, a distribution for its hyper-variables, and a utility for measuring information about the target parameters. Designs are found by approximating expected utility with Monte Carlo sampling and optimizing it using approximate coordinate exchange. Examples cover linear models, count responses, and time-to-event responses; the authors find that designs avoiding strong response-model assumptions can be less vulnerable when those assumptions are wrong.
narrate.key_results: In a 16-run example with 3 controllable variables and 10 linear-model parameters, the Gibbs designs under the two calibration-weight specifications achieved 85% efficiency relative to the D-optimal design for the reported information criteria; the D-optimal design had no pure-error degrees of freedom, while the Gibbs designs had 6. For the integrated squared-error loss example, the maximum-projection Latin hypercube design achieved 75% efficiency under the negative squared error criterion and 70% under the Shannon information criterion; the Gibbs design optimized for Shannon information achieved 88% under negative squared error, while the negative-squared-error design achieved 45% under Shannon information. In the time-to-event comparison, for run sizes from 10 to 50, the Gibbs design’s efficiency under the Bayesian utility rose from 0.037 to 0.175, while the Bayesian design’s efficiency under the Gibbs utility rose from 0.270 to 0.680. The count-response and time-to-event examples both showed Gibbs designs with more interior design points than their Bayesian-design comparators.

key_equations.explanation: The posterior density pi with subscript ell for parameter t given responses y and design X is proportional to the exponential of negative calibration weight w times loss ell, multiplied by the prior density pi with subscript ell.

key_equations.explanation: The target parameter theta with subscripts ell and D is the value t in parameter space Θ minimizing the expected weighted loss, with expectation taken over responses under designer distribution D indexed by hyper-variables r and design X.

key_equations.name: Gibbs expected utility
key_equations.explanation: The Gibbs expected utility U with subscript G for design X averages utility u over responses from designer distribution D and then over hyper-variables r from distribution C, evaluating utility at target parameter theta with subscripts ell and D.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the framework depends critically on specifying a designer distribution that is flexible enough to plausibly include the true response-generating distribution. They identify the design-dependence of target parameter values and sensitivity to calibration-weight specification as areas needing further investigation. Their proposed computation relies on approximations, including a normal approximation to the Gibbs posterior in the general approach.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The examples use selected simulated or constructed response-generating distributions, so they do not establish how well the method performs in real experiments where the designer distribution may also be misspecified. The paper does not evaluate practical constraints such as restricted treatment combinations or costs, and several examples use numerical optimization and repeated Monte Carlo calculations whose run-time requirements are not reported.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating target parameters with physical interpretations that do not depend on the design, including limits of target parameters as the number of runs grows. They also propose studying sensitivity to calibration-weight specification alongside research on automatic calibration methods, and encouraging developers of Bayesian design computation to extend their methods to Gibbs optimal design.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method in real quality-engineering experiments and compare decisions under a range of plausible designer distributions, including deliberate misspecification. It would also be useful to extend the framework to operational constraints and sequential design, and to provide software that supports implementation and reproducible comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces Gradient-based Survey (GBS), an adaptive paired-choice experiment for designing products with binary attributes. It targets the product with the highest expected choice rate against a baseline, and also extends the method to personalize products using observed respondent information. Instead of assuming a particular parametric utility function, GBS represents product features with Bernoulli random variables and updates their probabilities using a gradient estimated from respondents’ choices. Each question compares two partial product profiles generated using the current design parameters, and the responses guide the next update. Simulations show that the method can find strong designs with fewer respondents than flexible neural-network baselines and can scale to very large feature spaces.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 10 features, GBS identified optimal products across the tested utility types with fewer than 100 respondents; for linear utility, the performance gap from correctly specified models narrowed at around 70 respondents. The neural-network baseline required 500 respondents for the linear case and 4,000 and 2,000 respondents for the two more complex cases. With 100 features, GBS showed a similar performance pattern and identified an optimum from about 10 to the power of 30 possible choices in less than half a minute. In the personalized-product simulation, GBS achieved the highest average test utility among the compared methods, with utility improving as more respondents participated.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that GBS does not estimate a choice model and does not provide a complete ranking of all possible products. They note that explaining preferences may require other tools, such as saliency maps, rather than model parameters that represent preferences.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation is based on simulated data, so the reported efficiency and accuracy have not been established in real choice experiments. Although GBS avoids a parametric representative-utility model, its derivation uses a random-utility framework with independent type I extreme-value errors; the paper does not test how departures from that choice structure affect performance. The paper also does not report practical respondent-fatigue or survey-administration results for repeated adaptive questioning.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest extending the objective to account for product costs and prices, and handling budget constraints with methods such as projected gradient. They also discuss applying GBS to product-line design and identify combining newer discrete-optimization gradient estimators with choice experiments as an interesting future direction.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate GBS in real commercial or field experiments and compare it with established adaptive conjoint designs under the same respondent and survey constraints. Further work could test robustness to different choice-error structures and develop practical stopping rules or respondent-allocation procedures for sequential deployment.

narrate.summary: This paper extends stepwise uncertainty reduction (SUR) sequential experimental design to vector-valued Gaussian processes, with the objective of estimating excursion sets. It develops the connection between continuous vector-valued Gaussian processes and Gaussian measures on spaces of continuous functions, then formulates sequential selection using conditional distributions after noisy observations. The authors establish consistency results for two measures of excursion-set uncertainty: integrated Bernoulli variance (IBV) and excursion measure variance (EMV). Under the paper’s assumptions, both measures converge to zero for designs that approximately minimize expected remaining uncertainty, with the approximation error tending to zero.
narrate.key_results: For vector-valued Gaussian processes and orthant threshold sets, the authors prove that an approximately minimizing SUR design drives both IBV and EMV to zero almost surely. For IBV, the integrated squared difference between the excursion indicator and its estimated probability also converges to zero almost surely and in mean. For EMV, the conditional expected excursion-set measure converges to the actual excursion-set measure almost surely and in mean. These are theoretical results; the paper reports no numerical efficiency, run-size, or prediction comparisons.

key_equations.explanation: The EMV uncertainty H under Gaussian measure ν is the variance, across function paths f drawn from ν, of the μ-measure of locations u in domain X where f(u) belongs to threshold set T.

narrate.limitations_stated: The paper does not treat multi-objective optimization with vector-valued Gaussian processes. narrate.summary: This paper develops optimization methods for constructing D-optimal designs for linear and full quadratic response-surface models with many possible experiments. narrate.summary: This paper develops Bayesian optimal experimental design (OED) for a two-dimensional inverse problem in linear elasticity. The goal is to choose where to apply a finite number of boundary pressure activations so that boundary deformation measurements better estimate the Lamé parameters inside the body. The authors linearize the forward model around background parameter values and assume independent Gaussian prior uncertainty and measurement noise. They derive how measurements change with parameter values and activation positions, then use these derivatives to optimize an A-optimality objective based on posterior uncertainty. Numerical tests show that the proposed search methods reduce the objective, although local minima can prevent them from finding a global optimum.
narrate.key_results: For three activations in the acrylplastic-like case, exhaustive search on a 200-point grid per position found an objective value of 3.93; greedy sequential search gave 4.33, about 10% higher, while sequential search refined by gradient descent gave 4.01, about 2% higher. For ten activations, the basic sequential method gave 0.87, while both the refined sequential method and gradient descent from an approximately equidistant initial design gave about 0.82; the authors report this as about a 6% reduction from the basic method. The three-activation exhaustive search requires a number of evaluations that grows exponentially with the number of activation positions, whereas the sequential search requires a number growing linearly in the number of positions for a fixed grid. The numerical study used 20 measurement sensors, 50 parameter subdomains, and an approximately 1,632-triangle mesh, with the elasticity calculations implemented in COMSOL. For three activations, the optimized objective also varied across the tested background materials: 22.62 for the stiff material, 3.93 for the intermediate material, and 0.12 for the loose material.

narrate.summary: This paper is a systematic review of research on A/B testing in software systems, not a proposal for a new experimental design. It reviews how researchers choose what to test, define variants and measures, assign users, run experiments, and use the results. The authors screened research papers and analyzed 141 primary studies, grouping their findings by test targets, design choices, evaluation practices, stakeholder roles, and open problems. The reviewed studies most often tested algorithms, visual elements, and workflows or processes, using two-variant tests and equality hypothesis tests. The paper identifies opportunities to improve statistical practice, the experimentation process, and automation.
narrate.key_results: The review analyzed 141 primary studies and found that single classic two-variant tests were the most common type, with 95 reported occurrences among 155 test-type occurrences; multi-armed tests had 30 occurrences and sequences of tests had 24. The most frequent targets were algorithms, with 58 occurrences, visual elements, with 33, and workflows or processes, with 28. Equality hypothesis tests were reported 94 times, including 37 cases where the specific test was not named; bootstrapping appeared 11 times. Among reported uses of results, feature selection occurred 71 times and feature rollout 24 times; the review did not report a common sample size or a comparative estimate of design efficiency.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify possible researcher bias in selecting and interpreting studies, incomplete coverage of relevant publications, and the risk that lower-quality studies could weaken conclusions. They describe mitigation steps including a review protocol, cross-checking by multiple researchers, searches across major computer science libraries, citation snowballing, and a study-quality threshold.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is limited to English-language studies found by the authors' specified search strategy, and the search was conducted in October 2022, so relevant work outside that scope or published later may be absent. The reported occurrence counts summarize what papers described; they do not compare designs under common conditions or establish which design performs best, and many studies did not specify their exact statistical method.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further work on improving the experimentation process, including addressing interference between simultaneous tests, improving sensitivity, and providing guidance for choosing and designing metrics. They also call for more automation of experiment design and execution, and for broader use or tailoring of statistical methods such as bootstrapping.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to update the review with newer studies and test whether its patterns hold in application areas less represented than web, search, and commerce. Researchers could also develop and evaluate shared reporting guidance for sample assignment, duration, metrics, statistical methods, and outcomes in real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Scientific Value Function (SVF) for designing experiments whose purpose is to understand an experimental space rather than optimize one specified output. The function converts multidimensional observations, such as diffraction patterns or spectra, into a scalar value based on how distinct they are from existing observations and how close their inputs are to previously measured inputs. The authors use this value as the objective for a Scientific Value Agent (SVA), which combines a Gaussian process surrogate with Bayesian optimization to select measurements. They demonstrate the approach in simulated phase-mapping problems, an emulated temperature study of barium titanate, and a real nanoparticle dataset used for visualization. The simulated tests show roughly an order-of-magnitude improvement over grid search, while the barium titanate example shows that physics-aware observation representations can help direct sampling to subtle transitions.
narrate.key_results: In the simulated one-dimensional and two-dimensional phase-mapping studies, the SVA reduced reconstruction error by roughly an order of magnitude compared with grid search; the sampling comparisons averaged 300 independent experiments. In the two-dimensional example, a 250-measurement campaign concentrated measurements near the periodic phase boundary while still sampling surrounding regions. In the barium titanate study, adding a deep-learned observation representation helped the SVA sample phase changes, but grid search reconstructed the bulk phase compositions as well as or better than the SVA. In a real nanoparticle synthesis dataset of 375 experimental conditions, the SVF highlighted regions associated with stable absorption, gradual change, and dramatic local change, providing a visualization for expert review.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that ordinary distance measures do not capture the subtle barium titanate transitions well: without a deep-learned embedding, the SVA performed on par with conventional methods. narrate.summary: This paper applies multi-fidelity experimental design (MFED) to the WAVI ice-sheet simulator to predict sea-level contribution while reducing the cost of simulation runs. The design uses a Gaussian process (GP) over both the simulator inputs and fidelity, treating fidelity as a continuous dimension and measuring value by reduction in uncertainty about the highest-fidelity output. The authors propose MF-UCB, which selects a lengthscale from its learned posterior using a confidence parameter, then chooses a run by balancing its expected uncertainty reduction against its cost. They analyze the cost-adjusted greedy approach using submodular optimization results and discuss error from uncertainty in the lengthscale. In the available simulation dataset, lower-resolution runs are useful when partial melting is enabled, but not when it is disabled; the paper does not report a prospective run-budget or prediction-accuracy comparison.
narrate.key_results: The study examines pre-existing runs at 5 km and 10 km resolutions, rather than reporting a prospective evaluation of the proposed design. With partial melting enabled, the 10 km runs provide information about the high-fidelity output and are a better cost-adjusted choice, although the paper says the greatest information can come from the higher fidelity. With partial melting disabled, the learned relationship indicates that the lower-resolution runs are not informative, so the uncertainty-reduction criterion disfavors them. A 5 km run costs approximately ten times as much as a 10 km run; the paper reports no numerical prediction-error or total-budget savings comparison against another design.

narrate.summary: The paper studies experimental design for estimating two parameters while controlling the correlation between their estimators. The authors derive properties of a criterion based on the product of the two estimator variances, known as R-optimality, and compare it with familiar criteria and combinations of criteria. They also examine a compound criterion that balances D-optimality and R-optimality. Their comparisons find that R-optimality and standardized A-optimality often reduce correlation while retaining high efficiency, whereas D-optimality alone does not guarantee low correlation.
narrate.key_results: For simple linear regression, the paper reports that the R-optimal design has D-efficiency of at least 0.943, while the D-optimal design has R-efficiency of at least 0.919. In the Michaelis–Menten comparisons at the lower design bound of 0.05, the squared correlation was 0.66 for both R-optimality and standardized A-optimality, compared with 0.69 for D-optimality; the squared-correlation criterion achieved 0.64 but was less efficient on the other criteria. When the design space included zero, the squared-correlation and modified E-optimal criteria gave singular single-point designs. narrate.summary: The paper develops an active Bayesian design method for identifying unknown parameters in quantum many-body systems. It considers a coupled-cavity array, where cavity frequencies are inferred from transmission measurements, and a qubit array, where qubit frequencies are inferred from pulse and projective-measurement experiments. The method represents the evolving parameter distribution with a neural network using a conditional normalizing flow, and selects each next measurement setting by maximizing expected information gain. The authors evaluate it in simulations against fixed, random, and, for the qubit example, uniformly spaced measurement strategies. In both examples, active selection learns system parameters with fewer measurements than the comparison strategies, but the optimization takes substantial computation time.
narrate.key_results: For the simulated array of 6 coupled cavities, active selection learned the cavity frequencies faster than random selection and performed better than measuring repeatedly at one fixed setting; the comparison results were averaged over 3 runs. For the simulated 4-qubit array, each of 100 experiments used 100 repeated measurements to improve outcome statistics. To reach a total information gain of 10 in that example, the authors report that active selection needed about 10 experiments, compared with about 20 for random selection. A uniformly spaced sweep eventually learned the qubit parameters but required more experiments than random selection.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that updating the neural network and optimizing over measurement settings takes on the order of hundreds of seconds per measurement step, making the method uneconomical as implemented for scenarios where measurements take microseconds or extended measurement sequences last around a millisecond. They also note that application-specific assumptions create tradeoffs between approximation accuracy and computation time.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation uses simulated examples of only two particular system types, with known couplings and dissipation in the cavity case and known coupling in the qubit case; it does not validate performance on real devices or under model mismatch. The comparisons are also limited in scope, and the reported strategy results are averaged over only 3 runs, so they provide limited evidence about variability across systems and noise conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose training a neural network policy on simulated scenarios to choose measurement settings more quickly. They also suggest incorporating measurement costs, developing likelihood-free methods, and studying non-greedy strategies that account for a total measurement budget or target information gain. They envision extending the measurement choice to broader experimental setups as part of an autonomous scientific system.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the approach on real quantum devices and measure how robust it is to incorrect system models, drift, and non-ideal measurement noise. Further work could also evaluate practical constraints on settings and resources, and compare the method's parameter estimates and prediction accuracy across a broader range of system sizes and repeated simulation trials.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a method for choosing trial participants and treatment assignments to improve a specified downstream treatment-effect task. It develops the method for binary outcomes and binary treatments, with targets including mean squared error, average treatment effect squared error, area under the Qini curve, and Expected Response Under Proposed Treatments. The method maps features into bins using a variational autoencoder, then uses Bayesian updating and Thompson sampling to choose the next bin and treatment according to a score derived for the chosen target. The authors evaluate it on synthetic data and historical randomized controlled trial datasets from healthcare and marketing. They report that the task-specific designs often outperform randomized trial sampling, with the largest reported advantage on marketing tasks scored by area under the Qini curve.
narrate.key_results: For targeted marketing, the area-under-the-Qini-curve design generally matched randomized controlled trial performance with about an order-of-magnitude smaller sample across the three marketing datasets. For the average treatment effect squared-error task, the authors report a meaningful advantage over randomized trial sampling on three of the four datasets. The real-data evaluations included a stroke dataset of 9,208 rows, a Criteo training pool of 2,992,640 rows with a 4,000,000-row test set, and a RetailHero dataset with 100,036 training rows and 100,000 test rows. Experiments used 384 trials per experiment except for stroke, which used 1,000 trials; uniform sampling in the latent space performed on par with the task-specific design for the Qini-curve task.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method to estimate and test policy effects at different quantiles of outcomes in sequential online experiments. It focuses on temporal and spatial-temporal experiments, motivated by ridesharing policies and heavy-tailed driver income. The method models changing outcomes and states over time, and extends those models to include effects from neighboring regions. Under stated assumptions, the conditional quantile effect on cumulative outcomes equals a sum of effects estimated at individual time points. The authors apply the method to ridesharing field data and simulations, finding evidence of effects that vary across quantiles and regions.
narrate.key_results: In the temporal field experiment, the new policy’s direct effect on driver income was significant at most tested quantiles, with reported p-values from 0.002 to 7e-5 at quantiles 0.3 through 0.9; its indirect effect was not significant at the tested levels. In the experiment with 12 regions, estimated direct effects ranged from 1.566 to 8.414 and indirect effects from 14.153 to 21.320; both were positive at all reported quantiles, though the direct effect was not significant at the 0.1 and 0.2 quantiles. The identical-policy control experiment did not reject the null at any tested quantile. Simulations based on 500 replications reported type-I error rates approximately at the nominal 5% level, with rejection rates approaching 1 as the signal increased to 0.1; the scenarios used 20 or 40 days and time-alternation intervals of 1 or 3. The paper does not compare its method with competing estimators or designs.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential design method for experiments where one of several candidate models is assumed to describe the response, but the correct model is not known in advance. Its objective is to identify the true model while also obtaining high parameter-estimation efficiency under that model. At each stage, the method uses Thompson sampling to select a candidate model's optimal design, combines that design with a uniform design for model checking, and then updates model scores using a model-selection step. The designs from the stages are combined into a final design. The authors prove that, under a condition requiring reliable model selection, its efficiency for the true model approaches that of an optimal design and its model selection becomes consistent.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical results show that the expected number of stages selecting a design for an incorrect model grows at most on the order of log(T), and the expected efficiency has a lower bound approaching one as the number of stages increases. In the dose-response simulations, the method used 10 stages of 15 observations each, and its estimation efficiencies were generally higher than those of the robust, uniform, standard, and hybrid comparison designs; model-selection accuracy was often similar across designs. In the robust parameter design example, with 512 experimental units, the sequential design achieved D-efficiencies above 98% while requiring substantially less budget than the robust design. With 256 observations in that example, its efficiencies were approximately 97% when either M2 or M5 was the true model, and it exceeded the hybrid design at sample sizes of 48 and 80, respectively.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a bit-parallel tabu search (TS) method to find two-symbol supersaturated designs (SSDs) that are optimal under the E(s2) criterion and the minimax criterion. The designs have balanced columns, with equal numbers of plus-one and minus-one entries. The authors show that these designs correspond to resolvable incomplete block designs (RIBDs), allowing the search to work with blocks and their intersections instead of directly manipulating design columns. The search exchanges points between blocks, uses a tabu list to discourage repeated moves, and uses bit operations to speed up intersection calculations. It finds fifteen previously unknown designs with 16, 18, 20, 22, or 24 rows, each achieving the sharpest known E(s2) lower bound while also being minimax-optimal.
narrate.key_results: The bit-parallel TS algorithm found E(s2)-optimal and minimax-optimal SSDs for the fifteen previously unresolved sizes (N, m): (16, 25), (16, 26), (16, 27), (18, 23), (18, 24), (18, 25), (18, 26), (18, 27), (18, 28), (18, 29), (20, 21), (22, 22), (22, 23), (24, 24), and (24, 25). In every case, the designs achieve the sharpest known E(s2) lower bound and have smax no greater than 6. The authors report that bit-parallel intersection calculations improve performance by a factor of N for the cases studied, where N is less than 64. The most difficult reported case, with 16 rows and 27 columns, took 585.4 processor hours; independent parallel searches reduced the elapsed time to 16.1 hours using 40 threads. The authors report that the previous NOAp algorithms did not find these designs despite long searches, while the new algorithm also found the optimal designs those algorithms had found.
