narrate.summary: The paper introduces BO-Muse, a framework for combining a human expert with Bayesian optimization to find good settings for an expensive, unknown objective. At each iteration, the expert and the algorithm each suggest a design; both are evaluated, and the observations are shared to inform the next round. The algorithm uses an upper-confidence-bound strategy and increases its exploration to complement the expert’s presumed tendency to focus on familiar, promising regions. The authors analyze convergence and report sub-linear regret, with faster convergence under assumptions about expert performance. They evaluate the approach on benchmark functions, classifier tuning, and a simulated spacecraft-shield design task.
narrate.key_results: For four synthetic benchmark functions, BO-Muse generally reduced simple regret more effectively than the standard Bayesian optimization baseline and the other reported baselines; these comparisons averaged 10 randomly initialized runs, with a budget of 10 times the function dimension in evaluations. In classifier tuning, 8 participants were divided between the teaming and expert-only groups, with 3 initial designs and 30 further iterations per participant; the authors report that the teamed group outperformed experts working alone on both classification tasks. The classifier experiments used a public biodegradability dataset, and the plotted results also compare the team with an algorithm-only baseline. In the spacecraft-shield study, the design space contained 577,365 options; BO-Muse suggestions inspired an unusual design path, and the expert’s best identified shield weighed 13.8 kilograms per square meter. The theoretical analysis gives sub-linear regret even for arbitrary human suggestions, while faster convergence than either human or algorithm alone is conditional on the stated expert-model and exploration assumptions.

narrate.summary: This paper adapts asymptotic confidence sequences for randomized A/B tests in a commercial experimentation platform. The primary objective is to estimate the average treatment effect while allowing continuous monitoring and stopping based on the accumulating data. The method constructs intervals from arm-level sample means and variances, and also provides an approach for estimating relative effect, or lift, and a sample-size calculator. The authors implemented the method in Adobe products and evaluated it with simulations and thousands of real experiments. They report that it controls type-I error in their evaluations and supports flexible stopping, although it can require more observations than a well-planned fixed-horizon test.
narrate.key_results: In 10,000 simulated A/A tests with binary outcomes and a 10% conversion rate in each arm, the asymptotic confidence sequence kept cumulative type-I error below the 5% target; repeatedly checking a fixed-horizon test did not. For equal power, the authors report that the asymptotic confidence sequence generally needs two to three times the sample size of a fixed-horizon test. Its calculated sample sizes closely matched, and were conservative relative to, empirical sample sizes from 10,000 simulations. narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for off-policy evaluation (OPE) in contextual bandit experiments, where actions may be assigned by a policy that adapts as data arrive. Its objective is to estimate target-policy mean rewards, changing average rewards, and reward distributions while preserving valid uncertainty statements during continuous monitoring. The authors construct confidence sequences (CSs) from importance-weighted outcomes and variance-reducing reward predictions, using martingale-based testing methods. The methods allow predictable, changing logging policies and do not require a known uniform upper bound on importance weights, although each observed importance weight must be finite. The paper is a general inference methodology rather than a procedure for selecting factor settings or optimizing a classical experimental design.
narrate.key_results: The methods provide nonasymptotic coverage at arbitrary stopping times for fixed and time-varying policy values, and simultaneous coverage over time and quantiles for the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of rewards. In the simulations, doubly robust versions produce narrower sequences than importance-weighted versions when rewards are predictable; betting-based sequences are tighter than the closed-form plug-in sequences, while the latter are simpler to compute. For time-varying values, the empirical Bernstein sequence is tighter in the illustrated examples, while the iterated-logarithm sequence has width of order the square root of empirical variance times log-log growth, divided by sample size. The paper illustrates a 90% time- and quantile-uniform CDF band and states that its band is consistent, with an explicit rate of order log of sample size divided by sample size. It reports no general run-size recommendation or aggregate numerical efficiency percentage.

narrate.limitations_stated: The results assume that the target policy is absolutely continuous with respect to the logging policies, so that the importance weights are finite for observed data. narrate.summary: This paper presents a method for attributing the effect of simultaneous randomized online experiments to the individual experiments that produced them. It targets population outcomes, especially engagement, and aims to account for interactions among experiments rather than judging each experiment in isolation. The authors estimate outcomes for different treatment combinations and allocate their overall impact using weighted Shapley cost sharing or an alternative that divides each combination's impact equally among its active experiments. They also describe a conditional version for estimating shared impact within population subgroups. A synthetic example and a large Amazon Music experiment show that weighted Shapley allocation can reveal effects that marginal comparisons or equal sharing obscure.
narrate.key_results: In a synthetic experiment with covariate confounding, inverse propensity score weighting produced less variable, more precise estimates than sample means; equal cost sharing diluted attributed effects toward zero, while weighted Shapley sharing better separated them. The Amazon Music study used millions of observations for three simultaneous experiments run over two weeks in July 2021, and the combined exposure reduced overall click-through rate by 1.27 percent relative to no exposure. All three experiments were active for around 66 percent of the population. Weighted Shapley attribution estimated lifts of −10.19 percent for experiment 0, 7.93 percent for experiment 1, and 0.99 percent for experiment 2; the first two were significant, with reported 95 percent confidence intervals of (−12.31, −7.90) and (4.45, 10.97), respectively, while experiment 2 was not significant. The equal-sharing and marginal estimates were not significant for any experiment, and marginal estimates did not reveal the interaction that made experiment 0's negative effect disappear when the other experiments were also active.

key_equations.explanation: The impact Δ_l attributed to experiment l is the sum over treatment combinations T of their probabilities P(T) multiplied by l's conditional Shapley allocation φ_l^T(v).

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that exact Shapley computation has exponential runtime as the number of parallel experiments grows. They also identify missing treatment combinations as a problem and propose investigating approximation methods and missing-data issues. They state that they withhold exact details of the real-world experiment to protect sensitive business information.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-world demonstration covers three experiments on one platform and one engagement measure, so it provides limited evidence about how well the approach transfers to other settings or outcomes. As the number of experiments increases, the number of treatment combinations also grows, making it harder to obtain observations for every combination and to satisfy the required overlap of treatment assignment across covariates.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying approximate Shapley values and the missing-data issues that arise when some experiment combinations have not occurred. They also suggest combining their approach with newer causal estimation methods, including doubly robust and double machine learning methods.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method on additional platforms, outcomes, and experiment configurations, and assess whether the attributed impacts remain useful when experiments are constrained by operational or user-experience requirements. A practical implementation could also support updating allocations as experiments begin or end and report reproducible analyses while protecting sensitive data.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a computer-oriented method for designing sequential tests that can choose different group sizes as data accumulate. It considers testing two simple hypotheses with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, and aims to reduce sampling cost while controlling the two error probabilities. The design is constructed by backward induction on the likelihood ratio, with a numerical grid and interpolation used to approximate the value functions. For i.i.d. observations, the resulting tests have the form of sequentially planned probability ratio tests (SPPRTs). Examples for Bernoulli data show lower costs than selected existing plans and lower average costs than fixed sample size tests in the scenarios studied.
narrate.key_results: For the Bernoulli majority example, the proposed plan had average sampling cost (ASC) of 11,510, compared with 18,254 for the best plan reported by Schmegner and Baron; the respective average numbers of groups were 2.07 and 9.3, while the proposed plan used 944 observations compared with 892. The paper reports this as nearly 1.6 times lower sampling cost, reflecting the setup cost per group in that example. In the clinical-trial examples, adaptive plans using at most 3 groups had relative efficiencies of 1.13 to 1.41 under the null hypothesis and 1.52 to 1.65 under the alternative hypothesis compared with fixed sample size (FSS) plans; the 5-group example had efficiency 1.66 under the alternative. The clinical-trial comparisons also report savings of about 2 to 3 analyses or patients under the alternative with at most 3 groups, and up to 5 with at most 5 groups, compared with the cited plans.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that appropriate multipliers do not necessarily exist to make both error probabilities exactly equal to specified targets; they also note that discrete binomial probabilities can prevent exact matching. Their numerical results depend on a finite horizon and grid approximation, and they identify a larger horizon, a finer grid, and a denser set of eligible group sizes as possible ways to improve numerical characteristics.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The clinical-trial application reduces the stated composite hypotheses to two simple endpoint hypotheses, so the results do not establish performance throughout the indifference zone. The designs also assume that the observation model and group costs are known and that the eligible group sizes are feasible; practical constraints such as limits on interim analyses or changing recruitment conditions are not incorporated into the examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the method under broader observation models and practical constraints on group size, interim timing, and recruitment. Testing the designs in real clinical or quality-engineering studies would also help assess whether the model-based cost savings hold in practice.

narrate.summary: The paper develops rerandomization and covariate adjustment for split-plot experiments, where one treatment factor is assigned to whole plots and another is assigned to units within those plots. It studies a two-factor, two-level design and targets average treatment effects. The design accepts only allocations whose covariate contrasts meet a Mahalanobis-distance threshold, using either Horvitz–Thompson or Hajek estimates of those contrasts. For analysis, the paper studies fully interacted regression adjustment and introduces a projection adjustment that removes conditional bias associated with covariate contrasts. The theory and numerical examples show that rerandomization improves efficiency, while projection adjustment retains efficiency gains even when covariates vary within whole plots.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that both proposed rerandomization schemes improve the asymptotic efficiency of the corresponding Horvitz–Thompson and Hajek estimators. In simulations with 600 whole plots and 2,000 randomizations, rerandomization and adjustment reduced estimator variability; when covariates varied within whole plots, the projection adjustments improved efficiency while some regression adjustments could make it worse. In the field-experiment illustration, the analysis used 136 subdistricts and 550 villages from a study that began with 608 village projects, and rerandomization was evaluated over 1,000 repetitions. For the audit main effect, rerandomization reduced the Horvitz–Thompson estimator’s standard deviation and average confidence-interval length by approximately 8%; the Hajek estimator generally performed better, and several adjusted estimators performed best in that example.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that fully interacted regression adjustment does not guarantee efficiency gains when heterogeneous subplot-level covariates are used and can reduce efficiency relative to the unadjusted estimator. Its guaranteed efficiency improvement applies under conditions such as using only whole-plot covariates or having negligible within-whole-plot covariate variation; the projection adjustment is proposed for cases outside those conditions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical evidence covers selected simulated settings and one field-study dataset, rather than a broad range of operational split-plot applications. The field illustration fills in missing potential outcomes using regression and then evaluates repeated allocations, so it does not provide direct validation from repeated real-world implementations; a stringent acceptance threshold may also require substantial allocation rejection in practice.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the methods in prospective industrial or field experiments with operational constraints on which allocations are feasible. It would also be useful to examine how the approach performs for designs with more factors, limited covariate information, or sequential allocation decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a sequential method for choosing interventions that move a system’s mean toward a user-specified target. It studies linear causal models with additive Gaussian noise and assumes that the causal graph is known, while its edge weights are uncertain. The method updates a Bayesian model of those weights after each experiment and selects the next intervention by reducing uncertainty about which intervention is best. Its causal integrated variance criterion can be evaluated in closed form, and an output-weighted version focuses more on interventions expected to be near the target. Simulations and an analysis of melanoma perturbation data show that the proposed criteria generally find effective interventions with fewer samples than the compared approaches.
narrate.key_results: In the main simulation comparison, the authors tested 30-node causal graphs with 10 intervention targets, using 1 sample per time step; each method was run 20 times on each of 10 instances. Both proposed criteria reduced error in the target-mean estimate more consistently than the random, greedy, model-variance, and optimal-intervention-variance baselines, with output weighting generally improving on the unweighted criterion. Additional simulations varied graph size from 10 to 30 nodes, intervention-target counts from 1 to 15, and graph structure; the proposed methods were consistently among the best performers, with the output-weighted method doing better in higher dimensions. In the melanoma dataset analysis, the authors considered 36 genes, with 5,039 control cells and 30,486 singly perturbed cells; for the CDH19 target, the causal integrated variance method reduced target-mean error faster than random and greedy selection, using 10 interventional samples per time step and 50 runs after a warm-up of 100 observational samples. The authors report closed-form evaluation and computational complexity proportional to the cube of the number of variables; the most computationally intensive additional baselines relied on Monte Carlo estimation and took longer per iteration.

key_equations.name: Integrated-variance acquisition criterion

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors identify reliance on a known causal graph, a linear model with additive Gaussian noise, and causal sufficiency as limitations. Causal sufficiency excludes latent confounders and also restricts the setting in which only some system variables can be observed or intervened on.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The biological evaluation reuses an existing perturbation dataset rather than prospectively selecting and conducting experiments, so it does not directly establish that the sequential recommendations will work in a live experimental workflow. The biological setup also restricts testing to single-gene interventions and assumes each perturbation shifts its target gene down by its observational mean; the paper notes that this assumption can fail, which can undermine recommendations when effectiveness is not screened beforehand.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the method to settings where the causal graph is partially or entirely unknown, and to nonlinear models, potentially using kernels. They also identify settings with latent confounders or interventions available on only a subset of variables as directions for further work.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be prospective validation in which the method chooses interventions under real laboratory constraints, including cost, availability, and batch-size limits. Further work could also compare alternative target measures and optimization criteria under the same sequential evaluation protocol, while recording the number of experiments needed to reach a practical target tolerance.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for constructing informative experiments for discrete choice models, where participants choose their preferred alternative from a presented set. It targets locally D-optimal designs, which maximize information for specified model parameters. The authors represent the information matrix as a graph Laplacian and use a distance-matrix transformation to reformulate the design problem with fewer variables and sparse constraints. They use this reformulation in a gradient-based algorithm for general choice-set sizes and relate paired comparisons to estimation in Laplacian-constrained Gaussian graphical models. Simulations and two real datasets show that the method can compute designs and assess how much information existing designs lose relative to the optimum.
narrate.key_results: For the general method, tests with 8 or 10 alternatives and choice-set sizes from 3 to 6 reported duality gaps of zero or at most 2.00e-16; the second optimization step took from 0.02 to 49.31 seconds across the tested settings. In the climate-concern dataset, the study design had D-efficiency 0.95173, compared with 0.96643 for the complete design with equal weights and 0.99997 for a rounded optimal design. In the cricket paired-comparison dataset, observed-design efficiency was 0.77507, compared with 0.98792 for the complete design. In simulations with 6 alternatives and choice sets of size 3, as parameter variation increased, the equal-weight complete design’s mean efficiency fell from 0.9943 to 0.5414 and the optimal design’s mean support size fell from 19.9840 to 5.9170.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that their rational-form result for paired comparisons applies when the optimal design’s graph is decomposable. They conjecture, but do not prove, that optimal designs in the paired-comparison model generically have decomposable graphs.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The designs are locally optimal for specified parameters, so parameter-estimation error or changes in utilities may reduce their realized efficiency. The general-method performance study covers only 8 or 10 alternatives and a small range of choice-set sizes, and its design-recovery step becomes costly in some tested cases, taking 49.31 seconds for 10 alternatives and choice sets of size 5.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest studying the maximum likelihood degree of semidefinite Gaussian graphical models under lower-dimensional parameterizations as a possible route to proving their decomposability conjecture. They note that resolving it would also address a previously posed problem concerning four-cycle designs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to study robust or Bayesian designs that account for uncertainty in the estimated attractiveness parameters. Further work could also test integer-run implementations and operational constraints, and validate the efficiency comparisons prospectively in designed experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops compound optimal design criteria for response surface experiments where the fitted polynomial model may be contaminated by extra polynomial terms. The designs balance precision for estimating the fitted model’s parameters, the ability to detect lack of fit, and the effect of model misspecification on parameter estimates. The authors combine these objectives using weighted products of design efficiencies and construct designs with a point-exchange search, using a pure-error estimate of experimental error. They extend the criteria to blocked experiments and examine both a numerical example and a blocked animal-feed experiment. The examples show that the objectives can conflict, but that designs with useful compromises across them can be found.
narrate.key_results: For the numerical example with 5 factors and 40 runs, the design optimized for parameter precision had 47.77% efficiency for the lack-of-fit objective when the contamination scale was 1; at a scale of 1/q, that efficiency was 94.41%. Designs optimized for lack of fit had parameter-precision efficiencies of 43.70% and 39.66% at those respective scales, illustrating the trade-off. In the real blocked case study with 36 runs and 2 blocks, compound designs with two center points per block had relative efficiencies from 92.26% to 99.23% at scale 1 and from 94.95% to 99.29% at scale 1/q. The authors report that the center-point restriction caused losses no greater than 1.82% and 5.05%, respectively; searching for a design typically took 13–15 hours and sometimes took 20–24 hours.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the point-exchange search can miss the optimal design and that computation can be demanding, with searches sometimes taking 20–24 hours. They also note that evaluating the determinant-based mean squared error component by Monte Carlo sampling is time-consuming, and suggest a point-prior alternative when computation time is a concern.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The framework represents contamination through a specified set of nested polynomial terms and a chosen prior scale, so its conclusions may not transfer to other forms or magnitudes of misspecification. Evaluation is limited to two examples, and the real case study does not report a comparative analysis against conventional response surface designs or validation across repeated real experiments.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the mean squared error criteria to more complex treatment and experimental-unit structures, including crossed structures, networks, and sequential designs. They also identify prediction-focused criteria as objectives that could be incorporated into compound criteria.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could assess the designs under alternative contamination models and prior distributions, and compare them with standard response surface designs across a wider range of factor counts and run sizes. It would also be useful to test sequential design updates and evaluate the method in additional real experiments with different blocking and operational constraints.

narrate.summary: The paper studies D-optimal data fusion (DDF), which selects a fixed number of new data points to add information to an existing Fisher information matrix (FIM). Its objective is to maximize the natural logarithm of the determinant of the combined information matrix. The authors derive two convex integer-programming formulations and complementary versions, then develop local-search and randomized-sampling methods as well as an exact algorithm strengthened by additional inequalities and cuts. They evaluate the methods on power-grid sensor placement, choosing phasor measurement units (PMUs) to work alongside existing conventional sensors. The results show that the exact method solves the tested cases more effectively when strengthened, while local search is fast and produces strong solutions on much larger instances.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that DDF is computationally hard and that a polynomial-time method cannot guarantee a constant-factor approximation unless P and NP are equal. On the tested 118-bus and 300-bus benchmark instances, adding both submodular and optimality cuts enabled the exact branch-and-bound method to solve every tested case within the four-hour limit; without these cuts, many cases were not solved within that limit. On the 2,383-bus Polish system, local search took 9 to 51 seconds and had gaps of 0.98 to 8.02 against the continuous-relaxation bound, whereas randomized sampling took 424 to 1,768 seconds and had gaps of 14.24 to 149.43. On the smaller benchmark cases with known optima, local search usually matched the optimum in less than one second and was faster than the compared greedy method, which had the same gaps in those cases.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal limitations section. They report that the exact algorithm could not solve many large-selection cases on the 2,383-bus instance to optimality within the four-hour limit, so they assess approximation solutions using a continuous-relaxation bound instead.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The experiments focus on power-grid sensor placement and benchmark systems, so they do not establish performance in the paper’s other proposed settings, such as active learning. The objective assumes a positive-definite existing information matrix and represents each candidate’s added information as a rank-one contribution; the paper does not test how performance changes when these modeling assumptions or the information estimates are inaccurate.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors expect their methods to apply to cardinality-constrained machine-learning problems, including sparse principal component analysis, sparse regression, and sparse matrix completion.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the methods in active-learning and other experimental-design applications, and evaluate their robustness when the assumed information matrices or candidate contributions are misspecified. It would also be useful to assess operational constraints such as sensor budgets, restricted locations, and sequential selection in real deployments.

narrate.summary: This paper evaluates ways to choose c-optimal experimental designs when observations may be correlated within or between experimental units. It assumes a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) and uses an information matrix based on the covariance of the observations. The authors show that the c-optimal criterion is monotone and supermodular, then compare local search, greedy addition, and reverse greedy removal algorithms. They also extend the approach to designs that minimize a weighted average of criteria across multiple possible models. In the examples, local and reverse greedy search generally performed well, while greedy addition was less reliable; the reverse greedy method was often faster than local search.
narrate.key_results: For the cross-sectional cluster trial examples, the worst local-search design was less than 1% higher in variance than the best design; for cohort examples, it was up to 12% higher. In the reported examples, greedy-search designs reached as much as 345.6% relative efficiency, while reverse greedy and local search generally produced better designs. The local search had a theoretical upper bound of 1.5 relative to the global optimum, but the authors could not guarantee that any algorithm found the global optimum. In the comparison with rounded multiplicative designs for 6 to 30 clusters, the worst design was reported as only 2% higher in variance, and larger designs generally matched the combinatorial designs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that none of the algorithms is guaranteed to find the global optimum. The greedy method cannot start from the empty set for these problems because designs may have singular information matrices, and the reverse greedy method has no approximation guarantee under the criterion as defined. The authors also limit their robust criterion to weighted averages, noting that minimax criteria are not supermodular.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical comparison covers selected cluster-trial and geospatial examples with specified covariance structures and parameter settings, so it does not establish similar performance across the broader range of experimental designs. Results also rely on the chosen information-matrix approximations for nonlinear models and, in some evaluations, Monte Carlo integration; performance under substantial model or covariance misspecification is not established.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further research to determine whether these algorithms provide a viable alternative for Bayesian optimal design, including approximating parameter integrals with a weighted set of models. They also describe the use of discretized design spaces as a way to apply the methods to problems that are not inherently discrete.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could evaluate the algorithms under practical allocation constraints, such as minimum or maximum counts for selected experimental conditions, and assess whether those constraints change the comparative results. Sequential design use and validation on real experiments would also help establish how well the computed designs work beyond the paper's numerical examples.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for selecting volunteers across covariate-defined groups when a study budget limits how many can be enrolled. Its goal is to estimate regression parameters or treatment effects accurately under generalized linear models and multinomial logistic models, rather than to estimate a population mean. The authors choose allocations that maximize the determinant of the model’s information matrix, subject to constraints on group sizes and other feasible allocations. They construct a constrained lift-one algorithm that searches one group allocation at a time and adds a check and search-direction adjustment to handle constraints. narrate.summary: This paper develops design-based theory for rerandomization in cluster-randomized experiments, where whole clusters rather than individual units receive treatment. Its objective is to improve covariate balance and the precision of treatment effect estimates, using covariates measured at either the individual or cluster level. In Scenario 1, the standard deviation was 0.23 for the cluster-level weighted Euclidean design, compared with 0.29 for the cluster-level Mahalanobis design and 0.62 for each baseline estimator. In the child growth monitoring data, which included 41 communities in each arm, the standard deviation was 0.14 for cluster-level weighted Euclidean rerandomization and 0.25 for cluster-level Mahalanobis rerandomization; combining cluster-level rerandomization with regression adjustment reduced it to 0.07. narrate.summary: The paper designs flip-angle acquisition schemes for hyperpolarized magnetic resonance imaging to reduce uncertainty in the apparent pyruvate-to-lactate exchange rate. It uses a Bayesian optimal experimental design approach that maximizes mutual information between measured signals and uncertain model parameters. The design is optimized using a spatially invariant pharmacokinetic model, and then assessed with simulated data from that model and a spatially varying tissue model. The authors compare constant flip angles with schemes that vary across scans and also compare against angles similar to those used clinically. Constant angles of 35 degrees for pyruvate and 28 degrees for lactate give the best accuracy and precision in the tested noisy-data inference, although varying angles can yield higher mutual information.
narrate.key_results: The study optimized designs for 30 scans, with repetition times fixed at 3 seconds, over signal-to-noise ratios of 2, 5, 10, 15, and 20. For signal-to-noise ratio 2, the best constant-angle design was 35 degrees for pyruvate and 28 degrees for lactate; for signal-to-noise ratio 20, it was 3 degrees and 28 degrees, respectively. Across 25 noisy simulated datasets, the constant-angle design for signal-to-noise ratio 2 gave the best reported accuracy and precision, while time-varying designs had higher mutual information but were more sensitive to noise. The 35-degree and 28-degree design was comparable to the clinical comparison of 20 degrees and 30 degrees and performed better at signal-to-noise ratio 2. narrate.summary: This review examines the state and prospects of software packages for designing experiments in the R programming language. It analyzes package download logs, package descriptions and connections, and topic lists maintained by the Comprehensive R Archive Network. It also describes the interfaces of popular packages for factorial, recipe-based, and augmenting designs. The authors find that downloads are concentrated in a small set of packages, while the available approaches remain diverse and package development appears to occur in silos. They argue that a more consistent interface could help practitioners express experimental context and help developers build on one another’s work.
narrate.key_results: In 2021, 10 of the 102 packages accounted for 68% of downloads; the download Gini index ranged from 32.7% to 69.1% across the years 2013 to 2021 and exceeded 60% in each of the last six years. Compared with other topic lists, experimental design had less download inequality, but it had the lowest average number of contributors among the 39 topic lists and among the least within-topic package connectivity. The most downloaded packages were generally established packages, and the top 10 ranking remained largely consistent over the nine years examined. The interface review covers widely used packages for factorial designs, recipe-style construction, and design augmentation, rather than evaluating design algorithms against one another.
narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that volunteer-maintained topic lists may omit relevant packages, that using downloads from only the RStudio mirror may bias the findings, and that the analysis covers only packages for the R programming language. Because the evidence is observational and may be affected by changes in users and package management over time, they describe their conclusions as speculative rather than conclusive or generalizable.
narrate.limitations_unstated: Package downloads are only an indirect measure of use and do not establish which experimental designs practitioners actually choose or whether a package is suitable for a task; downloads can also be prompted by package dependencies. The analysis does not directly test the interfaces with users, and its detailed interface discussion focuses on popular packages, so it cannot establish how the broader package collection performs in practice.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest further exploratory analyses, extending the study beyond packages for the R programming language, and examining other aspects of interface design. They also advocate a consistent, extensible interface that can draw on existing packages and support contributions from other developers.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could survey or observe practitioners to test whether context-oriented interfaces improve the specification and selection of designs, and could benchmark package results on shared design tasks. It would also be useful to track packages and their use across platforms over time, including proprietary software, to test whether download patterns reflect practice more broadly.

narrate.summary: This paper develops estimation and inference methods for randomized experiments with multiple treatments assigned within matched groups. Their theoretical results and simulations show that fully blocked designs can improve efficiency over designs using a finite number of larger strata, while replication can improve finite-sample control of test size when there are many treatments or covariates.
narrate.key_results: In simulations based on 4,000 replications, the standard matched-tuples design had lower mean squared error than complete randomization, matched pairs focused on one factor, and the tested large-stratum designs across the reported model specifications; it generally also compared favorably with rerandomization, though rerandomization was slightly better in some cases. In a separate study based on 2,000 replications, null rejection probabilities for the tested methods were generally close to the nominal 0.05 level, and the matched-tuples design had the highest power in almost all reported model and parameter settings. In simulations with up to six factors and nine covariates, the standard design could be highly conservative: for six factors and nine covariates its null rejection probability was 0.003, while the replicated design's was 0.047; the replicated design generally had somewhat higher mean squared error but better size control in these settings. narrate.summary: The paper develops a robust version of expected information gain for Bayesian experimental design when the prior distribution may be uncertain. In the A/B test, increasing the radius from 0.001 to 0.1 improved estimates for designs that were strongly overestimated, without noticeably harming the other estimates. In the preference and pharmacokinetic tests, a radius of 0.1 could make the adjusted estimator cross the true information-gain value, so the original upper- and lower-bound interpretations no longer applied; for the pharmacokinetic test, the adjusted neural estimator was close to the true value.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a data-driven way to speed up optimal experimental design (OED) for uncertain Kuramoto oscillator models. The goal is to choose pairwise synchronization experiments that reduce uncertainty relevant to the control cost of achieving robust synchronization. A message-passing neural network (MPNN) predicts mean objective cost of uncertainty (MOCU) directly from a graph representation of the model, avoiding repeated sampling and differential-equation solving during design. Its training objective includes a constraint intended to preserve the expected direction of MOCU changes when uncertainty bounds are narrowed. In simulations with five- and seven-oscillator models, the approach produced OED performance virtually identical to sampling-based design while greatly reducing computation time.
narrate.key_results: For seven-oscillator models, MOCU prediction took an average of 19 seconds per model with the sampling-based method, while the MPNN processed the full test set of 2,000 models in 1.160 seconds; the paper reports a 32,758-fold speed-up. For one OED update, the sampling-based method took 2,995.8 seconds for seven oscillators and 1,345.4 seconds for five oscillators, compared with 0.0340 and 0.0321 seconds, respectively, for the neural method. The authors report four to five orders of magnitude acceleration and virtually identical uncertainty reduction to the sampling-based design in both simulations; random and entropy-based selection reduced uncertainty less effectively early in the sequence. Adding the constraint loss improved the share of cases in which predicted MOCU changed in the expected direction: for five oscillators, the reported rates were 0.9254 and 0.9178 for lower- and upper-bound updates, and for seven oscillators they were 0.8660 and 0.8475.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for sequential experimental design under the Bayesian optimal experimental design framework. It turns the design problem into a Markov decision process and learns a policy with reinforcement learning to maximize information about unknown model parameters across a sequence of experiments. The construction uses a learned summary of past experiments and outcomes, together with a reward that assigns each experiment its incremental contribution to the information objective. This approach can handle discrete design spaces and likelihood models without design gradients, unlike some earlier amortized methods. In the simulated tasks studied, it achieves strong information-gain results and proposes designs quickly after training.
narrate.key_results: For source location at 30 experiments, reinforcement learning achieved an expected information gain lower bound of 11.73 ± 0.040, compared with 10.965 ± 0.041 for deep adaptive design; their upper bounds were 12.362 ± 0.062 and 12.380 ± 0.086, respectively. For the constant elasticity of substitution task at 10 experiments, reinforcement learning achieved a lower bound of 13.965 ± 0.064, compared with 10.774 ± 0.077 for deep adaptive design. On the prey population task at 10 experiments, reinforcement learning reached 4.456 ± 0.032, while sequential Monte Carlo reached 4.521 ± 0.065, so the paper reports comparable performance rather than an advantage for reinforcement learning. In deployment, the prey task took 1.50 E-3 seconds per proposed design with reinforcement learning, versus 20.550 seconds for variational prior contrastive estimation and 81.252 seconds for sequential Monte Carlo.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for choosing where and when to acquire data to reduce uncertainty in climate-model parameters. It targets parameter estimation in a general circulation model (GCM), using a Bayesian design objective that favors designs expected to reduce parameter uncertainty. The method uses a simulated global climate record to assess candidate locations and seasons, then fits local inverse problems in parallel using the calibrate-emulate-sample (CES) framework. The authors test it with an idealized model of convection parameters, using both stationary and seasonally varying climate statistics. The method often identifies informative regions near the Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ), but the best location can depend on the width of the sampling region and the season.
narrate.key_results: The design stage requires on the order of 10^2 model evaluations, compared with the 10^5 evaluations the paper reports as typical for traditional Bayesian calibration; it requires no additional forward-model evaluations beyond those used by CES. For stationary statistics and a one-latitude design, the selected latitude was −19°, and the resulting posterior utility was 26.4; the equatorial comparison at −3° had utility 13.9, while the high-latitude comparison at −75° had utility 1.7. For seasonally varying statistics, the solstice-season designs near ±3° had reported utilities of 131.9 and 154.7, compared with 47.9 and 39.5 for secondary subtropical designs near ±30°. With a three-latitude stencil, the stationary design centered at −8° had utility 126.0, compared with 35.3 for the design centered at −3°; the authors also report that shorter averaging periods and narrower stencils can yield less informative, more multimodal posteriors.

key_equations.name: Design selection

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors focus on selecting one design at a time; selecting multiple simultaneous sites creates a combinatorial problem, and evaluating every candidate becomes inefficient for very large design spaces. They report that the method often predicts the ordering of design informativeness but does not necessarily predict the actual utility accurately, partly because of finite sampling and added model-error inflation. Targeting can also be less effective with noisy data, and the demonstrations use a perfect-model idealized setting.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The demonstration estimates only two convection parameters in one idealized model, so it does not establish how well the method transfers to comprehensive climate models or larger parameter sets. Its rankings also depend on the chosen climate statistics, prior, fixed covariance approximation, and candidate locations; actual field or high-resolution simulation choices may be constrained by cost and access in ways not represented in these tests.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose more efficient optimization methods for large design spaces, including approaches that accelerate determinant calculations or use utility surrogates. They also identify application to comprehensive climate models as an important next step, to test whether non-obvious optimal sites arise in more realistic settings.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method with real observations or high-resolution simulation data, including model mismatch that is not generated by the same model being calibrated. They could also compare alternative design objectives and operational constraints, and test repeated sequential acquisitions to determine whether updated posteriors lead to robust improvements.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how to construct nested sets of points that cover a compact domain evenly, using a chosen distance norm. Its objective is to keep the mesh ratio—the fill distance relative to the separation radius—small at every design size. The authors prove that no nested sequence can have an eventual mesh ratio below 2, and show that a greedy method that repeatedly selects the point farthest from those already chosen attains this bound. They also analyze relaxed selection, finite candidate sets, and a boundary-avoiding variant. The main finding is a theoretical guarantee for the greedy construction, with examples showing that boundary avoidance can improve coverage at the cost of worse uniformity for some designs.
narrate.key_results: For any nested sequence in a compact domain of positive volume, the limit superior of the mesh ratio is at least 2. The exact greedy method has mesh ratio at most 2 at every design size, fill distance no more than twice the best possible, and separation radius at least half the best possible. The relaxed method has mesh ratio at most 2/a, where a is its lower bound on the fraction of the current fill distance used when choosing the next point; the exact greedy method is the case a=1. In the two-dimensional unit-square example at n=80, the boundary-avoiding method has reported fill distance 0.0913, compared with 0.125 for ordinary greedy packing, while its mesh ratio is worse for some intermediate designs.

key_equations.name: Lower bound for nested sequences
key_equations.explanation: The limit superior is the eventual upper behavior, n indexes design size, MR is the mesh ratio, X_n is the design at size n, and 2 is the universal lower bound.

key_equations.name: Greedy point selection
key_equations.explanation: The next point x_{n+1} is chosen from domain X to maximize its minimum norm-distance from the existing design X_n, whose points are x_i.

key_equations.name: Uniformity guarantee
key_equations.explanation: MR is the mesh ratio for design X_n, and a is the positive relaxation parameter; setting a to 1 gives the exact greedy method's bound of 2.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that computing the fill distance can be difficult when the domain is continuous. They also state that a finite candidate set deteriorates the method's performance and that the algorithm degenerates once its candidates are exhausted.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The exact greedy rule requires finding a global farthest point, which may be difficult to do reliably in high-dimensional or irregular domains. The guarantees concern geometric coverage and spacing, rather than performance for a response model or a particular experimental objective, and the numerical illustrations cover only a few geometric examples.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.

Further work could also compare the designs in real computer experiments and provide an implementation that estimates the fill distance and reports the resulting guarantees.

narrate.summary: The paper develops computational methods for Bayesian experimental design when a model has nuisance parameters that affect measurements but are not targets of inference. Its objective is to choose designs that maximize expected information gain about the parameters of interest. The authors approximate the effect of small nuisance uncertainty by modifying the measurement likelihood, avoiding a separate sampling loop for nuisance parameters. They combine this approximation with either a Laplace approximation or importance sampling to estimate information gain. Their examples show that the methods can work accurately when nuisance uncertainty is sufficiently small, including for a simulated electrical impedance tomography experiment involving composite laminates.
narrate.key_results: For the linear Gaussian example, the Monte Carlo Laplace approximation and the importance-sampling estimator closely match the analytical expected information gain, with and without nuisance uncertainty when that uncertainty is small. In that example, the optimal number of outer samples grows at order tolerance to the power negative two for all three estimators, and the authors report that adding nuisance uncertainty does not change the total complexity; the importance-sampling estimator uses one inner sample except at small tolerances. In the electrical impedance tomography example, the approximation loses positive definiteness when nuisance variance exceeds about 9.03 × 10⁻⁷; at the tested small nuisance variance, the importance-sampling estimator generally needs one inner sample except for small tolerances, while the Laplace estimator cannot meet tolerances below its inherent bias. The simulated electrode design results favor large shifts and large electrode distances, with shift having the greater influence on information gain; the reported consistency checks show errors within the requested tolerance at the stated 95% confidence level.

key_equations.name: Expected information gain criterion
key_equations.explanation: Here I is expected information gain for design xi, theta is the parameter of interest, Y is the data, p(Y given theta and xi) is the likelihood marginalized over nuisance parameters, and p(Y given xi) is the data density marginalized over both parameter and nuisance uncertainty.

key_equations.name: Small-noise correction to measurement precision
key_equations.explanation: Here M combines the derivative of the forward model g with respect to nuisance parameter phi at zero and the square root of nuisance covariance Sigma_phi; C is the correction matrix; I is the identity matrix; and Sigma_epsilon is the measurement-error covariance matrix, whose inverse square root appears in the correction.

key_equations.name: Adjusted likelihood precision
key_equations.explanation: Here Sigma_eff is the effective measurement covariance after the nuisance approximation, Sigma_epsilon is the measurement-error covariance, M is the nuisance-sensitivity matrix defined above, and the superscript minus one denotes a matrix inverse.

narrate.limitations_stated: The small-noise approximation requires nuisance uncertainty to be small enough that the adjusted covariance remains positive definite; the paper gives the condition in terms of nuisance sensitivity and measurement-error covariance. The Laplace estimator also has an inherent bias that can make sufficiently small tolerances infeasible, and the authors did not account for the bias from one likelihood approximation in their numerical examples because computing it was demanding.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The methods are demonstrated on a linear Gaussian example and one simulated tomography setup, so their performance on real experiments and on substantially different model classes is not established here. The approximation relies on local sensitivity to nuisance parameters and Gaussian uncertainty assumptions, while the tomography design explores a restricted electrode configuration rather than a broad range of manufacturing, access, or cost constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the method on real measurement data and compare its design recommendations with experiments, especially near the positive-definiteness limit. Further work could also evaluate non-Gaussian or larger nuisance uncertainty and incorporate practical design constraints such as electrode access, setup cost, or sequential redesign after preliminary measurements.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for choosing validation points to estimate the integrated squared error (ISE) of a predictor trained on a fixed design. It assumes that the unknown function follows a Gaussian process (GP) model and uses a kernel-based maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) criterion that depends on the training design. The authors construct nested validation designs incrementally by kernel herding, and also propose weights to reduce the influence of validation points far from the training points. Their simulations indicate that both where validation points are placed and how they are weighted affect estimation accuracy. In the reported experiments, weighted kernel-herding designs estimate ISE more accurately than the compared random, low-discrepancy, and leave-one-out approaches.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 100 random functions, dimensions 2 through 10, a training design of 100 points, and a validation design of 50 points, the weighted kernel-herding design had the lowest mean absolute relative estimation error among the compared designs. Weighting also improved the kernel-herding, Sobol’, and random validation designs relative to their unweighted versions; the unweighted Sobol’ and kernel-herding designs tended to overestimate ISE, while unweighted random designs had substantial variability. Leave-one-out cross-validation strongly overestimated ISE in these experiments. Separate design comparisons used training and validation sizes of 50 and 25 or 50, and 200 and 100; kernel-herding constructions generally had good space-filling properties, while the minimum-norm variant had poorer space-filling performance.

key_equations.name: Integrated squared error
key_equations.explanation: The integrated squared error for training design X_n integrates the squared difference between predictor η_n and unknown function f over design space X under measure μ.

key_equations.name: Conditional covariance kernel
key_equations.explanation: K_{|n} is the covariance kernel conditional on training design X_n, K is the original covariance kernel, k_n contains kernel values between x and training points, and K_n is the training covariance matrix.

key_equations.name: Validation discrepancy criterion
key_equations.explanation: The squared discrepancy Δ² for validation design Z_m and training design X_n equals the squared MMD γ² between empirical measure ζ_m and target measure μ, using kernel C defined from conditional covariance kernel K_{|n}.

key_equations.name: Incremental herding construction
key_equations.explanation: At iteration k, the algorithm selects point z_{k+1} to minimize the difference between the potentials under current measure ζ_k and target measure μ, then updates ζ_k with step size α_k and a point mass δ at the selected point.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors assume a zero-mean Gaussian process with a known covariance kernel, though they note that covariance parameters can be estimated and that a parameterized mean can be accommodated. They state that the conditional kernel used for the discrepancy is not characteristic, and leave a fuller investigation of when zero discrepancy implies equality of measures beyond the paper’s scope. They also note that large candidate sets can be needed in higher dimensions, while separable kernels permit explicit calculations that address this computational difficulty.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The validation-performance experiments use simulated random polynomial functions rather than functions from real computer experiments, so the reported gains have not been demonstrated on operational engineering problems. The main prediction and validation constructions use Matérn covariance kernels, and the evidence does not establish how the method behaves when the assumed covariance model is substantially misspecified or when its parameters are poorly estimated.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify construction of validation designs for predicting the error process, as an alternative way to estimate integrated error, as work for a companion paper. They also point to further investigation of conditions under which the conditional discrepancy uniquely identifies the target measure, and describe the results as opening perspectives for constructing space-filling designs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the method on real computer experiments and compare its accuracy under deliberate covariance-model misspecification and noisy observations. It would also be useful to assess computational scaling and practical design constraints in higher dimensions, and to examine whether sequentially updated validation points and weights remain reliable as the training design changes.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a new way to make smaller, practical designs for complex experiments using a beta variational autoencoder (beta-VAE). It begins with a full factorial design after removing trials that violate constraints, then encodes those trials into a two-dimensional latent space. A user specifies a grid of points in that space, and the autoencoder decodes the points into experimental trials. The paper tests the method on a four-factor example and on tuning a convolutional neural network (CNN) for handwritten digit classification. In the application example, square and polar grids gave more systematic coverage than random subsets and produced validated accuracies close to the larger initial design.
narrate.key_results: For the CNN example, filtering the 7,200-trial full factorial design to satisfy constraints left 1,920 trials. The square grid used 64 trials, a 30-fold reduction, and had validated lower confidence limit (LCL) accuracy of 98.4%; the polar grid used 40 trials, a 48-fold reduction, and achieved 98.8%. The constrained initial design had 98.6% validated accuracy, while the three random designs with 64 trials achieved 98.3%, 97.8%, and 97.9%; the authors report that two random designs had notable differences between interpolated and validated results. The square and polar grids also matched the initial design's ranking of all nine factors by importance, while the random design showed some deviation.

key_equations.explanation: Gradient_Metric at grid coordinates x and y sums the absolute changes in each decoded factor level F_i over each transformed latent axis L_j; i indexes the nine factors, j indexes the two axes, and Δ denotes change.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that autoencoder training is stochastic, so latent representations vary between runs and may require hyperparameter tuning or repeated runs. Their visual and interpretive analysis is limited to two-dimensional representations, and decoded trials must still be checked for constraint violations and other design problems. They also describe the CNN example as illustrative, based on a small subset of available data and a lean training process, rather than as an optimized solution to digit recognition.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes primarily from one illustrative CNN tuning problem and one four-factor demonstration, so it does not establish performance across different experimental domains or response types. The comparisons do not include a broad set of established design methods, and generating fewer trials does not remove the cost of running the costly CNN training and its replications.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify further validation of input-data duplication as a needed topic, particularly for designs with many factors having high numbers of levels. They also suggest that other grid patterns, aggregation methods, and gradient summaries could be used.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare these generated designs with established fractional factorial, screening, and computer-experiment designs under the same factor constraints and run budgets. It would also be useful to test sequential use, in which observed responses guide later grid points, and to validate the method in real process experiments as well as on additional public datasets.

narrate.summary: This paper proves the existence of small ordered orthogonal arrays, a generalization of orthogonal arrays in which columns are grouped into ordered blocks. The objective is to use as few rows as possible while ensuring that every required selection of columns contains every symbol tuple the same number of times. The authors represent the required balance conditions as averages of functions and apply a probabilistic existence theorem due to Kuperberg, Lovett, and Peled. Their result gives an upper bound on the number of rows that depends mainly on the number of symbols, blocks, and the strength. The proof is nonconstructive, so it establishes that such arrays exist but does not provide a way to generate them.
narrate.key_results: For every parameter choice allowed by the paper, the authors prove that an ordered orthogonal array exists with the row-size bound given below. The bound is polynomially larger than the Rao lower bound, which scales with the number of symbols and blocks and has strength-dependent exponent t/2. The authors say their result improves an earlier upper bound based on the total number of columns, particularly when the number of blocks is large relative to the strength.

narrate.summary: The paper extends an existing method for designing neutron reflectometry experiments by using Fisher information to choose measurement conditions that reduce uncertainty across model parameters. It applies the method to lipid bilayers, a degrading lipid monolayer, and a thin magnetic layer. The authors scale parameter importance and choose designs that maximize the least-informed combination of parameters, using numerical optimization and simulations. They compare candidate contrasts, angles, counting-time splits, and underlayer properties, and use Bayesian sampling to check predicted improvements for selected bilayer designs. The results show that experiment conditions can substantially improve parameter precision and can make detection of a very small magnetic moment feasible within a practical measurement time.
narrate.key_results: For the two bilayer models, adding one optimized underlayer raised the minimum eigenvalue from 4.694 times 10 to the minus fourth to 4.016 times 10 to the minus third for the DMPC case, and from 1.312 times 10 to the minus third to 1.128 times 10 to the minus second for the DPPC/RaLPS case; the authors report that nested sampling also showed tighter parameter distributions. For both models, measuring heavy water and ordinary water was the best two-contrast choice; the optimized minimum eigenvalue increased from 4.957 times 10 to the minus sixth to 1.919 times 10 to the minus third for DMPC, and from 6.367 times 10 to the minus eighth to 2.771 times 10 to the minus third for DPPC/RaLPS, compared with using one contrast. The optimal two-angle designs used a low angle and a high angle: 0.82 and 4.00 degrees for DMPC, with 11.9 percent and 88.1 percent of the time, and 0.68 and 4.00 degrees for DPPC/RaLPS, with 8.9 percent and 91.1 percent of the time. For the magnetic example, the design identified a platinum thickness near 26 angstroms as optimal; compared with an 80-angstrom design, it needed several thousand fewer minutes to achieve comparable likelihood evidence for a moment of 0.01 Bohr magnetons per atom in a layer about 20 angstroms thick.

key_equations.name: Parameter importance scaling

narrate.summary: This paper develops optimal experimental designs for accelerated degradation testing of systems with two degradation components, modeled with Gamma processes. Stress levels are selected from a normalized design region, and measurements are assumed to be taken at fixed, known times. For independent components, the design minimizes the variance of an estimated failure-time quantile; for dependent components, the paper uses Frank or Gaussian copulas and develops determinant-optimal designs. It also derives determinant-optimal and c-optimal designs for a simplified version in which outcomes record whether each component has crossed its failure threshold. Numerical examples show the resulting support points and weights, and examine sensitivity to changes in assumed conditions.
narrate.key_results: For the independent-component example, with four observation times, the two marginal c-optimal designs put weights 0.79 and 0.21 on stress levels 0 and 1, and weights 0.91 and 0.09 on those levels, respectively. For dependent components with four equidistant observation times, the Frank-copula determinant-optimal design uses six points with equal reported weights of 0.166; the Gaussian-copula design uses the same six points with weights 0.20, 0.20, 0.16, 0.16, 0.18, and 0.09. With one measurement in the binary-outcome example, the determinant-optimal designs use four corner points with weights close to one quarter each; the c-optimal designs use four points, including an interior point, with different weights for the two copulas. The authors report that the binary c-optimal design performs well in sensitivity comparisons against equal-weight designs, but give no single numerical efficiency value.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that it is unknown whether the proposed copula specification yields a bivariate process with independent increments, except for the independence copula. narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical designs are local: they depend on nominal parameter values, and the examples use a grid with increments of 0.05 rather than demonstrating performance over a broad set of models or experimental settings. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the results to other marginal failure models, including Wiener processes, inverse Gaussian processes, and nonlinear mixed-effects degradation models.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could develop tractable dependent-outcome design methods for multiple measurement times and evaluate them with practical constraints such as limited stress combinations, test costs, and integer sample allocations. Comparisons across additional dependence models, criteria, and real experiments would help assess how well these locally optimal designs transfer to practice; sequential design and implementation software could also be investigated.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for selecting experimental designs that remain estimable when some runs are lost. It focuses mainly on linear models for factorial designs, while also illustrating the approach for polynomial models. The method represents dependencies among runs using circuits derived from the model matrix, then uses exchanges of design points to reduce the harmful circuits in a selected fraction. Simulations show that this exchange procedure often improves robustness relative to random starting fractions, and a reduced version can help with larger problems. Robustness and D-efficiency are equivalent for totally unimodular model matrices, but the paper shows that this equivalence does not generally hold.
narrate.key_results: In simulations using 1,000 random starting fractions, the main algorithm improved robustness in at least 95 percent of cases for nearly all reported full-factorial examples; the exception was the five-factor design with eight runs, where the fifth percentile of the change was negative. For the reduced algorithm on the five-factor main-effects model with ten runs, the mean robustness gain was 0.244, compared with 0.156 for the full algorithm. For a 40-run orthogonal array, all 1,000 starting fractions of size 22 were improved to robustness 0.1818, while almost all starting fractions had robustness zero; for size 23, all outputs had robustness 0.0474. In a 27-run orthogonal array example with 12-run subsets, mean robustness increased from 0.3197 to 0.4567. The authors report execution times below one second per fraction in their examples, and show that outside the totally unimodular case a D-optimal design can have low robustness.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that the point-loss score is only a first-order approximation to inclusion-exclusion and can be inaccurate when a fraction contains many circuits, because multiple circuits can correspond to the same minimal fraction. They also report that circuit computations grow rapidly with design dimension, that the reduced algorithm performs worse for small fractions, and that the exchange algorithm can encounter local minima.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The method assumes that the specified model is the model of interest; omitted effects or other model misspecification could change which circuits matter and which runs are robust. The evaluation uses simulations and selected design examples rather than real experiments, and the search does not account for practical restrictions such as unequal run costs or constraints on which treatments can be performed.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest placing the exchange algorithm within simulated annealing to address local minima. They also introduce circuit-based analysis of supersaturated designs as a direction requiring further theory, and point to possible applications in optimal designs and randomization for treatment allocation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to extend the search to designs with run-cost, availability, or randomization constraints while comparing robustness with other design objectives. The method could also be validated on real experiments with missing runs and assessed under plausible model misspecification.

narrate.summary: The paper develops stress-setting designs for accelerated degradation testing (ADT) of products with multiple competing degradation components. It models each component's repeated measurements with a linear mixed-effects model (LMEM), while assuming observation times are fixed and stress remains constant within each test unit. The objective is to estimate a chosen quantile of the system failure-time distribution under normal-use conditions as precisely as possible. The authors derive a locally c-optimal criterion based on the asymptotic variance of that quantile estimator. They construct designs analytically for one example and with a multiplicative algorithm for another, and compare their performance with equally weighted designs on the design-region vertices.
narrate.key_results: In Example 1, with two stress variables and a series system, the reported optimal approximate design assigns weights 0.67, 0.11, 0.19, and 0.03 to the four vertices (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), and (1,1); its reported median failure time is 5.2. In Example 2, for a 2-out-of-3 system, the corresponding weights are 0.60, 0.03, 0.13, and 0.24, and the reported median failure time is 2.43. Both examples use three measurement times, 0, 0.5, and 1, and the paper reports that their optimal designs generally outperform the equally weighted vertex design in the presented efficiency comparisons. The paper does not report a fixed number of test units or numerical efficiency values in the text.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the machine-learning regression-adjusted treatment effect estimator (MLRATE) for estimating the average treatment effect (ATE) in randomized experiments. It uses machine-learning (ML) predictions of outcomes from covariates that are independent of treatment assignment, then includes those predictions in a linear regression adjustment. Cross-fitting generates predictions using data outside each observation’s split, helping prevent overfitting bias. The authors establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid confidence intervals (CIs) under stated conditions, and show that the method’s asymptotic variance is no greater than that of the difference-in-means estimator. In simulated data and A/A tests on Facebook metrics, the method reduced uncertainty compared with both difference-in-means and adjustment using only the pre-experiment outcome.
narrate.key_results: In the simulation with 10,000 observations and 100 covariates, nominal 95% CIs had empirical coverage of 95.18% for MLRATE with gradient boosted regression trees (GBDT) and 95.34% with elastic net; their average CI widths were 0.62 and 0.86 times the difference-in-means width. Across 48 Facebook metrics, MLRATE reduced variance by 72–74% on average relative to difference-in-means and by 19% relative to LinInteract, the adjustment using the pre-experiment outcome alone. Average CI width reductions were 50–51% relative to difference-in-means and 11–12% relative to LinInteract. Matching the precision of MLRATE with GBDT would require, on average, 5.44 times the sample size for difference-in-means or 1.56 times for LinInteract.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The theoretical guarantee depends on randomized treatment, finite-moment and other regularity conditions, and convergence of the fitted prediction functions to a limit; it does not establish a finite-sample no-harm guarantee. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest exploring more sophisticated prediction methods and incorporating additional covariates. They specifically mention synthetic-control-inspired strategies that use contemporaneous outcomes for individuals outside the experiment.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further evaluation could test coverage and variance reduction in actual randomized experiments, across organizations and outcome types, while comparing additional adjustment methods and prediction algorithms. Practical studies could also examine constrained or delayed feature availability and sequential experiment use, including the computation and operational effects of generating and reusing cross-fitted predictions.

narrate.summary: This paper extends mean objective cost of uncertainty (MOCU)-based optimal experimental design (OED) by using machine learning (ML) to speed up the selection of experiments for uncertain Kuramoto oscillator models. The objective is to reduce uncertainty that affects the control cost of achieving global frequency synchronization. The method trains a one-hidden-layer neural network to classify whether a model with a given control strength will synchronize, replacing repeated differential-equation simulations inside the control-cost search. Candidate experiments isolate oscillator pairs and observe whether they synchronize, then update the uncertainty about their coupling strength. In simulations with five- and seven-oscillator models, the method closely matched the original design performance while greatly reducing computation time.
narrate.key_results: For the five-oscillator case, estimating expected remaining MOCU took an average of 0.1110 seconds with the machine-learning method and 818.7 seconds with the simulation-based method; their estimates had a Pearson correlation of 0.9849. For the seven-oscillator case, the corresponding times were 0.6953 seconds and 3,684.9 seconds, a reported speedup of 5,298 times, with a correlation of 0.9606. In experiments repeated across 100 randomly sampled true models, the MOCU-based designs, including the machine-learning design, reduced uncertainty substantially faster than entropy-based or random selection and showed nearly identical average design performance to the original method. The machine-learning design identified the first best experiment in all 100 five-oscillator evaluations and in the reported seven-oscillator sequence comparisons; the paper’s abstract reports speed improvements of up to 154 times without degradation of design performance.

narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose using deep neural networks to discover useful relationships among parameters in non-homogeneous Kuramoto models with multiple oscillators.
