narrate.summary: The paper introduces a family of optimal experimental design criteria for choosing a limited set of experiments to estimate the coefficients of a linear model. It assumes independent, zero-mean Gaussian noise and uses elementary symmetric polynomials to create criteria between A-optimal and D-optimal design. The authors construct designs using a convex relaxation followed by sampling, or a greedy procedure that removes experiments from an initial set while preserving feasibility. The criteria include A-optimal and D-optimal design as endpoint cases and offer intermediate choices. The authors report theoretical performance guarantees and experiments in which greedy designs have quality comparable to Fedorov exchange designs while taking less time.
narrate.key_results: On synthetic data with 500 candidate experiments and 30 parameters, the paper compares design budgets from 40 to 200 and reports that greedy design performs comparably to Fedorov exchange. For the reported setting with polynomial order 10 and precision density 0.6, greedy took 0.28 seconds at budget 40 and 52 seconds at budget 200; Fedorov exchange initialized from the greedy design took 66 and 130 seconds, respectively, while uniform initialization took 1,600 and 4,700 seconds. The authors also prove approximation guarantees for their greedy method and a probabilistic guarantee for sampling from the relaxed solution under a stated conditioning assumption. On the Concrete Compressive Strength dataset, with 1,030 possible experiments and eight physical parameters, A-optimal design had the smallest reported prediction error, while higher polynomial orders increased design-matrix sparsity with a marginal decrease in predictive performance.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal block designs for estimating direct treatment effects when treatments can also affect plots to their left, right, above, and below. It studies a two-dimensional layout with block effects and allows a general within-block covariance structure for the errors. The authors define a design measure over possible block arrays, show that symmetric designs provide a complete class, and derive conditions that characterize universally optimal designs even when the design is not symmetric. Their construction identifies a restricted set of useful arrays and then solves for their proportions. The results give exact universally optimal designs in some settings and highly efficient designs in others, particularly when exact universal optimality is unavailable.
narrate.key_results: For three treatments in blocks with three rows and three columns, the paper reports 19,683 possible arrays and 3,281 distinct symmetric block sets; increasing the number of columns to four raises the number of symmetric block sets to 88,574. In the two-row, three-column example with two treatments, a universally optimal exact design can use four blocks, whereas a symmetric exact design requires at least 16 blocks. For settings with at least as many treatments as plots per block, the authors report efficiencies of 0.9997 and 0.9999 for two example designs, while noting that exact universally optimal designs rarely exist in this case. narrate.summary: This paper develops sequential experimental designs for fitting sparse polynomial chaos expansions (PCEs) to computational models. Its objective is accurate prediction across the input space while limiting the number of model evaluations. The method begins with a space-filling design, uses least angle regression (LAR) to select a sparse polynomial basis from the observed responses, and then adds points selected using regression optimality criteria, including the S-value criterion. The authors compare the approach with space-filling and other sequential designs on four numerical models ranging from three to sixty-two input dimensions. The sequential S-value design generally gives the most accurate and stable predictions in those comparisons.
narrate.key_results: The study compares designs over 50 replications on four benchmarks: the three-dimensional Ishigami function, an eight-dimensional Sobol function, a ten-dimensional truss model, and a sixty-two-dimensional diffusion model. The sequential S-value design is reported to outperform the alternatives in prediction accuracy and to show less variability between replications; it also has a consistently smaller information-matrix condition number in the Ishigami comparison. The reported sequential runs start with 40 points and add 20 at a time for Ishigami, 100 and 50 for the eight- and ten-dimensional examples, and 100 and 20 for the diffusion example; the plotted design sizes reach 160, 1,500, 450, and 300, respectively. Sequential D-optimal designs perform poorly in the reported comparisons, while sequential maximin designs are useful at low to moderate dimensions but erratic at high dimension.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a method for predicting quantitative outcomes when high-resolution measurements are costly but threshold-based, categorical measurements are easier to obtain. It is demonstrated on molecular features for predicting antimalarial potency and aqueous solubility. The method extracts eigenvectors of feature correlations within coarse-label groups, then uses the quantitative measurements to fit the importance of those features in a quadratic model. This combines a linear model fitted to quantitative data with interactions informed by the coarse data. The authors report improved prediction over quantitative-only models in their examples and show how the method behaves in simulated energy landscapes.
narrate.key_results: For antimalarial potency, the dataset included 1,528 active compounds and quantitative potency measurements for 1,189 compounds; the authors report that combining coarse and quantitative data could achieve similar predictive accuracy with about an order of magnitude fewer quantitative measurements. For aqueous solubility, the method achieved a mean absolute error of 0.61 and a coefficient of determination of 0.85 using 90% of the 1,144-molecule dataset; the paper compares this favorably with a reported coefficient of determination of 0.83 for kernel partial least squares. In a simulated stratified-sampling example, using 500 quantitative measurements with the combined method recovered the interaction matrix with a mean absolute error of 0.12, compared with 0.31 using quantitative measurements alone. narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for designing order-of-addition experiments, which study how the sequence of applying components affects a response. Its objective is to estimate effects efficiently while using fewer runs than a full set of component orders. The design represents each order through pairwise ordering factors and seeks balance among those factors, including through a new order-of-addition orthogonal-array definition. The author uses D-optimal search algorithms to find designs and also considers secondary balance measures, process factors, and restrictions on allowable orders. The paper reports useful balanced designs in 4, 5, and 6 components, and near-balanced designs in 7 components.
narrate.key_results: For 5 components and 15 runs, the paper found designs with a mean variance-inflation factor of 2.17 and D-efficiency of 0.96, compared with Van Nostrand’s design, which had a mean variance-inflation factor of 3.28 and D-efficiency of 0.79. The paper reports 12-run order-of-addition orthogonal arrays for 4 and 5 components and 24-run arrays for 5 and 6 components. For 7 components, no 24-, 36-, or 48-run orthogonal arrays were found in the reported searches; the best 24-run design had D-efficiency 0.990 and an average strength-2 chi-square measure of 0.07. The paper also demonstrates augmenting a 24-run, 5-component design with process factors and adapting the search to restricted component orders.

narrate.limitations_stated: The author says the D-criterion is limiting for very small designs when the model matrix lacks full column rank. narrate.limitations_unstated: The searches rely substantially on the main-effects model for pairwise ordering factors, while interactions may matter; the paper suggests interaction-aware analysis but does not evaluate how the proposed designs perform under such models. The failure to find larger-component orthogonal arrays in a finite search does not establish that none exist, and the numerical comparisons cover selected examples rather than a broad range of real experimental settings.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author proposes investigating whether D-efficiency of 1 implies D-optimality, finding closed-form constructions, and determining the largest component count for which arrays exist at given run sizes and strengths. The paper also calls for catalogs covering restricted orders and process factors, accessible software, structural study of non-isomorphic designs, and efficient chi-square search algorithms.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the designs in real experiments and compare their estimation performance when pairwise-order interactions or other response models are important. Research could also examine practical randomization and operational constraints, and assess whether designs can be augmented sequentially as experimental knowledge changes.

narrate.summary: The paper designs geographic clusters for randomized experiments in which users may move between regions, causing treatment interference. In the United States cut-size comparison, GeoCUTS had cut sizes 4 percent of the reported reference for both highly active and highly mobile data, compared with 7 percent for DMA and 15 percent or 14 percent for the grid, respectively; the paper also reports that GeoCUTS and linear embedding had the best cut sizes among the compared methods.

narrate.summary: The paper develops theory for weighted optimal experimental design in a linear model with parameters of interest and nuisance parameters. Its objective is to estimate a chosen system of estimable functions, possibly assigning different importance to those functions, using eigenvalue-based criteria such as A-optimality and E-optimality. The paper proves that this weighted objective is equivalent to ordinary optimality for an appropriately defined system of functions, and gives a construction that also works from a specified weight matrix. It extends the weight-matrix definition to singular matrices and systems that span only part of the estimation space. The main finding is theoretical equivalence, allowing methods already available for standard optimal design of functions to be used for weighted design.
narrate.key_results: For eigenvalue-based criteria, the paper proves that the information matrix for a system of estimable functions and its corresponding weighted information matrix have the same nonzero eigenvalues, including multiplicities. It also shows how to construct a system of estimable functions from a specified weight matrix so that the weighted and standard criteria are equivalent. The proposed weight matrix for a system of interest is the product of its coefficient matrix and its transpose; it applies even when the system is rank-deficient or the weight matrix is singular. The paper interprets weighted E-optimality as minimizing the largest weighted variance over functions in the weighted space, and weighted A-optimality as minimizing an average variance for an appropriately sized system of functions. It reports theoretical results and illustrative examples, but no numerical efficiency, run-size, or prediction comparisons.

narrate.summary: This paper reviews Bayesian experiment design and develops an approach for finding designs for multivariable generalized linear models (GLMs). narrate.summary: The paper develops condition-number optimal designs, called K-optimal designs, for estimating regression parameters in linear models driven by Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes and sheets. It compares these designs with determinant-optimal, or D-optimal, designs for temporal sampling and spatial regular grids. The designs are constructed by deriving the information matrix from the OU covariance structure and optimizing either its condition number or determinant. The paper also studies equidistant designs, including grid refinement and expansion of the sampling region. Its main finding is that K-optimal designs can give lower estimation error than D-optimal designs for large covariance parameter values, when a non-collapsing K-optimal design exists.
narrate.key_results: For the restricted three-point temporal design, the D-optimal point is always at the midpoint, while a non-collapsing K-optimal design exists only when the covariance parameter is below 0.5718 or above 4.9586. For two-point temporal designs, the paper proves that a unique K-optimal design exists; for increasing-domain equidistant designs, the determinant criterion increases with spacing while the condition-number criterion has at least one global minimum. In the simulations, 10,000 samples were used for each example; for the temporal design, K-optimal performance was similar to D-optimal performance at small covariance values and superior in the upper parameter range. For the spatial nine-point designs, reported relative efficiencies of K-optimal versus D-optimal mean squared errors ranged from 88.90% to 115.33% in the displayed large-parameter table, with values below 100% indicating lower error for the K-optimal design. narrate.summary: This paper studies whether experimenters can monitor A/B tests continuously and stop them early when using Bayesian hypothesis testing. It considers a normal-mean model, first with a specified treatment effect and then with a composite alternative that assigns a normal prior to the effect. The method calculates the Bayes factor using all observations collected up to the stopping time, with a stopping rule based only on information already observed. The authors prove that the posterior odds retain their Bayesian interpretation under any such proper stopping rule that stops in finite time with probability one. Simulations illustrate the result and show that early stopping can reduce the amount of data collected while changing rejection rates and power.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 100,000 runs, a sample size of 100, and a Bayes-factor cutoff of 9, the fixed-horizon design had a false rejection rate of 0.018, power of 0.465, and false discovery rate of 0.037. With one-sided early stopping, these were 0.060, 0.599, and 0.09; two-sided early stopping gave 0.060, 0.598, and 0.09. The average run length with early stopping was about 55 rather than the fixed sample size of 100; early stopping occurred in 59.5% of runs under the alternative in the one-sided design and in 64.9% under the alternative and 65.0% under the null in the two-sided design. The paper also reports a simulation for a composite alternative with sample size 1,000 and a normal prior with standard deviation 0.1; its figures illustrate that the observed ratios between alternative and null runs track the calculated Bayes factors under both fixed-horizon and early-stopping designs.

narrate.summary: This paper develops methods for placing a fixed number of design points to cover a design region as uniformly as possible in the worst case. The target is a minimax design for computer experiments and other coverage tasks, including sensor placement. For a 7-point two-dimensional design, its minimax distance was within 0.001 of the reported global minimum. With 100,000 representative points, reported computation time ranged from 15 to 90 seconds in two dimensions and from 4 to 8 minutes in eight dimensions; binary integer programming took nearly 30 minutes per design, while principal points and fast flexible space-filling designs were faster but generally had worse minimax results. For 60-point designs in eight dimensions, the projection refinement improved projected minimax and average-distance measures relative to the compared designs, but performed worse on the projected maximin measure.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a randomization-based method for estimating causal effects in a two-factor, two-level split-plot experiment. It targets the population average effects of each factor and their interaction, including when treatment allocations are unbalanced. The design assigns one factor at the block level and randomizes the other factor among units within each block; the authors derive sampling variances from between-block and within-block potential-outcome covariances. They also construct conservative variance estimates and corresponding interval estimates. Simulations report better coverage than the comparison methods in many of the settings studied, particularly where those methods under-cover.
narrate.key_results: The method gives unbiased estimates and a closed-form sampling variance that separates between-block and within-block contributions; under strict additivity, balanced designs minimize the reported sampling variances. Simulations used 1,000 randomizations per setting, a nominal 95% interval level, and block and within-block sizes of 40 and 80. For potential-outcome type II under strict additivity with sizes 40 and 40, coverage for the whole-plot effect was 95.0% for the proposed method, compared with 0.0% for complete-randomization, generalized linear model, and mixed-model intervals; the other two effects had 100.0% coverage for all four methods. Under type II with no additivity assumption, proposed-method coverage was 99.3%, 99.7%, and 98.7% for the whole-plot, sub-plot, and interaction effects, compared with 33.9%, 42.3%, and 36.8% for complete-randomization intervals. The authors report similar overall patterns for sizes 80 and 80, though those results are not shown.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not give a formal limitations section. They state that space limitations constrained further development and identify extensions to other split-plot forms as areas for further exploration.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The simulations use balanced factor allocations, even though the method is intended to handle unbalanced allocations, and use only two reported block and within-block sizes; they do not validate the method on a real experiment. The analysis assumes equal block sizes, so its results do not directly establish performance for unequal-sized blocks, and the interval justification is asymptotic as the numbers of blocks and units per block increase.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending Bayesian causal inference to split-plot designs while preserving frequency properties, developing randomization tests for sharp unit-level null hypotheses, and extending the results to multi-level factors, more factors, and more complex split-plot designs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could develop and validate variance estimates for unequal block sizes and for practical constraints beyond the allocation imbalance treated here. Sequential use of the procedure and validation on real industrial or engineering experiments would also help establish its practical performance.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal designs for estimating a single regression parameter when observations have first-order or second-order autoregressive errors. It first finds signed weights that make a signed least-squares estimator attain the same variance as the best linear unbiased estimator at a fixed set of observation points. For increasingly dense, equally spaced points, it derives continuous approximations to the optimal designs, using a density over the interval and weights at its endpoints; the second-order case also involves endpoint derivative terms. The authors then use these approximations to construct practical designs with a small number of runs and a modified weighted least-squares estimator. In the examples, this procedure approaches the full-grid estimator closely in one case, while its accuracy depends on the regression function and design in another.
narrate.key_results: For the first example, with a constant regression function and second-order errors, the proposed weighted least-squares estimator has variance 0.80170 for K=2, compared with 0.80158714 for the best linear unbiased estimator using the same K+4 design; the ordinary least-squares variance is 0.914. For K values from 2 through 5, the proposed estimator's variance ranges from 0.80170 to 0.80161, while the corresponding best linear unbiased estimator variances range from 0.80158714 to 0.80158466. In the second example, with a squared regression function, the proposed estimator's variance ranges from 0.40218 to 0.40139 for K from 2 through 5, whereas the best linear unbiased estimator on the same designs ranges from 0.37079053 to 0.37065785; ordinary least squares has variance 0.723 at K=2. For the full set of 101 potential points, the reported best linear unbiased estimator variances are 0.80158449 in the first example and 0.37055791 in the second, close to the respective continuous-model optimal variances of 0.8 and approximately 0.36543.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors restrict their study to a one-parameter regression model with first-order or second-order autoregressive errors. Their continuous approximation for first-order errors requires a positive autoregressive parameter; they note that negative values lack a continuous real-valued analogue and are harder to analyze. The derivations also assume equally spaced observation points and a regression function that is nonzero throughout the interval, with differentiability requirements for the approximations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The practical comparison covers only two numerical examples, both with second-order errors of a particular autocovariance form, so it does not validate the procedure broadly across error structures or regression functions. The proposed construction relies on signed weights and, for the second-order case, approximates endpoint derivatives using nearby observations; constraints on allowable run locations, nonnegative weights, or measurement costs could therefore change its practical performance.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the finite-run procedure across a wider range of regression functions, autoregressive parameters, and second-order covariance forms, including cases excluded from the continuous approximations. Study how to adapt the designs when run locations or weights are constrained in practice, and test the estimator and design in real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops particle swarm optimization (PSO) to search for locally D-optimal designs for generalized linear models (GLMs) with binary responses and mixtures of discrete and continuous factors. The objective is parameter estimation, with the design chosen to maximize the determinant of the information matrix at specified nominal parameter values. PSO searches continuous factor settings directly and assigns design weights while evaluating candidate designs against the equivalence theorem. The authors test the method in simulations and apply it to odor-removal, electrostatic-discharge, and constrained plastic-molding design problems. They report that PSO finds efficient designs, often with fewer support points than comparison designs, and can accommodate irregular design spaces.
narrate.key_results: For two continuous factors, PSO found 1,000 designs in 30.41 seconds; comparison methods took 37.68 seconds or more at the coarsest reported resolution, and some methods were unavailable or much slower at finer resolutions. In the odor study, the PSO design had 15 support points, while temperature-discretized factorial designs had 48 to 496 points and relative efficiencies of 56.10% to 58.96% compared with the PSO design. In the electrostatic-discharge study, PSO produced a 14-support-point design, and the original 80-setting design had 32.85% relative efficiency compared with it. For an all-discrete simulation of 10,000 designs per factor count, PSO took 10.347, 39.391, and 239.350 seconds for two, three, and four factors, respectively; Lift-One was faster in those comparisons.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that for criteria without the convexity properties that support an equivalence theorem, there is no such theorem available to verify the design; confirmation then depends on theory, which they say is feasible only for relatively simple models. Their main results are locally optimal and therefore depend on chosen nominal parameter values.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-world applications use published studies and selected nominal parameter values, but the paper does not report running the proposed designs and comparing outcomes from newly conducted experiments. The performance comparisons cover a limited set of model structures and algorithms, so the reported speed and efficiency advantages may not carry over to other constraints, parameter settings, or practical run costs. The designs are approximate and would need integer run allocations for implementation, which can change their achieved efficiency.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose applying PSO to other design problems, including exact designs for correlated responses and minimum-bias designs. They also suggest applications to healthcare studies with mixed discrete and continuous factors.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate how rounding approximate weights to feasible integer run counts affects efficiency under practical run-size and resource constraints. Further work could also test sequential updating of nominal parameter values and validate the proposed designs in newly conducted industrial experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper develops designs for screening variables and estimating effects when responses follow generalized linear models (GLMs). It focuses on binomial responses with logistic regression and Poisson responses with log-linear regression, using a Bayesian information capacity (IC) criterion to make designs useful across candidate models and uncertain parameter values. Logistic designs are found by numerical optimization, while the Poisson designs use an analytical construction for minimally supported designs. The authors pair these designs with all-subsets model selection, using penalized likelihood and a generalized information criterion (GIC) for logistic regression and maximum likelihood and the Akaike information criterion (AIC) for Poisson regression. Simulations show that screening can work effectively for both response types, though logistic regression is more challenging and generally requires larger experiments.
narrate.key_results: In logistic-regression simulations, Bayesian IC designs achieved power above 80% with 30 or 50 runs and above 90% with 80 or 100 runs; each simulation condition used 1,000 generated data sets. Compared with locally D-optimal designs for the largest model, the Bayesian IC designs generally had higher power and lower type I error and FDR. For Poisson regression, the authors studied five-variable designs with 16 runs and 10-variable designs with 32 runs; power was almost uniformly high and type I error rates were below 0.2. For the Poisson designs, reported minimum design efficiencies exceeded approximately 0.4 and mean efficiencies exceeded approximately 0.55; fractional factorial designs had much lower efficiencies, despite similar model-selection performance, and therefore were expected to estimate the selected model poorly.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors restrict the model spaces considered, either by limiting the number of variables or by assuming factor sparsity. They state that larger model spaces may make all-subsets selection impractical, and that larger designs are needed for good logistic-regression model selection than for Poisson regression.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results rely on simulated data generated under the assumed link functions, model forms, and bounded prior distributions, so performance under misspecified links, different coefficient distributions, or real experimental conditions is not established. The examples also focus on main effects and bounded factor settings, which limits how directly the reported designs apply to settings with interactions or other practical treatment constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose further study of the GIC penalty with penalized maximum likelihood and of experiments where the link function must also be selected. They also suggest scalable alternatives to all-subsets selection, evaluation of Bayesian and shrinkage methods, and design methods that jointly address model discrimination and parameter estimation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the designs in real screening experiments and assess their robustness when the assumed priors or response models are inaccurate. It could also study practical restrictions on treatment settings and run allocation, and whether designs can be updated sequentially as screening data accumulate.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes nested orthogonal arrays for designing space-filling experiments that support estimation of main effects and interactions. The method combines balance from orthogonal arrays with the fine, individual-factor coverage of Latin hypercube sampling. It constructs a design with nested arrays of strengths 3, 2, and 1, using finite-field array constructions and a mapping that refines factor levels. The authors aim to improve the coverage of factor levels while reducing correlation between estimates of first-order terms and their interactions. They report that simulations show the proposed designs outperform strength-2 orthogonal arrays and Latin hypercube sampling, but give no numerical performance results.
narrate.key_results: The authors report that their nested orthogonal arrays consistently outperformed strength-2 orthogonal arrays and Latin hypercube sampling in their simulations. They provide no numerical efficiency, estimation-error, prediction, or run-size savings results, so the reported comparison is qualitative. As a construction example, they show a 64-run design with 5 factors that can be viewed at strengths 3, 2, and 1, with 4, 8, and 64 levels respectively.

narrate.summary: This paper develops stopping rules for an automatic experimental design method that uses real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and Bayesian optimization. The method models the relationship between audio-visual stimulus settings and a target brain response with a Gaussian process (GP), then uses expected improvement to select new settings. The target is to maximize the difference in activity between the occipital and superior temporal brain regions. The authors test two rules on data from an earlier study: stopping when consecutive settings are close, and stopping when the probability of improvement falls below a chosen threshold. Both rules appear useful for many of the tested runs, and the authors report that stopping earlier in those runs would not have impaired prediction accuracy.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation used data from five subjects and their initial two runs, except that one subject completed only one run. In most runs, the Euclidean distance between successive settings reached zero, while the probability of improvement at those points was below 0.05. The authors report that scanning could potentially have been reduced by up to seven observations, or approximately 2/3 minutes, in some runs without reducing prediction accuracy. In three runs, the distance remained above zero, suggesting that further observations might have improved predictions.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The empirical evaluation is based on a small group of five subjects and data from a single audio-visual task, so it provides limited evidence about performance across populations or other experiments. The task also has a hypothesized optimum and a discrete 19-by-19 stimulus grid, which may make the reported results less representative of settings with unknown optima or larger, constrained design spaces.

narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could test the rules prospectively with more participants and tasks where the optimum is not specified in advance. It would also be useful to evaluate stopping rules under practical constraints on allowable stimuli and to compare their performance and run savings against fixed-length experiments.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how much of a discrete parameter space is expected to be covered by Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) and orthogonal sampling (OS). Its objective is to estimate coverage after a specified number of trials, including coverage of lower-dimensional projections relevant to experimental designs. The authors count how often points or projected point combinations occur in samples, then use inclusion and exclusion to derive expected coverage and bounds. They also compare the theoretical results with simulations. They find that LHS and OS have the same expected full-space coverage under the stated conditions, while projected coverage depends on the dimension of the projection rather than the full space.
narrate.key_results: For full-space coverage, the paper derives an approximate expected coverage of 1 minus the exponential of negative k times lambda, with lambda equal to 1 divided by n raised to d minus 1; the result is the same for LHS and OS when n equals p raised to d. For a two-dimensional projection, the same coverage form applies with lambda equal to 1 divided by n, independent of the full-space dimension. The authors state that the projected-space result extends to a projection of dimension t, with lambda equal to 1 divided by n raised to t minus 1. Simulations for a five-dimensional space examine projections of dimensions 2, 3, and 4 at coverage levels of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, and are reported as consistent with the theory.

narrate.summary: The paper studies how linear codes can form orthogonal arrays, with codewords used as the array rows. It establishes results for codes over any finite commutative ring with identity and for the Gray map images of linear Z4 codes. The authors prove that an array's strength is determined by the minimum weight of the code's dual, using Hamming weight for general finite rings and Lee weight for the Z4 Gray map result. The proofs use algebraic properties of finite rings and known relations between Lee-weight enumerators and their transforms. The paper is theoretical and reports no experimental designs or empirical performance results.
narrate.key_results: For a linear code over any finite commutative ring with identity, the orthogonal-array strength is one less than the minimum Hamming weight of its dual. For a linear Z4 code, the strength of its Gray map image is one less than the minimum Lee weight of the dual code. The paper further states that if the original code has strength t, then its Gray map image has strength between t and 2t + 1, inclusive. These are theoretical results; the paper reports no run-size comparisons, efficiency measurements, or experimental validation.

key_equations.name: Strength for codes over finite rings
key_equations.explanation: Str is orthogonal-array strength, C is a linear code over a finite commutative ring with identity, w_H is minimum Hamming weight, and C⊥ is the dual code.

key_equations.name: Bound on Gray map image strength
key_equations.explanation: t is the strength of the original Z4 code C, Str is orthogonal-array strength, and C′ is its Gray map image.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say that similar connections probably do not exist for codes over integers modulo n or more general rings, because there is no analogue of the Gray map. They also leave open which pairs of strengths for a Z4 code and its Gray map image can be realized.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The results establish algebraic relationships but do not show how to select a code for a practical experiment or assess whether its run count and factor-level structure are feasible. narrate.summary: This paper extends a studentized permutation test to longitudinal and repeated-measures split-plot designs with factorial effects. It tests hypotheses about group means, such as time effects and interactions, using a WTS and critical values from permutations of all pooled individual observations. The model permits non-normal outcomes and different, unrestricted covariance matrices across groups, while assuming independent observation vectors across subjects. The authors derive the asymptotic validity of the method and compare it with the asymptotic WTS and ATS through simulations and a laboratory example. The permutation method generally brings small-sample error rates closer to their target while retaining the WTS's large-sample properties.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with 10,000 generated datasets and 1,000 permutations per analysis, the target type-I error rate was 0.05. For the group-by-time interaction with eight repeated measurements, the asymptotic WTS had error rates of about 0.36 to 0.47 in several settings, whereas the WTPS rates in those settings ranged from 0.037 to 0.068. Across the simulation settings, the reported median distance between WTS and chi-square quantiles was 9.179, compared with 0.8948 between WTS and WTPS quantiles. The paper reports that the WTPS and WTS have asymptotic relative efficiency 1 and the same local power; in the power simulations, the ATS had slightly higher power for normal data, while the WTPS had higher power and controlled the error rate for log-normal data. In the leukocyte oxygen-consumption example, the tests gave similar conclusions: treatment, staphylococci, and time effects were significant, as was the treatment-by-time interaction.

narrate.summary: The paper develops Bayesian optimal designs for experiments whose statistical models depend on solutions to nonlinear ordinary differential equations. It targets parameter estimation and model selection, including an experiment on serine transport across human placental membranes. The method represents numerical-solution uncertainty with a probabilistic Gaussian-process solution, estimates expected design utility by nested Monte Carlo sampling, and searches for designs using approximate coordinate exchange. Precomputing covariance quantities reduces the computational work of these searches. Across several examples, the resulting designs outperform uniform or previously proposed designs under the tested objectives.
narrate.key_results: In the computational method, the authors reduce the repeated work from cubic to quadratic in the differential-equation grid size per Monte Carlo draw, after a one-time cubic-cost precomputation. In the placenta study, designs were found for 2 to 7 placentas, each with 8 observations at common times; under each of the four objectives, the optimal design with 2 placentas outperformed the original design with 7. At 7 placentas, the parameter-estimation designs generally used early observation times and treatments unlike the experimenters’ original treatments, while the model-selection design placed most observation times later in the interval. In a separate misspecification check, using the simpler model caused about a 6% loss in expected squared-error utility; the information-gain difference was within Monte Carlo error, and the absolute-error loss was smaller than the squared-error loss but larger than Monte Carlo error.

narrate.summary: The paper develops sequential experimental designs for identifying which of several unknown response surfaces is smallest at each location in a continuous input domain. Its objective is to reduce the integrated cost of choosing the wrong surface, rather than to estimate every surface equally accurately. The authors model each surface using a Gaussian process (GP) and choose the next location and surface to sample using uncertainty-reduction or gap-based rules. The proposed methods adapt sampling both to difficult locations and to the particular surfaces that are most informative there. In the reported numerical studies, adaptive designs generally had lower ranking loss than uniform and space-filling designs, with the stepwise uncertainty reduction method performing particularly well in the one-dimensional example.
narrate.key_results: In the one-dimensional example with 200 total design points, the stepwise uncertainty reduction (SUR) method had true loss 1.19E-3, compared with 2.64E-3 for uniform sampling, 1.91E-3 for non-adaptive Latin hypercube sampling, and 1.50E-3 for the upper confidence bound (UCB) method with the reported tuning value of 1. The SUR method's empirical loss was 0.96E-3 in that comparison, and the methods were each run 100 times. In the two-dimensional, five-surface example with 500 design points, true loss was 3.17E-3 for SUR and 2.97E-3 for UCB, compared with 5.47E-3 for uniform sampling and 4.72E-3 for non-adaptive Latin hypercube sampling. In the epidemic-control example, the authors used 200 design sites and 100 batched simulator samples per site to estimate the boundary between intervention and no intervention.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that SUR requires known sampling-noise variances when its acquisition score is optimized. They report that UCB performance is sensitive to its tuning schedule, and that estimating GP parameters can worsen performance; in the example, this also suggests that a stationary GP model may not fit the response well. narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence is limited to synthetic benchmarks and a simulated epidemic-control case; the paper does not report validation in a physical or industrial experiment. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying fixed-confidence ranking procedures that stop based on achieved accuracy rather than a preset sample budget, including criteria based on changes in empirical loss. narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could evaluate the methods on real experiments and compare realized decision costs, not only simulated ranking losses. narrate.summary: This paper develops a measurement and analysis method for benchmarking blocking collective Message Passing Interface (MPI) operations and comparing MPI libraries. Its objective is to make performance comparisons fair, statistically supported, and reproducible rather than to optimize a product or process. The method models clock drift, uses hierarchical clock synchronization, collects repeated measurements across separate benchmark launches, randomizes test order within each launch, and removes outliers. It compares the resulting distributions using the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney test. In the reported tests, its approach produced more reproducible results than the Intel MPI Benchmarks and SKaMPI, at the cost of longer benchmark runs.
narrate.key_results: The authors found that measured run times from separate benchmark-program launches often differed significantly, with reported differences commonly around 3%–5%; collecting data from multiple launches was therefore important. In one studied case, 500 observations were needed for the sample means to appear normally distributed, rather than the commonly assumed 30. Across 30 repeated trials, the authors’ method had a maximum relative run-time difference of less than 5% at a message size of 2^14 bytes, while the Intel MPI Benchmarks 4.0.2 and SKaMPI 5 showed greater variation, especially for smaller messages. For a tested 512-process configuration, HCA clock synchronization achieved higher precision than the clock-offset-only methods; the tested HCA settings took at most 10 seconds to synchronize, compared with at least 30 seconds for the Jones and Koenig method in the cited comparison.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a linear programming relaxation of the orthogonal-array existence problem, for designs with a specified number of runs, factors, levels, and strength. It uses a recurrence and inequalities derived from an earlier result to remove selected variables from the integer formulation. The authors prove that the resulting polytope is full dimensional and that its distinct defining inequalities are facets, apart from a stated degenerate case where some facets repeat. They also characterize the polytope's coordinate-permutation symmetries and prove that, in the nontrivial cases, these symmetries permute factors and nonbaseline levels. Their computational comparisons show that the reduced formulation is often slower for enumeration because it has a smaller symmetry group, though there are exceptions.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that the polytope is full dimensional and that each distinct defining inequality is a facet; facets repeat only in the stated case with strength one less than the number of factors and two levels. The permutation symmetry group of the polytope is characterized exactly: for the nontrivial cases it has the structure of factor permutations combined with permutations of the nonbaseline levels, while the paper gives separate results for boundary cases. The authors numerically verified their facet and symmetry findings for two-level cases with 4 to 13 factors, three-level cases with 3 to 8 factors, and four-level cases with 3 to 6 factors, over the strengths specified in the paper. In the enumeration table, the original formulation took 1,683.95 seconds for the OA with 20 runs, 10 factors, two levels, and strength two, compared with at least 37,214 seconds after variable deletion; however, for the OA with 64 runs, 7 factors, two levels, and strength four, deletion reduced time from 98.83 to 15.45 seconds. The table therefore supports the authors' conclusion that the smaller formulation is usually slower in their comparisons, but not universally so.

narrate.summary: This paper develops experimental designs for building surrogates of expensive computational models, focusing on Gaussian process (GP) regression and pseudospectral polynomial approximation. For GP regression, it chooses simulation inputs by minimizing integrated posterior variance (IVAR), a measure of uncertainty across the input domain that also corresponds to expected integrated prediction error. The design is constructed by optimizing all selected points together, or in batches, using a sample-average approximation and gradient-based optimization. The authors also use kernel eigenfunctions to explain when GP regression and pseudospectral approximation produce the same or different results. In their tests, IVAR designs generally improve prediction over entropy- and mutual-information-based designs, while GP regression can outperform adaptive polynomial approximation for some functions, especially when inputs interact strongly.
narrate.key_results: For 40-point designs on the two-dimensional circular domain, simultaneous IVAR design took 11 seconds, compared with 10 seconds for entropy design and 79 seconds for mutual-information design; greedy IVAR designs adding four points or one point at a time took 29 and 65 seconds. In tests on 1,000 functions sampled from the GP prior, full IVAR and its greedy variants had lower average relative prediction error than entropy and mutual-information designs; full IVAR also performed better than the space-filling designs in the reported comparisons. For the one-dimensional sine example using 20 points, relative error was 8.7 × 10⁻³ for pseudospectral approximation and 1.8 × 10⁻³ for GP regression on the same quadrature points, while GP regression on IVAR points achieved 1.0 × 10⁻⁵. For the three-dimensional Ishigami function, GP regression reached relative error 10⁻² after 50 function evaluations, whereas adaptive pseudospectral approximation required 100 evaluations to reach the same error.

narrate.summary: This paper presents a construction for sliced space-filling designs for computer experiments. It combines pairs of orthogonal Latin squares at two component orders using a direct product, then rearranges rows and applies projections to obtain doubly orthogonal quasi-Sudoku Latin squares. These squares, or orthogonal arrays formed from them, can be converted into space-filling designs by relabeling levels and adding random jitter. The resulting full designs have uniformity in one- and two-dimensional projections; the slices have guaranteed two-dimensional uniformity, and the quasi-Sudoku-square construction also provides slices with one-dimensional uniformity. The method is derived theoretically and is illustrated with a construction of order 12.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves that orthogonal pairs of Latin squares at component orders m and n yield orthogonal quasi-Sudoku Latin squares of order mn, with projections that establish double orthogonality. It also proves that the construction can produce a quasi-sliced orthogonal array with m²n² rows, four columns, and strength two. The example uses component orders 4 and 3 to construct squares of order 12, and gives a projected sliced array with 36 rows and four columns. The paper reports projection-uniformity guarantees, not empirical prediction errors or comparisons against alternative designs.

narrate.summary: This paper proposes a way to perform sensitivity analysis for computationally expensive, deterministic objective functions after searching for their minimum. Optimization and Objective-Oriented Adaptive Experimental Design (O3AED) reuses the optimization evaluations as initial points for a surrogate, then adds points selected for the intended analysis. For global analysis, the authors use Extended Fourier amplitude sensitivity test (FAST) on the surrogate; for local analysis, they introduce MultiVariate Multi-Steps Local sensitivity analysis (MVMSL), which perturbs one, two, or three parameters at a time and considers multiple perturbation sizes. Their objective-oriented design chooses added points from the local perturbation samples, rather than aiming for a globally accurate surrogate. narrate.summary: This paper studies two-stage adaptive dose-response designs for Phase II pharmaceutical studies, with the aim of estimating the full dose-response curve efficiently. It compares updating the second-stage allocation using a maximum likelihood (ML) point estimate with updating it using the full posterior distribution of the parameters. The model used for design is a four-parameter sigmoid Emax model, and the design objective is D-optimality. To make Bayesian design calculations faster, the authors approximate posterior samples with a weighted set of k-means cluster centers. In simulations, Bayesian updating generally performed better than ML updating, especially when the interim analysis occurred early, while the benefit of adaptation depended on the starting design.
narrate.key_results: The evaluation covered 448 scenarios, with 5,000 simulated trials per scenario and total sample sizes of 150 or 250. Bayesian updating generally had higher second-stage design efficiency and lower variability than ML updating, with the clearest advantages at early interim analyses; the two approaches became more similar as the first-stage sample increased. The advantage of adapting was strongly dependent on the starting design: starting design C had efficiencies from 0.03 to 0.22 across the four simulated dose-response profiles, while several other starting designs had efficiencies above 0.8 in some profiles. For the posterior approximation, the reported average relative efficiencies were 0.915, 0.961, and 0.976 for first-stage sample sizes of 15, 60, and 150, respectively; in one scenario, its average design-calculation time was 7.7 seconds versus 124.9 seconds using the full posterior.

narrate.summary: The paper develops universally optimal block designs for estimating direct treatment effects when treatments can affect plots immediately to their left and right. It also studies a model in which the left- and right-neighbor effects are equal. The design calculations allow an arbitrary positive definite within-block covariance matrix and cover general numbers of treatments and plots per block. The paper also shows that, for persymmetric covariance matrices, a design’s efficiency under the equal-neighbor model is at least its efficiency under the separate-neighbor model.
narrate.key_results: For a four-treatment, four-plot example with 10 blocks, the reported A-, D-, E-, and T-efficiencies are 0.9943, 0.9946, 0.9682, and 0.9949. With five treatments and five plots per block, a particular symmetric-block design has efficiency 0.9999 under all four criteria when the adjacent-plot covariance parameter is 0.5, while the compared type-I orthogonal-array design has efficiency 0.8232; at parameter value 0.9, that array design’s efficiency falls to 0.3395. narrate.summary: The paper introduces a general way to represent practical experimental-design restrictions as limits on the use of multiple resources. It develops a tabu search heuristic, drawing on the Detmax procedure, to construct efficient exact designs for a finite design space under those restrictions. The search moves between feasible designs by adding or removing one run, uses a tabu list to discourage revisiting designs, and favors moves whose approximate-design extensions appear promising. The authors demonstrate the method on block, quadratic regression, and nonlinear regression examples using D-optimality. Their numerical results show that the heuristic produces highly efficient designs and often matches or outperforms methods tailored to narrower constraint types.
narrate.key_results: For a block model with 16 treatments and run sizes from 15 to 120 blocks, the heuristic generally matched or exceeded simulated annealing, with reported exceptions at sizes 28, 36, 53, 54, 55, and 78; it also found theoretically D-optimal designs for the listed run sizes from 64 through 120. For a quadratic model, across cost limits from 1,100 to 3,900 price units in increments of 50, all computed designs had D-efficiencies above 99.99% relative to approximate optimal designs; the authors report that the heuristic also outperformed the integer quadratic programming and mixed integer second order cone programming results for this example. For the nonlinear sampling-time model, the heuristic was as good as or better than the competing specialized heuristic in all but 24 of 1,680 results; at starting time 35, its designs had 94.46% efficiency relative to that competitor, though the authors report finding the optimal design after 200 to 300 seconds. At starting time 72, the heuristic’s design had 99.56% efficiency relative to the approximate optimum, compared with 94.09% for the competing heuristic.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an experimental-design framework for comparing simulated molecular-cloud spectral data cubes and assessing which physical inputs change their appearance. It studies four two-level factors: the input Mach number, magnetic-field strength, initial velocity-spectrum shape, and temperature. The authors compare three measures—principal component analysis (PCA), the spectral correlation function (SCF), and the Cramer two-sample statistic—and analyze their responses with factorial designs. They use a full factorial design and a smaller fractional factorial design, then compare these with the one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) approach. All three measures respond to changes in input Mach number and temperature, while the smaller factorial design recovers the main conclusions with fewer simulation runs than the full design.
narrate.key_results: The full factorial design used 16 runs for four factors at two settings each; its half-sized fractional factorial design used 8 runs, compared with 5 runs in the OFAT design. The fractional design gave results consistent in direction and relative magnitude with the full design, although some effects—particularly for PCA—were less significant; it required only 3 more runs than OFAT. Across the three measures, input Mach number was the dominant effect and temperature was also significant, while magnetic-field strength and velocity-spectrum shape were not significant main effects in the full factorial analysis. OFAT appeared to show a magnetic-field effect, but the full design associated this pattern with interactions, including an interaction between magnetic field and input Mach number. The simulations produced 384 synthetic data cubes from 16 simulations, 8 time outputs, and 3 viewing orientations.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The study covers only four factors at two settings each, and its conclusions may not transfer to broader factor ranges or other simulation setups. narrate.summary: The paper studies exact designs for estimating parameters of a shifted Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) sheet, a stationary Gaussian field with exponential correlation, when measurement locations must increase in both coordinates. In the thermal-field example, the reported efficiencies are 0.99, 0.978, and 0.999 for the three listed correlation-parameter settings. narrate.summary: The paper develops graph cluster randomization for estimating the average effect of a treatment when people’s outcomes can be affected by their neighbors’ treatment assignments. It models exposure as a set of assignments under which an individual’s outcome is assumed to match the outcome in the all-treatment or all-control universe. The method groups nearby vertices into clusters, randomizes treatment at the cluster level, and uses exposure probabilities to construct an unbiased Horvitz-Thompson estimate when the exposure model is correctly specified. The authors give an exact dynamic program for probabilities under several neighborhood exposure conditions and propose a three-net clustering procedure for graphs with restricted neighborhood growth. Their main theoretical finding is that this clustering can give variance that grows linearly, rather than exponentially, with vertex degree under the stated graph and outcome conditions.
narrate.key_results: For a cycle graph, the derived variance is minimized when clusters contain three vertices, matching the size of a vertex’s neighborhood in that graph. For powers of a cycle with degrees from the tested cases, simulations used 5,000 vertices and one million cluster randomizations; the cluster size giving the reported linear-in-degree behavior was 2k + 1, where the degree is 2k. The authors prove a linear-in-degree variance upper bound for their three-net clustering on restricted-growth graphs, while vertex-level randomization under full-neighborhood exposure has a variance lower bound that grows exponentially with degree. For neighborhood exposure probabilities under cluster randomization, the exact dynamic program runs in O(dmax s) time, where dmax is the maximum degree and s is the number of clusters connected to the vertex.

narrate.summary: This paper develops simulation-based Bayesian design methods for models that can be simulated but whose likelihood is not available in analytical form. They test the methods on a quadratic regression example where the exact answer is also available. The two-stage approach recovers the known optimal designs in one and two dimensions, while the direct approach becomes difficult when the utility target is raised to higher powers.
narrate.key_results: In the direct method, chains of 10^8 iterations took 2.25 to 3 minutes; across the tested tolerance values, acceptance rates ranged from 0.0048 to 0.0170 and integrated autocorrelation times ranged from 44.01 to 12.28. For the two-stage method, posterior particle sets of 5,000, 10,000, and 20,000 gave results close to the exact posterior; in the one-dimensional example, computing 20,000 particles took 13.71 minutes compared with 3.41 minutes for 10,000, with little reported gain from the larger set. In the two-dimensional example, posterior sets of those sizes took 0.85, 3.35, and 13.39 minutes, respectively, and the design samples for J = 200 concentrated near the exact optima, (0, 1) and (1, 0); the longest second-stage run took 1.19 minutes. narrate.summary: This paper develops space-filling Latin hypercube designs (LHDs) for computer experiments, starting from nearly orthogonal arrays (NOAs) constructed from stars in finite projective geometry. Its construction connects the randomization restrictions represented by randomization defining contrast subspaces (RDCSSs) to the columns of an array, then converts that array into an LHD. The authors give conditions guaranteeing that these arrays exist and propose three guidelines for choosing the generators that produce them. In a worked example, designs following all three guidelines have larger reported distance measures than examples violating one or more guidelines. The paper considers deterministic simulators and does not assume a particular response or prediction model.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical results guarantee NOAs with 2 to the p runs, 2 to the t levels per factor, and strength 2 for every t less than p, up to 2 to the quantity p minus t plus 1, minus 1 factors. For a 16-run, three-factor example, the design following all three guidelines has a minimum interpoint distance (MID) of 0.2724 and an average interpoint distance (AID) of 0.6910; examples violating the first or second guideline report MID values of 0.1875 and AID values of 0.6896 or 0.6867, while the example violating the third reports 0.1531 and 0.6793. The simulation generates 100 random arrays for each of the three single-guideline violations and the no-violation case, and both distance measures favor designs satisfying all guidelines. In that comparison, violating the third guideline is most damaging, while the relative damage from violating the first or second is not consistent across both measures.

narrate.summary: This paper evaluates how dependence between users and items affects uncertainty estimates in online experiments that aim to estimate treatment effects. It develops a crossed random-effects framework and compares independent-observation, one-way, and multiway bootstrap methods for constructing confidence intervals. The evaluation uses Facebook click data for advertisements, search results, and News Feed stories to create same-versus-same (A/A) tests, along with simulations from a probit random-effects model. The authors find that ignoring dependence can substantially inflate false positives, while accounting for dependence among users assigned to conditions is often adequate under the sharp null. When treatment effects interact with items, accounting for both users and items can be important for reliable coverage.
narrate.key_results: Across all three datasets, the independent-observation bootstrap performed poorly, and its nominal 95% confidence intervals became increasingly anti-conservative as data accumulated. After two weeks, the paper reports that a search comparison between equivalent user groups could reject the null nearly 50% of the time using that method. In the A/A evaluations, each bootstrap method was assessed using 500 comparisons and 500 reweightings per comparison; user-level intervals had advertised or conservative error rates under the sharp null, while multiway intervals were conservative. In simulations, a nominal 95% interval from the user bootstrap covered the true value only 87.5% of the time for item-effect standard deviation 0.5 and treatment-control item-effect correlation 0.75, whereas the multiway bootstrap remained mildly conservative.

They also note that the paper focuses on false-positive rates and confidence-interval coverage, rather than missed effects or errors in estimating effect direction and magnitude.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The operational data come from one company and concern click-through outcomes in three product areas, so the empirical findings may not transfer to other industries, outcome types, or dependence patterns. The synthetic tests and simulations also cover selected assignment structures and modeled item interactions, rather than a broad range of real treatment effects and operational constraints.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose developing more sophisticated ways to perturb existing data and using additional parameters estimated from real experiments to make evaluations more like field outcomes. They also identify assessing missed effects and other estimation errors, combining bootstrap methods with precision-improving design or adjustment, and reducing multiway interval width as relevant directions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could validate the bootstrap comparisons in randomized field experiments across different industries and outcome types, including settings with more than two dependent unit types. It would also be useful to evaluate how practical assignment constraints and sequential experiment decisions affect the methods' uncertainty estimates.

narrate.summary: This study examines how compiler options affect the energy use and execution time of embedded software. The authors test the GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), ten benchmarks, and five embedded platforms, using physical power measurements. They treat compiler options as factors that can be enabled or disabled and use fractional factorial designs to study their effects and interactions without testing every possible combination. The results show that energy and execution time usually move together, but that exceptions occur, including when hardware features change power use without changing runtime. The authors find no option that consistently improves results across all tested programs and platforms.
narrate.key_results: Fractional factorial experiments examined options enabled at three GCC optimization levels; the paper reports 82 options across those levels, of which 20 appeared among the most effective options in the results table. The study reports 2,048 separate runs for its significance analysis and uses the Mann–Whitney test to assess whether an option has a significant effect. In one Blowfish case on the Cortex-M3, disabling a branch-probability option reduced energy by 4 percent, while a four-option exhaustive case study showed that individually beneficial changes could interact and produce a worse combined result. On the Cortex-A8, the authors report that multiplication on the SIMD unit used about 20 percent less power than multiplication on the standard unit, although vectorization did not improve execution time in the benchmark case they investigated.

narrate.summary: This paper develops an approximate method for finding E-optimal designs for weighted polynomial regression on an interval. The objective is to improve parameter estimation by maximizing the smallest eigenvalue of the design's information matrix. The method uses Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization to construct an approximate Tchebycheff function, selects its local maxima and minima as experimental conditions, and calculates design probabilities from those points. The authors compare the resulting designs with exact designs where available and with designs found by long-run random optimization otherwise. Their numerical examples report designs close to E-optimal for the tested weights and model dimensions.

For the other reported examples, the largest efficiency loss is 8.720 × 10⁻⁵ and the smallest is 2.998 × 10⁻⁹; these efficiencies are assessed against designs obtained by random optimization run for a long time. The tested general weights include the exponential weight and a product of square-root factors. narrate.summary: This paper derives a minimal Markov basis for conditional exact tests of main effects in half-fraction factorial designs with two-level factors, where the design resolution equals the number of factors. The observations are modeled as independent Poisson counts, and the tests condition on the sufficient statistics for the main effects. The authors prove that the required basis can be formed from square-free degree-2 moves, giving a closed-form structural result instead of requiring a general-purpose algebraic computation. A chemical-reaction example illustrates use of the basis to estimate a conditional test p-value by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling.
narrate.key_results: The main theorem establishes that square-free degree-2 moves form a minimal Markov basis for the stated class of designs. The paper reports minimal basis sizes of 3, 30, 195, 1,050, and 5,103 moves for designs with 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8 factors, respectively. In the chemical-reaction example, 30 moves were used with 10,000 retained samples after 10,000 burn-in samples; the estimated p-value was 0.96, compared with the asymptotic p-value of 0.9712. The likelihood-ratio statistic was 3.37, and the authors concluded that the main-effect model fit the data adequately.

narrate.summary: This paper develops gradient-based methods for Bayesian experimental design when the objective is expected information gain about unknown model parameters. It presents Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation and sample average approximation combined with the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno method. The methods use gradients derived from a nested Monte Carlo estimate, with a polynomial chaos surrogate to make repeated model evaluations and gradient calculations less costly. The authors test the methods in a simulated environmental-monitoring problem: choosing one sensor location to infer a contaminant source location from measurements generated by a diffusion model. In that example, both methods tend to identify domain corners as informative sensor locations, and Robbins-Monro generally obtains lower error than the sample-average approach at comparable computational effort.
narrate.key_results: The comparison used 1,000 independent optimization runs for each method across outer sample counts of 1, 11, and 101 and inner sample counts of 2, 11, 101, and 1,001. The polynomial chaos surrogate used a total-order polynomial of degree 12 and 1,000,000 forward-model evaluations; reported relative L2 errors ranged from 6 × 10^-3 to 10^-6. In the sensor-placement example, the four corners of the square domain were optimal and the center was worst; with the largest sample counts, approximately 250 runs selected each corner. The authors report that Robbins-Monro consistently achieved lower mean square error than sample average approximation with Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno at comparable computational effort, while noting that the advantage was small and could depend on the problem and implementation. Deterministic Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno runs usually found a local maximum in fewer than 10 iterations, whereas Robbins-Monro runs could continue to the 50-iteration maximum used in the experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a potential-outcomes framework for causal inference in full factorial experiments with K factors, each at two levels. It defines factorial effects for individual units and for finite or hypothetical superpopulations, rather than defining effects only through a regression model. The framework uses balanced treatment assignment and develops estimation and inference through Neymanian, Fisherian, and Bayesian approaches. Examples show how it can distinguish estimands that ordinary regression may conflate and can support inference about finite-population effects and summaries other than averages.
narrate.key_results: Under complete random assignment with equal replication, the paper derives an unbiased estimator of each finite-population average factorial effect and its sampling variance. In a simulated two-factor experiment with 20 units, the estimated effects were 2.98, 1.74, and 0.36; the reported 95% Neymanian intervals were [1.93, 4.03], [0.69, 2.78], and [-0.69, 1.40], while the corresponding Fisherian intervals were wider: [1.02, 4.61], [0.01, 3.65], and [-1.38, 1.91]. For a simulated manufacturing example with 800 springs and 100 replicates per treatment combination, Bayesian estimates for two effects were 0.24 and 0.10; the finite-population intervals were [0.18, 0.30] and [0.05, 0.13], compared with superpopulation intervals of [0.16, 0.31] and [0.01, 0.15]. narrate.summary: This tutorial presents an algebraic method for identifying polynomial regression models on experimental designs and understanding aliasing. For a given design, it forms the ideal of polynomials that vanish at its points, chooses a monomial ordering, and computes a Gröbner basis. The monomials in the resulting quotient basis give a saturated, hierarchical model with as many terms as design points. The paper also explains how normal forms describe aliasing and how varying term orderings produces an algebraic fan of models. Examples range from factorial and screening designs to Latin hypercubes, Latin squares, and response-surface designs.
narrate.key_results: The paper surveys the method and illustrates it with design examples rather than conducting a comparative performance study. For the 7-factor, 15-run screening design, it reports 18,368 identifiable models grouped into 25 equivalence classes, with model total degrees from 21 to 31. For a Plackett-Burman design with 8 runs and 7 factors, it reports 610 identifiable hierarchical models in 4 classes, with total degrees from 7 to 10. The two 6-run Latin hypercube examples identify 27 and 11 models, respectively; the authors also report that computing an algebraic fan can be expensive.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a sequential experimental-design method for predicting the output of a costly computer code using a hierarchy of code fidelity levels. It uses a multi-level co-kriging model, in which each level is linked to the preceding level through an autoregressive relationship. The construction is recursive, so the multi-level predictor and its uncertainty can be obtained through a sequence of kriging models. The design selects an input with the largest predictive variance and uses the variance contributions from different code levels to guide which level to run. The paper gives a level-selection illustration for two levels but reports no empirical performance study.
narrate.key_results: The theoretical derivation shows that the multi-level co-kriging model can be constructed recursively and is equivalent to constructing independent kriging models level by level. Predictive variance at a level is decomposed into a contribution propagated from the preceding level and a contribution from the current level. The proposed design chooses the input with the largest predictive variance, then considers the level contributions together with a cost-precision criterion. For two levels, the paper compares the high-level predictive variance at the selected point with the integrated mean squared error to guide whether a high-level run is worthwhile. No numerical efficiency or prediction-accuracy results are reported.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for selecting experiments to infer parameters in nonlinear models that may be expensive to simulate. The method uses a Bayesian objective: choose the experimental conditions expected to provide the greatest information about the parameters. It estimates this objective with nested Monte Carlo sampling and uses polynomial chaos surrogates to reduce the cost of repeated model evaluations. Stochastic optimization is used to search design spaces, including designs that plan several experiments together. Demonstrations use a simple nonlinear model and simulated shock-tube combustion data, where the authors find informative designs and substantial computational savings.
narrate.key_results: For the combustion example, the single-experiment optimum was around 975 K and equivalence ratio 0.5; inference at that setting produced a tighter posterior than at the two alternative settings tested. For two-experiment optimization, the Nelder–Mead nonlinear simplex method performed better overall than simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation in the reported study of 100 independent optimization runs. A design with two experiments on the favorable design ridge produced a tighter posterior than the tested four-experiment factorial design. With 5,000 noisy-objective evaluations and 10,000 inner samples per evaluation, using the full model would require 50,000,000 model evaluations, compared with 10,000 evaluations to construct the surrogate; the authors estimate a speedup of roughly 3.5 orders of magnitude and a saving of 49,990,000 model evaluations, or roughly four months of serial computation. A lower-order surrogate with order 6 and 10,000 quadrature evaluations still found reasonable designs, but its parameter-inference posteriors were substantially less accurate than those from the higher-order surrogate with order 12 and 1,000,000 quadrature evaluations.

narrate.summary: The paper develops construction methods for balanced mixed-level supersaturated designs used to screen many factors with relatively few runs. It targets designs that are optimal under the average nonorthogonality criterion or the chi-square criterion, while avoiding fully aliased columns. The methods combine smaller equidistant designs with normalized difference matrices using group-based operations. The authors prove conditions for column aliasing and show how the nonorthogonality of constructed designs is controlled by that of their source designs. They provide theoretical results, examples, and tables of newly constructed optimal designs.
narrate.key_results: The authors establish that certain constructed designs are optimal when their row coincidence numbers meet stated balance conditions, and prove that the constructions can avoid fully aliased columns. One example produces an 18-run design with 12 three-level factors and coincidence numbers of 3 and 4, optimal under both criteria. Another produces a 24-run design with 24 two-level and 5 three-level factors, optimal under the average nonorthogonality criterion with constant coincidence number 13. The paper reports theoretical construction results and design tables, not empirical screening or prediction comparisons against competing designs.

key_equations.explanation: The construction combines source design F and the transpose of normalized difference matrix D over group A; m is the factor count of F, r and q specify the difference-matrix parameters, and lambda is the constant coincidence number of F.
