narrate.limitations_stated: The authors note that nonorthogonality can be severe when there are many more factors than permitted runs and may prevent existing methods from identifying active factors correctly. They describe analysis of data from supersaturated designs as an important and challenging topic for further research.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The optimality results depend on balanced source designs and particular coincidence-number conditions, as well as suitable difference matrices; the paper does not establish that such ingredients exist for every desired mix of levels and run size. The designs are assessed theoretically rather than through screening studies or real experiments, so the paper does not show how they perform when effects are sparse, the model is misspecified, or run-order and other practical constraints apply.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify analysis of data from supersaturated designs as a continuing research challenge, particularly when the number of factors greatly exceeds the number of runs. They suggest that research on high-dimensional, low-sample-size data may be relevant.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future studies could compare the resulting designs’ factor-screening performance under different sparse-effect models and under model misspecification, rather than relying only on the paper’s design criteria. Research could also extend the constructions to practical randomization or resource constraints, evaluate sequential use, and provide software and validation on real experiments.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a method for choosing observation times in random-effects models when measurements from the same subject may have correlated errors. Its objective is efficient parameter estimation, including estimation of pharmacokinetic parameters and the area under a concentration curve. The authors approximate nonlinear models by a local linear model, derive an asymptotic optimal design density, and obtain finite-run designs from the density's quantiles. They demonstrate the method with linear and nonlinear examples and with data from oral and intravenous pharmaceutical studies. The derived designs generally perform well, while equally spaced designs can be inefficient in some cases.
narrate.key_results: For the nonlinear compartmental example with six observations, the equidistant design had about 50% D-efficiency, compared with close to 90% for the design derived from the asymptotic density, for both ordinary and weighted nonlinear least squares. In the two pharmaceutical trials, the derived designs had ordinary least squares efficiencies of 0.99 and 0.95, and weighted least squares efficiencies of 99% and 97%. The expert-selected trial designs had ordinary least squares efficiencies of 0.96 and 0.92, whereas equally spaced designs had efficiencies of 0.97 and 0.41. Thus, the equally spaced design performed well for the oral application but poorly for the intravenous application.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a general construction for building large designs for deterministic computer experiments from smaller designs. It focuses on orthogonal Latin hypercubes, which are useful for estimating effects in polynomial models, and also discusses nearly orthogonal and cascading designs. The construction combines component matrices using a Kronecker product and a scaled addition, while stacking provides designs at additional run sizes. The authors prove that an orthogonal Latin hypercube with more than one factor exists for every run size of at least four except those of the form four times an integer plus two. Their results show how to construct designs with many factors, including run sizes that earlier methods did not cover.
narrate.key_results: The existence result rules out designs with more than one factor only at run sizes of the form four times an integer plus two, among run sizes of at least four. In the paper's comparison at 32 runs, the proposed methods provide 12 orthogonal factors, compared with 8 for Ye and 11 for Cioppa and Lucas; the Steinberg and Lin method provides none in that comparison. At 256 runs, the proposed methods provide 192 factors, compared with 14 for Ye and 29 for Cioppa and Lucas, while Steinberg and Lin provide 248. The authors also give a construction that repeatedly expands suitable smaller designs and prove lower bounds on the number of factors for several families of run sizes.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors say that space limitations lead them to omit the discussion of cascading Latin hypercubes and to give only a brief account of nearly orthogonal designs, referring readers to a thesis for more detail. They also note that their factor-count lower bounds depend on the small designs found by computer search and could improve if better search results become available.

The reported factor counts depend in part on available component designs, and the paper provides no runtime evaluation or validation using a real simulator or response data.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors identify a generalized construction for space-filling designs as part of their research plan and say they intend to write a future paper on it. For cascading designs, they refer readers to the thesis for the omitted discussion.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to evaluate the constructions under practical factor constraints and compare their prediction or parameter-estimation performance on actual simulator studies. Further work could also develop accessible software and investigate sequential construction, where new runs are added while retaining the desired balance and orthogonality properties.

narrate.summary: This theoretical paper studies how to choose experiments when only a limited number can be run, with the goal of improving parameter estimation. It considers a family of design objectives based on the eigenvalues of the combined information matrix, with a parameter that connects rank maximization to a trace-based criterion. The author proves that these objectives are submodular and examines both greedy selection and rounding solutions from a continuous relaxation. The results give approximation guarantees for these methods, including guarantees that improve as the criterion parameter approaches one. The paper presents theoretical derivations rather than experimental validation on data.
narrate.key_results: For replicated and binary designs, greedy selection achieves an approximation factor of at least 1 minus 1 over e; for a run limit of N, the paper also gives the stronger finite-run factor 1 minus (1 minus 1 over N) raised to N. For binary designs, selecting the N largest continuous-solution coordinates achieves a factor of at least (N/s) raised to (1-p), provided p is no greater than 1 minus the natural logarithm of N divided by the natural logarithm of s. For replicated designs, the proposed incremental rounding method has a parameter-dependent guarantee that tends to one as p tends to one, and it is better than the greedy guarantee in many settings identified by the paper. For budgeted designs, the paper cites an adapted greedy guarantee of about 0.35 and a guarantee of 1 minus 1 over e when greedy selection is combined with enumeration of triples.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The guarantees depend on the assumed information matrices and spectral objective; the paper does not test how they hold when the statistical model or information matrices are misspecified. It also gives no runtime or real-experiment validation, and practical constraints beyond the stated run-count and budget limits are not assessed.

narrate.summary: The paper designs a numerical algorithm for finding D-optimal approximate designs on finite design spaces for linear models. Its objective is to allocate design weights to maximize the determinant of the Fisher information matrix, supporting precise parameter estimation. The cocktail algorithm combines the vertex direction method (VDM), nearest neighbor exchanges (NNE), and the multiplicative algorithm (MA). The exchange step helps remove poorly placed support points and quickly redistribute weight among nearby points, while the other steps help preserve access to the full design space and improve the criterion. The paper proves monotonic convergence and reports that the method is substantially faster than the compared algorithms in its numerical examples.
narrate.key_results: The cocktail algorithm is proved to converge monotonically, and the paper states that its limit points are D-optimal under the stated full-rank condition. For design space X1 with n = 500 points, the cocktail algorithm took 0.96 seconds and 16 iterations, compared with more than 762 seconds and more than 10,000 iterations for the multiplicative algorithm and more than 555 seconds and more than 10,000 iterations for the vertex exchange method. For X3 with n = 200, the cocktail algorithm took 1.21 seconds and 29 iterations, while the vertex exchange method took 127.2 seconds and 5,324 iterations; the multiplicative algorithm exceeded 382 seconds and 10,000 iterations. Comparisons with general-purpose optimization methods also favored the cocktail algorithm in the reported cases, though the author cautions that implementation details can affect such comparisons.

key_equations.name: Cocktail algorithm update
key_equations.explanation: Here w at iteration t is the current weight vector, w at iteration t plus one is the updated vector, and the operators apply the vertex direction method, nearest neighbor exchanges, and multiplicative algorithm in that order.

narrate.limitations_stated: The paper notes that choosing an ordering that captures neighborhood structure is an open practical issue for design spaces with multiple factors. It also says that extending the approach beyond D-optimality may require numerical one-dimensional maximization instead of the available closed-form exchange step, and that the convergence proof does not readily extend to a version using a vertex exchange step in place of the vertex direction step.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical study uses a limited set of finite, discretized model spaces, so its speed results do not establish performance for broader model classes or continuous spaces. The experiments optimize approximate weights rather than evaluating the effects of rounding them to an actual finite-run experiment, and the timing comparisons may depend on implementation and computing environment.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author suggests extending the algorithm to other optimality criteria and nonlinear problems. The paper also points to extension for nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation with censored data.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to assess how rounding approximate weights into feasible run counts affects parameter-estimation performance, including under practical constraints on factors and randomization. Further work could also test sequential updates and validate the algorithm in real experiments, rather than only on numerical design spaces.

narrate.summary: The paper develops constructions for nested space-filling designs used when a computer model can be run at different levels of accuracy. The setting is a less expensive, lower-accuracy experiment and a more expensive, higher-accuracy experiment, with the higher-accuracy runs forming a subset of the lower-accuracy runs. The authors construct nested orthogonal arrays by building nested difference matrices from finite-field multiplication tables and combining them with orthogonal arrays using Kronecker products. They also give constructions using existing arrays and discuss nonprime-power and mixed-level cases. The resulting designs guarantee uniform coverage in low-dimensional projections, but the paper does not report empirical performance comparisons.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that combining a nested difference matrix with an orthogonal array yields a nested orthogonal array, and give additional construction results for mixed levels and nonprime-power numbers of levels. One example produces a 64-run, 4-factor array with 8 levels containing a subset of 32 runs that becomes a 4-level orthogonal array after level collapsing. Another example gives a mixed-level array with 144 runs containing a nested array with 72 runs. These are theoretical construction results; the paper does not compare measured efficiency, estimation accuracy, or prediction accuracy against other designs.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the orthogonal arrays constructed in the article have strength 2, which guarantees uniformity only in two dimensions.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper establishes combinatorial properties but does not report empirical comparisons of coverage, modeling accuracy, or computational cost for actual computer experiments. The constructions also depend on suitable arrays and level projections, and their resulting run sizes may be large for some choices of parameters.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose constructing multiple designs from a given nested array, optimizing designs using distance or correlation criteria, and extending the constructions to higher strength and nested nets. They also identify studying sampling properties, nesting more than two accuracy levels, and using coding-theoretic techniques as future directions.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could assess these constructions against alternative space-filling designs using practical constraints such as fixed run budgets, parameter bounds, or infeasible combinations. Software that automates construction and verifies the nested coverage properties, followed by validation in real computer experiments, would also help establish practical usefulness.

narrate.summary: This paper develops quarter-fraction, two-level nonregular factorial designs using linear codes over the integers modulo four. The construction uses a generator matrix made from an identity matrix and one additional column, then maps the code to a two-level design; the paper also studies half-fractions of these designs. The authors derive how the frequencies of the values in the added column determine the designs’ word lengths, aliasing, resolution, and projectivity. They use these results to construct designs optimized for maximum resolution, minimum aberration, or maximum projectivity. The designs often match or improve on regular designs of the same size, and some attain minimum aberration or maximum projectivity among all designs.
narrate.key_results: The paper proves that the construction’s word lengths and aliasing are determined by the counts of values in the added generator column, and gives formulas for resolution and projectivity for both full designs and half-fractions. Among the constructed designs, the authors identify maximum-resolution and minimum-aberration designs, and show that some of these have minimum aberration among all possible designs; other constructed designs have maximum projectivity among all possible designs. In the reported comparison, the 64-run, 8-factor design has resolution 5.5 and projectivity 5, compared with resolution 5 and projectivity 4 for the regular minimum-aberration design of the same size. More generally, the maximum-resolution designs in the table have resolution at least as large as their regular counterparts, while maximum-projectivity designs generally have higher projectivity, sometimes at the cost of lower resolution.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that they do not know whether their maximum-resolution designs have maximum resolution among all possible designs, although catalogs suggest that several small designs do. They also note that extending the results to one-sixteenth fractions using two added columns is more complicated because of the sixteen possible combinations of those columns.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The construction is restricted to a particular family of two-level designs generated by an identity matrix plus one column, so its optimality results do not establish that it is competitive for other design structures or practical constraints. The paper provides theoretical results and design comparisons rather than validation in real experiments, and the full-design run count grows rapidly with n.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose investigating one-sixteenth fraction designs constructed with an identity matrix plus two added columns. They also leave open whether the maximum-resolution designs identified in the paper are maximum-resolution designs among all possible designs.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful extension would evaluate these designs under model-specific estimation or prediction criteria, including practical constraints such as restricted factor combinations or blocking. Further work could also provide accessible construction software and validate the designs through sequential or real experimental applications.

narrate.summary: The paper develops a fast way to construct space-filling Latin hypercube designs (LHDs) for deterministic computer models. It considers black-box models whose outputs are assumed to depend nonlinearly on only a few inputs, with the goal of supporting a cheap, unbiased, low-uncertainty predictor. The proposed algorithm adds points one at a time, preserving the LHD property while seeking points at least a chosen distance from existing points. The resulting designs are called space-filling Latin hypercube designs (SLHDs). The reported results show improved inter-point distances over random LHDs for the examined dimensions, with construction times reported for several design sizes.
narrate.key_results: For designs with a run count approximately ten times the input dimension, the paper reports SLHD construction times of 40 seconds for 100 points in dimension 10, 60 seconds for 140 points in dimension 14, and 200 seconds for 200 points in dimension 20 on a 2.1 GHz personal computer. The authors report that 90% of the SLHD inter-point distances are higher than most distances in random LHDs, indicating better filling of the design space. For dimensions 2 through 10, the paper also lists reference minimum distances for exact maximin LHDs, but does not report that the SLHDs attain those values. The authors describe their algorithm as more efficient than generating many random LHDs and choosing the best, but provide no timing comparison for that alternative.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the exact maximin distance is unknown, so the target distance must be selected heuristically. If the algorithm cannot place another point at the target distance, it reduces that distance; the authors note that this can result from poor placement in earlier iterations.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evaluation focuses on geometric distances and does not demonstrate that the constructed designs improve prediction accuracy or uncertainty for computer-model outputs. The reported timings are not compared quantitatively with competing construction algorithms, and the paper does not assess performance under practical restrictions on allowable input combinations.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors suggest further improving the designs by applying local search or simulated annealing.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to compare prediction error and uncertainty across SLHDs, random LHDs, and other space-filling designs on representative computer models. Further work could also evaluate constrained or sequential design settings and provide a reproducible implementation and broader runtime comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper designs and reports a real experiment to find cartridge settings that minimize shot-group spread for one Savage 10FLP rifle. The objective is to minimize the mean radius of shots around the center of each seating-depth and powder-charge combination. The authors used a full factorial design with six seating-depth levels, ten powder-charge levels, and cartridge lot as a blocking factor; they also measured thirteen cartridge covariates. They analyzed the data using analysis of variance (ANOVA) and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA). The smallest observed mean radius occurred at a seating depth of 0.030 inches and a powder charge of 25.9 grains.
narrate.key_results: The authors prepared 400 cases across 60 factor combinations and analyzed 380 shots after invalidating 20; each combination had between five and eight cases. The overall ANOVA model was statistically significant, with a reported p-value of 0.0008; powder charge was significant at 0.0378, and its interaction with seating depth was significant at 0.0006, while seating depth alone was not significant. In the ANCOVA, primer weight was the only significant covariate, with a reported p-value of 0.0072; the authors report that the 3.1-grain primer level had a smaller observed mean radius than the 3.2-grain level. The smallest observed mean radius was 10.62 millimeters at 0.030 inches seating depth and 25.9 grains powder charge, compared with 12.60 millimeters for the second-smallest setting and 40.97 millimeters for the largest; the paper does not compare design efficiency against alternative designs.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a space-filling design method for computer experiments when the relationship between inputs and response is not yet known. Their numerical comparisons find that these designs spread points evenly and perform well against commonly used space-filling designs, including in a ten-dimensional example.
narrate.key_results: The comparisons include 20 designs of size 30 in dimension 3 and 20 designs of size 100 in dimension 10. narrate.summary: The paper develops algorithms for computing bounds on the run count of mixed-level orthogonal arrays (OAs), which are designs whose columns can use different numbers of levels. The authors rewrite the bounds as expectations over a random walk whose step costs depend on the alphabet of each column. This representation leads to an exact recursion, a large-deviations (LD) approximation, and an importance sampling (IS) estimator for the bounds. Numerical examples show that the recursion is much more tractable than direct summation for many alphabet groups, and that the simulation estimates are close to the exact values in the examples tested.
narrate.key_results: For an example with 4 alphabet groups and 80 columns, direct evaluation and the recursion both gave a Rao bound of 190,051; the LD estimate was 689,760, while IS estimates based on 2,000 paths were about 1.82 to 1.94 times 10 to the fifth. For an example with 40 groups and 800 columns, direct evaluation was estimated to require about 10 to the 41 operations, whereas the recursion computed the exact Rao bound, 2.57 times 10 to the 38, in under a second. In that example, the LD estimate was 1.82 times 10 to the 38, and IS estimates from 1,000 paths were 2.35 to 2.58 times 10 to the 38, with reported standard errors of 0.14 times 10 to the 38. For the corresponding GV example, the exact bound was 3.13 times 10 to the 71 and the LD estimate was 2.85 times 10 to the 71; reported IS estimates were 2.8326 to 3.5288 times 10 to the 71.

narrate.summary: The paper develops optimal slide designs for complementary DNA (cDNA) microarray experiments in which treatment combinations have a factorial structure. It focuses on the baseline parametrization, which defines effects relative to control or baseline levels, and aims to estimate main effects and interactions precisely. For saturated experiments, the authors derive lower bounds on each effect’s estimation variance and construct designs that attain all the bounds at once. They then propose augmenting these saturated designs to find efficient nearly saturated designs, and extend the results to models with dye-color effects. The results show that designs optimal under the baseline parametrization can differ from familiar balanced designs, and establish strong optimality for dye-swapped designs at the minimum run size under the dye-effect model.
narrate.key_results: For the 2 by 2 factorial, the authors derive weighted-optimal design measures and report that, with interaction weight 2 and 22 slides, a rounded design has 99.44% efficiency relative to the optimal design measure. For general factorials with one fewer slide than the number of treatment combinations, their construction attains the variance lower bound simultaneously for every main effect and interaction. In complete enumerations, augmentation of those saturated designs gives weighted-optimal designs for the 2 by 2 factorial at 4, 5, and 6 slides and for the 2 by 3 factorial at 6, 7, and 8 slides, for the reported weights 1, 2, and 3. With dye-color effects, at least twice the saturated run size is required to estimate all effects, and dye-swapped versions of the constructed designs attain all the corresponding variance bounds; for a 2 by 2 factorial, an augmented dye-swapped design is confirmed optimal at 8 slides for weights 1, 2, and 3.

narrate.summary: The paper develops conditional exact tests for factor effects in two-level fractional factorial experiments with discrete responses. It considers independent Poisson models for counts and logistic models for binomial responses, where the response is a count out of a known total. A Markov basis supplies the moves that keep samples within that conditional space, and sampled test statistics are used to estimate p-values. In the wave-soldering example, the estimated conditional p-value differs substantially from the large-sample result, showing why exact conditional calibration can matter for these data.

The estimate used 100,000 burn-in steps followed by 1,000,000 Monte Carlo samples, and its estimated standard deviation was 0.0045. The authors report that the asymptotic distribution understated the upper-tail probability and overstated the evidence against the null model in this example. Their design-to-contingency-table correspondences also identify settings where existing Markov-basis results apply; for the illustrated 16-run null model, a minimal basis has 35 moves.
